column4: Julie Aldredge stated that over the weekend a rumor began that the City would be closing down the Marshall White Center (MWC); this led concerned residents to begin a petition drive and that has gone nationwide due to social media sharing. She noted that she understands this is just a rumor, but it has brought attention to the fact that a significant portion of the Center is still closed to the public; this has fueled rumors that the entire Center may eventually be closed. She indicated she is present tonight to encourage the Mayor and Council to re-open the entire Center and make it the vital part of the community that it once was. Mayor Caldwell stated that he was alarmed to hear the rumor and learn of the petition; when Administration did learn of this information, they issued a public statement regarding the recent investments into the Center. This year alone, $421,000 was invested from the Ogden City 2019-2020 budget to replace the roof among other upgrades to the facility. In addition to the roof replacement that is cunently underway, the recent Center improvements also include a new parking lot, outdoor basketball courts with new flooring and backboards, a newly refinished gymnasium floor, expanded boxing facilities and new boxing equipment, a new picnic shelter, new scoreboards, and new gymnasium bleachers. He stated the City simply does not have the $2 million needed to rebuild the pool at this time and for that reason the City continues to work to explore other options in the community. He concluded he is not sure where the rumor came from, but he can confirm that the City is absolutely committed to preserve the Center; the City would not have spent over $400,000 in the last year if that were not the case. Ralph Price congratulated those members of the Council and the Mayor who were recently re-elected to their position. He then stated he appreciates the concern the Council has shown in regard to his recent medical trials and surgeries. He is happy to be able to continue to advocate for improvements in the community and he will continue his meetings with local educational partners to make educational opportunities available to the homeless population. He stated a lot of great work was done last year and he encouraged the Council to continue that work in the new year. He then mentioned the passing of a local legend, Joe McQueen. He asked that the Council do something to officially honor his life and contributions to the community. He also commented on the rumors relating to the closure of Marshall White Center and asked that the Mayor and Council continue to pursue improvements to the Center and opportunities for rehabilitating the swimming pool. Angel Castillo also congratulated the Mayor and Council members on their re-election. She then echoed the comments a made about the Marshall White Center; the rumor has gained media attention and there will be a news story on local channel soon. This is an issue she and the 45 ladies from Fern's Happy Hour have been talking about for the last year. She appreciates the information posted by City Administration regarding the money that has been spent to improve the facility, but she does not appreciate the reactionary nature of City Administration. She would prefer the City be proactive in addressing this issue. If a real solution had been presented to the public, the rumor would not have been started. The community wants a definitive answer about this issue and she fully supports the concept of partnering with a community anchor institution. She referenced the book called Palaces for the People in regard to social infrastructure; the City needs places for people to gather free of charge and gain access to healthful activities to better their life. The community needs to know they are supported by the Council and City Administration in regard to the Marshall White Center facility; clear communication regarding this support is needed. She understands government moves very slowly, but people want to be informed. She recommended that the Council support reopening the pool and ensuring that the Center is fully operational for the community it serves. Malik Dayo quoted the website Change. Org, which is where the public petition opposing the closure of Center has been hosted. The website indicates the Marshall White Center opened its doors to the community it serves in 1968. The Marshall White Center is a community recreation center in Ogden named in honor of Utah's first black police officer to be killed in the line of duty, Det. Sgt. Marshall N. White, a Military Veteran who's watch ended October 18,1963. The Center was the first home to Ogden's Head Start Program and for 51 years the center has been a multi-generational landmark in the lives Ogden City's children - the Baby Boomers, Generation X and the Millennials. For five decades the facility has encapsulated the hearts of the inner-City youth to whom it has provided a safe haven and often times a place of refuge with a plethora of services including, but not limited to: numerous programs providing youth with structured after school and summer programs, culinary classes, and recreational classes with focus on health and fitness. The facility includes a gym complete with basketball court and boxing ring, a weight and exercise room, park grounds with tennis courts/basketball courts. Lastly but not least, there is an indoor pool that has been closed for more than year due to structural damage that would be catastrophic without repair. Estimates ofrestoration have been quoted at $500,000.00; an amount that the building's owner/operator Ogden City Corporation, has been reluctant to fund despite its Fiscal Year (FY) 2020 City Budget of$186,178,525.00. Mr. Dayo stated that$500,000 is the price ofahomein Ogden and he is disgusted at the leadership of the City that is opposed to paying that amount to repair the facility. He then discussed police matters; arrest rates by ethnicity were last reported in an editorial in the Standard-Examiner in July of2010. Former Chief Greiner responded to this editorial. The editorial indicated that the Latino population at the time was 23 .6 percent, but that Ogden Police had reported that Hispanic juveniles accounted for 53. 7 percent of their aiTests during that period. Proposed Ordinance 2020-1 designating the Stone/Brown/James Home, located at 159 West 2nd Street, as a local historic resource A memo from the Community and Economic Development Department regarding a proposed historical resource designation came before the Council for consideration. The memo stated petitioners Richard and Tammy Creeger are proposing the home located at 159 West 2 nd Street, known as the Stone/Brown/James home, be listed as a local historic resource on the Ogden City Register of Historic Places. The designation would require any significant changes proposed for the building, including demolition, to be approved by the Landmarks Commission through the approval of a Certificate of Historic Appropriateness. The designation would help ensure the preservation of the building and would help to ensure that any changes proposed would maintain the character and historicity of the building. The City's Landmarks Commission has reviewed the proposed designation and has forwarded a recommendation of approval finding that the building meets both the historical and architectural criteria listed in the City's code for local designation. Chair Nadolski then introduced in writing proposed Ordinance 2020-1, entitled: "An ordinance of Ogden City, Utah, designating the Stone/Brown/James home. She wondered why City Council work session meetings are not being streamed or broadcast. column4: Malik Dayo stated he attended an NAACP meeting last week and learned something new about the Marshall White Center; it is the only building standing in the State of Utah that is named for a person of color. Most of the individuals in the City Council have served more than one term and if they continue to let the facility fall into disrepair, that does not speak well about the leadership of the City. This should be prioritized as an emergency issue that needs immediate attention. He stated that Ogden is approximately 31 percent Hispanic and there are 143 sworn officers. He understands there are nationwide challenges in recruiting and retaining public safety employees, but he wondered how many of the City's 143 officers are persons of color and what recruiting efforts have been taken to ensure that the population of the Police Department is reflective of the City population. Ralph Price echoed the comments made by Mr. Dayo regarding the Marshall White Center; this is a hub for the minority community, and it is important to preserve it. It is a place where youth and adults from diverse backgrounds can learn to have pride in themselves and their culture. He then thanked the City for work that has been done to improve roadways in the City, but he recommended an emphasis on clearing and improving sidewalks to make it easier for those using a cane or a wheelchair to navigate them. He stated he has been forced into the road many times due to the sidewalk condition and he has been struck by a vehicle five times. He encouraged the City to pay more attention to pedestrian accessways for those with disabilities. He concluded he is excited to see more positive work done in the City in 2020.

She has watched the decline of their property over the past 10 years and explained when they passed, they had no water, electricity, or heat in their home. They had been assigned a social worker with Weber Human Services, but they did nothing for them. column4: Shirlene Hill stated that she is the owner of the property referenced by Shelby. She asked what the City Council is doing. She noted that downtown Ogden is classified as "City Central", but she inquired as to the boundaries for that defined area. She asked what can be done to help elderly residents who intend to live their lives out in their homes in Ogden. The elderly couple referenced by Shelby could not take care of themselves and there are many others like them who live in rental units managed by landlords who do not take care of the property. There are ways to help people get through the last few years of their life, but those things are not being employed. She asked what the City can do to help address this issue. If the Council cannot help those who need to be helped, she wondered how they can beautify Ogden. She has lived in her home for 30 years and has seen this problem several times.

column4: Alicia Washington stated she is the owner/operator of Good Company Theater and she addressed the topic of discussion in tonight's work session relating to amendments to the City's arts ordinance. Having served on the Arts Advisory Committee, she has been amazed by the quality applications for arts funding. Good Company Theater started by receiving arts project grants from the City and the Theater complied with guidelines for grant awards, which included having non-profit status. She found fiscal sponsorship from other arts organizations and this was a very difficult process. It was difficult for her to hear that there were other arts entities that received the same consideration and grant awards without having complied with those same regulations. It made her re-assess the work being done by the Arts Committee or any sub-committees. Opening the grant program to arts entities that are for-profit seems to change the quality of the program in her opinion. She offered suggestions such as requiring that for-profit entities pair with non-profit entities for the purpose of applying for arts funding from the City; this would ensure responsible spending of arts funding. column3: stated she understands that members of the Council have begun discussions with City Administration and other community p
column4: Angel Castillo stated she understands that members of the Council have begun discussions with City Administration and other community partners about the Marshall White Center; however, this issue has been on the community's mind for two years and they deserve answers about the timeline of the project. She is very uncomfortable with the message that the City does not know what they will do about the project. She then referenced discussions in tonight's work session about the potential need to update the City's General Plan and zoning ordinance; the Planning Commission is forced to deny applications on a regular basis because they do not conform with the zoning ordinance and she finds it unacceptable that something so important has not been updated because the Planning staff does not have the time or resources to address it. The City needs to find a way to reduce the burden on essential staff so they can work on vital projects. The City is losing revenue associated with projects that can not move forward because of City ordinances. She then noted that one of the topics raised by Council member White during the work session is a concept called 'soft density'; this provides a plethora of options for increasing density in single-family homes and encompasses land uses such as accessory dwelling units (ADUs), tiny homes, and smaller footprints for a single dwelling. If property owners and developers can be allowed to build smaller units or build on smaller lots, housing will become more affordable in the community. There is not just one answer to the housing affordability issues the City is facing, but a combination of the types of things she has discussed in relation to inclusionary zoning and soft density would be a move in the right direction.

column3: thanked the Council and Mayor for their support of the joint proclamation declaring Febmary as Black History Month in Og
column4: Ralph Price thanked the Council and Mayor for their support of the joint proclamation declaring Febmary as Black History Month in Ogden City. He encouraged everyone to engage with the minority community throughout the month of February; this would communicate to the residents in the City that actions are more important than words and they truly believe it is important to recognize and acknowledge the lives of many pioneers who promoted the recognition of Black History in Ogden City. He stated that the City's Marshall White Center was named for a fallen African American police officer; he recognizes that improvements have been made at that facility, but more can be done to make it functional and able to provide a benefit to the community. He would like for the month of February to be meaningful and serve as an actualization of things that are being done to benefit the African American community.

column3: addressed the Council regarding certain policy issues that they have direct control over. As the City's budget process b
column4: Angel Castillo addressed the Council regarding certain policy issues that they have direct control over. As the City's budget process begins, she would like for the Council to consider what it will cost to provide the Planning Division the resources they need to update the City's General Plan and development code. The Council has talked about adjusting the code to allow for smaller lot sizes and smaller home footprints and she is supportive of these adjustments to allow developers to build homes that are more affordable for residents of the community. She encouraged the Council to reach out to the Planning Division to gain a better understanding of the support and resources they need to complete tasks assigned to them. The City has not updated its General Plan in over 20 years and there is the potential for the City to be negatively impacted by the outdated plan. She would like for the City to be proactive rather than reactive in its planning efforts. She then noted she would also like the Council to consider regulations for predatory loan operations; there are 25 loan businesses listed in Ogden and one of those offers a 299 percent annual percentage rate (APR). Utah Law indicates the maximum APR a lender can charge without a contract is 10 percent, but predatory lenders have gotten around that by requiring borrowers to sign contracts allowing them to charge these astronomical rates. If an individual borrows $1,500 from this lender, their monthly payment would be $400. The City should take a stance against this practice and place a sunset date on this type of business operation in the City. If the Council truly cares about its residents, particularly those that live at or below the poverty level and that are preyed on by these lenders, they should take a stand and not allow them to take advantage of citizens. column4: Ralph Price stated he would like for Ogden City and Weber County to provide for acceptance ofbusiness donations that could be used to improve facilities in the area that serve the population. There are businesses in the community willing to contribute to causes that will provide for feeding, clothing, or housing those in need. Many people in Ogden do not have the ability to better their own situation and allowing donations from businesses would provide some discretionary funding to give residents access to programming intended to educate them and help them improve their future.

column4: Angel Castillo stated she was pleased to hear that others in the community recognize the need for more affordable housing and different housing options. She expressed the utmost respect for Planning Manager Montgomery and his staff, and indicated she did not feel the planning staff had been given the resources they need to adequately perfonn their role of planning for the future growth of the community. The fact that the City has several outdated community plans has been raised several times and has been a point of contention for developers and residents alike. The City could allocate $500,000 to pay for an outside consultant to rewrite its General Plan, which would take a year to 18 months or they could hire three new planners to do the work in 2 to 2.5 years. She would rather be proactive and both hire the consultant and two planners in order to appropriately respond to growth. The Council heard from a realtor tonight who confomed her statements in the past that there is not enough affordable housing in the community. The City needs not just affordable housing, but different housing types for students, elderly residents, and the working-class residents of the community who earn $25,000 to $35,000 annually. She encouraged the Council to carefully consider this issue in their upcoming budget planning process.

column4: Joanne Lawrence stated the last time she attended a City Council meeting it was in response to hearing a rumor about the closure of the Marshall White Center; at that time the public was told that City Administration and the Council would be discussing their plans for addressing the swimming pool at the Center, but she has not heard that discussion has taken place. She would like an update on that matter. Other after school programs in the area have been defunded and cancelled; there is a need for programming for the youth in this area.

column4: Ralph Price discussed the Marshall White Center as well and indicated it has been a source of pride for the minority community of Ogden; he is disappointed that the City Council has not done anything to respond to the requests from the community to repair and reopen the pool. He asked the Council to do what they can to support the community and respond to their requests for infonnation. He concluded by inviting the City Council to attend an upcoming NAACP meeting that will be hosted at the Eccles Center.

column4: Angel Castillo stated she has been talking to the Council for nearly two years about police salaries and the need to increase the affordable housing stock in the City. The topic of affordable housing continues to be a point of contention for the Council, the Planning Commission, and developers and that is because the City's current General Plan is hobbling all partners. She stated she is a fan of historic homes and properties, but it is appropriate to consider soft density in residential neighborhoods and higher density uses along transit lines. The only way that can be accommodated is to allocate funding for an update of the General Plan; the City could hire a private consultant for $500,000 and it would take them 1.5 years to complete the work or three additional planners could be hired and it would take them 2.5 to 3 years to complete the task. She would like the City to be proactive rather than reactive and pursue both options; this will help the City 'dig itself out of its current situation' and facilitate both commercial and residential development that can meet the needs of each of the neighborhoods in the community. Affordable housing is not just high-density apartment complexes; it can include things like tiny homes and accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and those things are not allowed by the current General Plan. Growth projections indicate the City's population will increase dramatically by the year 2050 and the City should do the responsible thing of allowing growth while taking care of current residents.

column4: Bill Hart stated that he is connected to the Anderson property on 2 nd Street; the property has been valued by the Anderson family for generations, but at one point in time, the City amended its land use ordinances to prohibit animal keeping- specifically horses - on the property. This is contrary to the Council's sentiment of maintaining the history and character of the neighborhood, which is gone. The area is in 'bad shape' and has been so for a long time. Now there is an opportunity to improve the area of the neighborhood that abuts 2 nd Street and Wall A venue and he hopes the City can come to an agreement to make development a possibility. He stated the area needs to change; it has already changed dramatically as a result of the City's acquisition of Business Depot Ogden (BDO); the installation is nearly built out and is a great income stream for the City and its residents. This asset could be enhanced by developing new housing in the neighborhood where people that are working at BDO could live and enjoy a short commute.

column4: Shelly Hart stated that she is Lyman Anderson's daughter and she fought with him for years about joining with other residents in the area to pursue historic preservation of the property; however, that never occmTed. She resents the fact that the comment has been made that she is selling her property for financial purposes. She is selling it because she cannot afford to maintain it any longer; there is no access to water and sewer for the home and she cannot take care of the 1.5-acre property surrounding the home. She loves the history of the area and would like to see it maintained as long as possible, but she has no one to live in the property any longer and if development of the adjacent properties occurs, her property will be landlocked. It is important to her for the area to be viable, but property owners' rights should not be impeded in the name of historic preservation. She admires the residents of the area that have fought for the Lynn Community Plan to be upheld, but there comes a point in time when compromise is needed; that time is now for her. It is not in her plan to live in the home on 2 nd Street. She is a resident and she asked that the Council also represent her and her rights.

column4: Tammy Creager thanked the Council for their action on the proposed development of property on 2nd Street. She encouraged the City to utilize Redevelopment Agency money to preserve the Bingham Fort historic area, which could be a true asset not just for the residents of the Lynn Community Plan area, but for the entire City.

column4: Alicia Washington stated she looks forward to seeing a transmittal from the Planning Commission to recommend an increase in the allocation of funding for the Marshall White Center. She said there are many discussions taking place in the community regarding what the City's CIP Plan accomplishes and now is the time for transparency as the Plan moves forward. It is also a good time to engage local groups who are interested in the Center. The City must honor populations that have contributed to the community for generations and they feel disregarded by a five-year funding recommendation of$90,000. She hopes that the Council will take the sentiments of people of color in the community into consideration. This is a significant moment in the growth of the community's diversity, and she urged the Council to handle this moment with care.

column4: Angel Castillo stated that the public does not understand how difficult the job of City Council member is. There will always be winners and losers in the decisions made by the Planning Commission and City Council. During the last Planning Commission there were about 50 people present to speak to the CIP agenda item. She tried to explain the CIP process to them, but everyone was concerned about the fact that the CIP only includes $90,000 for the Marshall White Center; however, that does not mean that is the only funding the Center will get because this is a five-year document that is independent of the City's annual budget. She understands that the CIP and budget processes are long, but it would have been helpful for the Planning Commission to have access to a thorough study of the Marshall White Center that could be relied upon for long tenn funding Minutes of Special Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, March 10, 2020 Page 80 recommendations. She stated that the Center is a priority for many residents. The pool seems to be the most impmtant component for many residents and regardless of the option chosen by the City, it will be necessary to provide a pool at the Center or ) elsewhere. The pool must also be accessible and that is not the case for most YMCA facilities. She stated the bottom line is that • the residents want an answer that they have been asking for for nearly two years.

column4: Betty Sawyer stated she raised her family on 28 th Street in Ogden and her kids rode their bikes to the Marshall White Center nearly every day of their lives. She is here to speak about the community's concerns and desires relative to the Center. She understands that the Planning Commission will be making a recommendation regarding CIP funding for the coming year and she hopes that the Council will greatly consider any project relating to the Center. She indicated that many residents are emotionally attached to many areas or prope1ties in Ogden and that is true for the Marshall White Center. She hopes that members of an advisory committee or the public in general will not be discouraged from acting upon their emotions. She indicated that it is appropriate to properly fund the Center so that it can continue to operate. She concluded that one of her greatest mentors once told her to not just listen to what a person says, but to watch what they do. This person also told her to follow the money and in looking at the City's five-year CIP plan she sees that there is just $90,000 for bicycles, cabinets, and weight equipment, she can only think that the City is not committed to the Center. She asked that the City meet the residents half-way and make a good faith effmt to provide significant funding to the Center and update or replace the swimming pool. It is necessary to start somewhere, and the citizens need to hear actual plans about the swimming pool.

column3: stated he represents an Ogden company, KBR, and they would like to build new hangars at the Ogden Airport for private fl
column4: Ethan Kendrick stated he represents an Ogden company, KBR, and they would like to build new hangars at the Ogden Airport for private flights. They are ready to break ground immediately upon receiving approval. He would like to build a hangar large enough to house four jets and he needs advice on how to proceed. Mayor Caldwell referred Mr. Kendrick to the Community and Economic Development Department and noted staff can counsel him on how to proceed with executing a land lease and applying for building approval.

column3: said he wished to talk about the Marshall White Center. As the City enters its budget development process for 2020-2021,
column4: George Green said he wished to talk about the Marshall White Center. As the City enters its budget development process for 2020-2021, he would like the Council to consider increasing the funding allocation for the Center. In 2020, the Center only received $90,000 while the allocation for a dog park in the City was $340,000. Higher funding amounts were given to the two golf courses in the City. He noted the Marshall White Center is located in the lower part of Ogden and is named after an African American police officer who was killed in the line of duty, but all the City can come up with for the Center is $90,000. It is the only building with a black person's name on it in the entire State of Utah. He understands the City would like a Young Men's Christian Academy (YMCA) building in the City to replace the Marshall White Center, but that type of facility will not meet the needs of the low-income residents in Ogden. He expects the City to do better for the residents living around Marshall White ) Center. There are many senior citizens who use the swimming pool and rely upon it for exercise and social interaction. He advised the Council to take action to avoid that Center being eliminated, which would be a great disservice to many. Chair Choberka stated the Council has not received the proposed CIP Plan for FY 2020-2021, but once they receive it, they will review it. She invited Mayor Caldwell to discuss the process Administration follows to identify and prioritize CIP needs in the community. Mayor Caldwell explained that department directors provide their recommendations to City Administration for review and prioritization. The Marshall White Center received $750,000 in the last few years and there are no plans to eliminate it or replace it with a YMCA. The City has received an engineer's estimate of$2 million to replace the pool and it will take a great deal of consideration and effort to secure funding for such a costly project. He noted that the CIP Plan is a five-year docmnent, but sometimes it is necessary to adjust the Plan in order to be responsive to the market, which is very dynamic. He appreciates the comments and concern from the community, but he can guarantee that the City has no plans to eliminate the Center. Chair Choberka added that Administration is fonning a Marshall White Center Advisory Board, which will be tasked with providing recommendations regarding the future of the Center and the City is looking for applicants for that Board.

column3: stated that the Marshall White Center is the only government owned building in the State of Utah named for a person of c
column4: Malik Dayo stated that the Marshall White Center is the only government owned building in the State of Utah named for a person of color. He then noted that residents have witnessed the taking of homes from people who could not take care of them. A store on Monroe Boulevard was given 90 days to complete repairs before the building would be taken. Yet, the City has had more than two years to determine how to take care of the Center and this is a double standard. He then addressed traffic stop data for the Ogden Police Department. He stated ifhe were stopped by a police officer, he would be considered white as would other Hispanic individuals in the community. This means there is no way to access accurate minority traffic stop data for the Department. He wants to know why accurate tracking is not taking place. The data that is being collected leads to disproportionate incarceration and unequal justice.

column3: asked the City Council to do their jobs; if they cannot do their job, they should step aside so that someone else can. T
column4: Amy Wicks asked the City Council to do their jobs; if they cannot do their job, they should step aside so that someone else can. The first part of doing the job is understanding the role and responsibility of the position of Council member. Under Ogden's form of government, there are checks and balances; the City Council determines the direction of the City by establishing policy and setting the City budget. If a pro grain or service is discontinued or significantly changed, there should be transparency. The Council should know about these things before they are reported on in a newspaper article. The Council should be part of discussions about something like discontinuing a recycling program before reading in a media piece that recyclables are being dumped at the landfill. If there was difficulty in providing this service, it absolutely should have been discussed during the budget process; steps should have been taken to ensure that things the City should be doing can be accomplished within the budget. She noted she realizes there are many challenging things happening in the world right now that need to be addressed, but that is no excuse for failing to make sure that important budget discussions occurred this year. The City knew last year that there were some issues with the recycling prograin and she is absolutely disgusted with what has gone on. She asked how much time and effort has Minutes of Special Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, July 14, 2020 Page 235 been wasted by residents preparing and sorting recyclable materials, only for those items to be dumped at the landfill. She asked how long the diligently recycled materials have been delivered to the landfill before some overpaid City bureaucrat decided to let citizens and the Council know that recycling is no longer happening in the City. She noted the City lacks any real leadership on this and other important issues. People elected Mayor Caldwell to run the City and make important decisions; they did not elect Chief Administrative Officer Johnson. People elected the Council to set policy and adopt a budget and then hold City Administration to those policies and the budget. Residents pay for recycling as part of their solid waste fee and if the domestic recycling business is not sustainable because materials are being shipped the China, efforts should be made to support innovators that are making use of recyclables here rather than lying to residents and dumping their recycled waste at the landfill. If the existing company contracted to provide the recycling service cannot fulfill the terms of the contract, City Administration needs to find another contractor to do it. The service should not have been discontinued without robust discussion or even notice to the residents. She is appalled by the violation of public trust and the lack of transparency surrounding this issue. She asked that the Council do their job and take steps to ensure the recycling program is reinstated; it is irresponsible to continue to allow useful materials to be sent to the landfill. She challenged the Council to do their job and hold City Administration accountable for this gross violation of public trust. Heath Satow echoed Mr. Knuth's comments; he applied to be a member of the MWC Advisory Board and has received no response whatsoever from the City. He then addressed the discussion regarding the ADU land use, noting that housing is an issue that impacts the whole City and the Council should be talking about the issue on a great scale rather than narrowly focusing on the Southeast Ogden Community Plan area. He then stated that like Ms. Wicks he is also very concerned about the lack of transparency by City Administration; lack of transparency is a form of description and if residents are deceived about what is going on in the City, no one can be held accountable for the decisions being made in their names. Last March the residents were told that recycling would briefly be delivered to the landfill as costs for recycling had increased by 47 percent. Mr. Johnson decided against asking residents to pay an estimated $.12 per month and, instead, decided to deliver recyclables to the landfill. At the time Mr. Johnson told KSL.com that the City was committed to offering a recycling program. After two weeks, the claim was made that Ogden City's recycling program was back and that is the last that residents heard. Now, residents are learning that Administration has been dumping recyclables at a landfill for the better part of a year and that practice continues to this day; he is more than upset that the efforts of residents to recycle have been wasted and that nobody in the City felt the need to infonn residents. Many people make purchasing decisions based upon the ability to recycle a product's packaging and not telling residents what was happening is a blatant violation of public trust. He asked for greater transparency, better communication, and more accountability moving forward on this and all other issues. Rose (no last name given) stated she is also commenting about the recycling program; today's media information about the issue includes a claim that Recycled Earth was violating its conditional use permit because trucks were being directed to dump outdoors and that is why, since March 3, 2020 recycling materials have been delivered to the landfill. It sounds as if a decrease in demand for recyclable materials has caused Recycled Earth not to process as much as in the past, which means this is an issue if unsustainability in that Recycled Earth only has a certain amount of space to store recycled materials. However, they are still accepting recycled materials from Hooper, Roy, Marriott-Slaterville, and Huntsville's recycled materials. In April of2019 there was a news article titled "Recycled Earth is focused on low cost of recycling, not just fee hikes". The article has photos showing recyclable materials being stored and sorted in the open air, which makes her wonder why there was only a violation in March of this year and not before. She then asked how close the City is to reaching a shmt-term solution with Recycled Eaith to allow recycling to continue; what solutions have been considered and does this include the construction of more buildings. Finally, in the City's press release the statement is made that if the recycling provider raises their dumping fees, the City will need to detennine how to absorb the increases or pass them on to residents in a higher monthly charge for solid waste and she asked what the Council or City Administration has done to secure estimates for recycling service by other providers. In 2019, Recycled Earth increased the fee charged to South Ogden City by $1 to $2 per month; she would have been happy to pay that same increase as an Ogden resident if it meant that her recycled materials would be delivered to a recycling plant. Angel Castillo also discussed recycling; the Facebook post that she shared about Ogden halting recycling had 263 likes, 150 cmmnents, and 156 shares. This means people are upset to learn that the City has not been recycling for nearly a year and even more upset that Administration felt that residents did not need to know about this change. She stated the City has a Sustainability Committee that Council member White fought very hard to bring to fruition and that committee did not even know about this issue. She is also under the impression that the Council did not know about the issue either. Sustainability is a very important issue to so many and she asked how the Administration dared to keep that information secret. She understands that Recycled Earth's fees have increased due to the changes in the recycled material market; recycled materials are a cmmnodity and prices can vary from month to month - Recycled Eaith posts the fluctuations on a monthly basis. What she does not understand is why Administration would not ask the citizens if they would be willing to pay an additional charge to recycle. She cited a project completed by a student at Weber State University (WSU) whereby she polled the residents of the City to determine what they would be willing to pay for recycling; most people are willing to pay up to $5 per month. When she spoke to Recycled Eaith yesterday, they informed her that their current fee is just under $.82 per week and decreasing, which is well under the $5 fee residents were willing to pay. She is aware that every bit of material placed in a recycling bin is not recycled, but if even half of that material were diverted from the landfill, she would be happy. Little things add up to big things and this is especially tme in terms ofrecycling efforts. She concluded she is disappointed, yet again, by the lack of transparency of City Administration. She is Minutes of Special Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, July 14, 2020 Page 236 offended that Administration treats the residents like children and only shares infonnation when they deem it is necessaiy to share it. She stated the City's Sustainability Committee should have been very involved in this decision and she asked what is happening, why it is happening, and how the residents can be assured that it will not happen again. Montana Evans also commented on recycling; this can be an expensive endeavor, but is something that should be considered in the budget because not doing it is more expensive in the long run. She stated that as a member of the community, she would be willing to pay more per month to maintain the recycling program. She echoed the concerns expressed by others about the lack of transparency of City leaders; residents need to be informed and allowed to make their own decisions, especially on such an important issue. She asked if there is a date and time that residents can expect this matter to be addressed and if there are channels that the residents can follow for an update.

column3: stated he also wished to comment on recycling; his research has shown that recycling is not beneficial to the environmen
column4: Payton Moss stated he also wished to comment on recycling; his research has shown that recycling is not beneficial to the environment nor is it beneficial to the budget. It is a service that should be eliminated from the City's budget and those funds could be better allocated to the Green Waste Facility of the City, which is already underfunded. If anyone were looking for solutions, one good option would be to eliminate the blue recycling bin and give residents a second garbage can, while directing them to utilize public recycling services for cardboard and plastic similar to the public service for glass recycling. The City could also consider incentives for companies to not use recycled materials in the City and encourage different packaging that can be easily broken down in the landfill or otherwise reused in the home. He then concluded that the last subject he wished to discuss is the need for sidewalks around Weber State University (WSU); furthermore, eliminating the single-fainily home/ADU distinction and allow multiple families to live in single homes throughout the City would be a more cost effective solution to address housing versus an ordinance that requires a lot of paperwork and funding on the City's side.

column3: stated he is an Ogden resident and the Chair of the Ogden Diversity Commission and he wished to comment on an issue rais
column4: Taylor Knuth stated he is an Ogden resident and the Chair of the Ogden Diversity Commission and he wished to comment on an issue raised during tonight's work session meeting relative to the process for selecting members of the Marshall White Center (MWC) Advisory Committee. He stated he has had a few residents reach out to him and the Diversity Commission relative to the manner in which Advisory Committee members were selected; the MWC serves a critical cultural and historical significance role in the community and surrounding neighborhoods. He wished to stress the importance of an open, transparent, and communicative process relative to selection of Advisory Committee members. He has yet to be informed by any of the 17 applicants for the Advisory Board positions that they were notified that their application was received. This is a fairly egregious oversight and those that have applied for the positions have expressed a position of distrust in the process. A process that is not open and transparent is not a process that anyone should be standing behind at this point. The Council needs to ask for more in this type of process to ensure adequate representation on this very critical Committee. This body will provide the long-tenn strategy for the MWC and if the process to recruit members that will develop that strategy is not transparent from the very beginning, it is not one that will have community support. He then addressed the Southeast Ogden Community Plan planning process and indicated that it seems that the saine people are participating on several different committees involved in the creation of the Plan; when creating community plans, they should be by and for everyone, not just those that have the time to be involved.

column3: stated she is present to restate the comments she made during the July 14, 2020 meeting urging the Council to do their j
column4: Amy Wicks stated she is present to restate the comments she made during the July 14, 2020 meeting urging the Council to do their jobs and hold Administration accountable for taking care of important City functions, like the recycling program. If Administration cannot make the program work, they need to take the blue recycling bins away from residents; otherwise, residents are simply getting a second garbage can at no cost. Asking people to continue to sort recyclables that are only going to be sent to the landfill is offensive and absurd. She understands the fear of breaking the habit ofrecycling, but Ogden residents are smart people who will be able to resume sorting recyclable materials when a program is reinstated. She understands that a new program may look different than the previous program and the City will need to educate residents on what can and cannot be recycled, so she asked that the City not waste the residents' time by asking them to continue to sort materials that will only be taken to the landfill. She encouraged the City Council to evaluate refuse rates and reduce those rates if the recycling program will not be resuming soon. Many residents are now forced to consider private recycling programs and this will increase their costs that could be offset by a reduction in refuse rates. She stated that COVID-19 should not be used as an excuse to delay action on this matter; it is not necessary to visit vendors of other recycling options in person and those types of visits and meetings could be held virtually just as Council meetings have been for several months. Heath Satow echoed Ms. Wick's comments regarding recycling. He then noted that he is disappointed that Council member Hyer did not issue an apology for his 'flag stunt' during the last City Council meeting. He was very angered by that and feels that Council member Hyer's actions were divisive; he noted he would like an explanation from Council member Hyer. He then noted that he has heard the Mayor mention on multiple occasions that he has no authority to require masks in public and that is an issue left to the Utah Governor; however, the Governor wants City leaders to ask him for pennission to regulate masks in public and Ogden's Mayor has not done that. Every other city that has asked has been granted permission and he wished to clarify that for the Mayor and others listening.

column3: stated that the City Council needs to strongly consider how to proceed with allowing and regulating Accessory Dwelling U
column4: Angel Castillo stated that the City Council needs to strongly consider how to proceed with allowing and regulating Accessory Dwelling Units in the City; there is a pending ordinance in place that would abolish multi-family housing in Minutes of Regular Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, August 4, 2020 Page 251 commercial districts. While she understands some of the City's motivation behind that issue and the need to regulate design standards, her biggest concern is limiting multi-family housing that typically serves lower income families. It is important to provide multi-family uses along the City's transit corridors and she asked that the Council consider data in support of enabling developers to build quality affordable housing. This is an extremely important decision and she looks forward to hearing from Council members about their plans to provide affordable housing to the citizens of Ogden.

column3: stated she will be in attendance every week until the Council addresses the issues regarding the City's recycling progra
column4: Amy Wicks stated she will be in attendance every week until the Council addresses the issues regarding the City's recycling program. Last week City Administration made a commitment to fix the City's website to provide updated infonnation about the status of the recycling program, but that did not happen. It should not be so hard to fix the website and she asked City Administration to do their job and not lead people to believe they are recycling. She also challenged the mindset that recycling should be a revenue generating program for the City. Residents had their utility bills raised from around $25 in 2005 to about $7 5 at present day. The $7 5 fee is for the lowest water tier and the smallest trash can. Many services have been provided and recycling should be considered one of those services that is benefiting the community and its future. She encouraged the Council to hold Administration accountable for their commitments and get a timeline for addressing the matter. Recycling is one of the few things that the City should be providing for residents. She then addressed the matter of a mask mandate and noted that judging from viewing City Council meetings, some Council members do not understand basic science and support wearing masks, but she encouraged the City to listen to the Governor and those that have indicated that masks help to keep the community safe and prevent the spread ofCOVID-19.

column3: stated that she is not pleased about the Council's action to place a limit on the number of AD Us that will be allowed i
column4: Angel Castillo stated that she is not pleased about the Council's action to place a limit on the number of AD Us that will be allowed in the Southeast Ogden Community Plan area. She revisited some of the affordability issues that she believes should be driving decisions in the City. Population growth is imminent and most of that growth will be living outside of the Salt Lake area; she has seen this happen to other communities that have been unprepared and that is why she thinks it is so important for the City to provide workforce housing; this is defined as housing for those in the medical profession, teachers, police and firefighters, and graduate students. From 2017 to 2020, the average home price has increased by 37 percent; in 2019, the median price for a single- family two-bedroom home is $270,000 and prices rise from there for larger homes. Households must earn between 59 and 97 percent of the area median income to fmd affordable housing and make a down payment and the City is not accommodating for that; this cannot be done by building more single-family homes. Multi-family housing is the answer; she fully supports locating multi-family developments along transit lines and she applauds the emphasis on that in the Southeast Ogden Cmmnunity Plan, but Minutes of Special Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, August 11, 2020 Page 260 she feels that ADUs should have also been allowed because it is a way to provide affordable housing without negatively impacting the neighborhood. She urged the Council to consider housing affordability in all land use decisions they make for the City.

column3: stated she is present to remind the Council that the City still does not have a recycling program, but residents have bl
column4: Amy Wicks stated she is present to remind the Council that the City still does not have a recycling program, but residents have blue bins that they are diligently using to sort recyclable materials and place them at the curb for collection, only to have that material taken to the landfill. Last week she mentioned there were several pages on the City's website that have not been corrected and led people to believe that the City is recycling; the Mayor offered a rebuttal indicating that has been fixed, but that is not the case. There was only a brief mention of the issue on the newsflash section of the website and the information is not indexed or available on the pages where people would typically look for recycling program details. He has sent an email to the entire Council and the Mayor with links to the sections of the website that need to be fixed and she has not received a response. There has been an effort made to correct the website, but the work is not thorough and is not done and she asked that the Council task one of their communications staff to examine the website closer to find areas in need of conection. She then echoed the comments made about renters; renters are not bad people. There are a lot ofrenters in the community and there is a desire to provide quality rental units for them. For the City to think that single-family home development is viable at this time is absurd and short sighted. Development plans need to be reflective of population growth projections and that means that higher density developments are needed. The development patterns of single-family homes on quarter-acre lots are not the future for Ogden as the City is nearly built out.

column3: stated she is pleased the Council is willing to participate in strategy sessions to discuss housing development for the
column4: Angel Castillo stated she is pleased the Council is willing to participate in strategy sessions to discuss housing development for the future of the City. She stated that accessible work force housing is desperately needed in the City; this is housing for people like teachers, first year nurses, grad students, and adjunct professors at the local college. These are people earning less than $50,000 per year, but it is important that these people have homes they can afford in the community, and that means less than 60 percent of their income. She wants people graduating from Weber State University to be able to stay in Ogden or for future generations of Ogden residents to remain in Ogden near their family. She understands the concerns about the quality of development projects and that can be addressed by tightening design standards to ensure quality multi-family housing. If the use is located along traffic lines, many of the concerns that have been expressed about this use will be addressed. These are issues that need to be discussed now before the City is at a point that movement is not possible. She looks forward to hearing the Council discussions about these important topics.

column3: stated he has some questions about the topics discussed in tonight's work session; he asked how the City will go about p
column4: Harvey Day stated he has some questions about the topics discussed in tonight's work session; he asked how the City will go about prosecuting restricted people who try to buy firearms, though they may not know there are restrictions on their ability to buy a firearm. He asked for the City to consider ways of making that information readily available so that people who may not know that there are restrictions on their ability to buy a fireann are not at risk of being prosecuted. He then addressed the concept of an outreach pro grain for people experiencing homelessness, noting it is important for the City to try its best to address the deficiencies that may exist in some individuals lives and the systems that should exist to help keep them in their homes rather than treating them or their behavior as criminal. These people should be acknowledged as part of the community with empathy, compassion, generosity, and open arms. Another thought on law enforcement outreach programs is that if there is a dedicated program to help young and disenfranchised community members understand the nature of policing and why they may have negative views of officers, benefits can be yielded. He asked if the City Council understands why the negative relationship may exist; he asked the same of law enforcement officials and other community members and wondered how the community can Minutes of Regular Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, August 18, 2020 Page 271 expect law enforcement officials to meet the community halfway to assure a sense of trust and respect without first examining the culture of policing in the community. All should feel responsible for how law enforcement officials are handling the community's most innocent and vulnerable citizens. Lastly, there are many renters in Ogden and he asked that they not be painted as second- class citizens; none of them are second class citizens are contributing to the community via prope1ty taxes and other fees.

column3: stated that he was pleased to hear during tonight's work session that the Police Chief and Mayor have already learned so
column4: Heath Satow stated that he was pleased to hear during tonight's work session that the Police Chief and Mayor have already learned so much from the bias training that so many begged the Mayor to implement during his campaign last year. He only wished the Mayor had been more proactive rather than reactive on the issue as doing so may have saved a life. He then recommended that the training could be more effective if it were done with officers who have bias training experience; this type of bias training is used across the nation with great effect. He then stated he wished to spend the rest of his time tonight to express his concerns about allowing a single neighborhood to remove itself entirely from the burden of the growing population pressures in the community. Housing prices are skyrocketing in Ogden while wages have been viitually stagnant in comparison. The great promise of outdoor companies drawing hi-tech companies with better paying jobs has never been realized under this Administration's tenure; he has concerns that he was not heard clearly last time and he wished to be more clear tonight. He asked if Ogden is a city or a mere collection of neighborhoods; if the City is going to address rising housing costs due to increased population, it is necessary to pull together as a City rather acting as a collecting of disparate neighborhoods following every localized desire with no guidance from the top. As discussed tonight, some said they do not want more apartments while others are expressing pressures for more affordable housing, all while allowing push back regarding ADUs. There is going to be growth and the City needs leadership on this issue, though there clearly is none. He stated this may be because the community is not being heard. He feels he was not heard last time as the Mayor said in his comments that there were some accusations made toward him and that he did not paiticipate in the Community Plan process; the Mayor indicated that he 'sat on his hands' and let the community around him decide what they wanted to do and he thought that the accusations were unfair. He stated it is not the Mayor's job to sit on his hands and let every community decide what is best for the City as a whole; but, more importantly no accusations were ever made. He stated he was the only person who mentioned the Mayor when he spoke about the Southeast Community Plan in his public comments, and his words were: "I just wanted to say we have growing populations in Ogden and by allowing a single neighborhood- of the wealthiest residents, including the Mayor- it places all the population burdens on the rest of Ogden, putting the burden on poorer neighborhoods." He stated he only referenced the Mayor lived there and no accusations of any sort were made. He would like the Mayor to address the concerns about population growth before it is too late rather than focusing on an imagined personal slight. He asked that the Mayor be more proactive and less reactive, the City needs vision now more than ever.

column3: thanked the Council for discussing the recycling matter in the work session tonight. She then stated that she would echo
column4: Angel Castillo thanked the Council for discussing the recycling matter in the work session tonight. She then stated that she would echo Council member Hyer's comments from the work session regarding the importance of paying close attention to a very complex topic that the Planning Commission has been and will be discussing over the next few weeks regarding housing opportunities in commercial zoning designations. She stated this is a big issue for the future of commercial development and any opportunities to locate housing in areas of the City that are more closely located to transit options.

column3: stated that he read the documentation regarding the recycling program that was presented during tonight's work session;
column4: Heath Satow stated that he read the documentation regarding the recycling program that was presented during tonight's work session; the documentation indicated that the program was suspended March 3, but it was 19 weeks later, on July 13, when the City provided a press release regarding that fact. Press releases are intended to inform citizens of what the City is up to, but what was not mentioned in the recycling update is that the press release was issued almost a week after the newspaper article was published regarding the City's problems with recycling. It is also his understanding that the City's Sustainability Committee learned about the program's suspension via that same news article. He stated that issuing press releases only after being 'busted' by local newspaper is not how good government works. He requested that the City Administration be more transparent on literally every issue in the City, particularly when the information is embanassing. The citizens should be treated like adults as they can handle the truth. The City should also actually use its advisory committees to make better decisions. He read an abbreviated description of the role of the Sustainability Committee: "the members ofthis Committee provide policy and program Minutes of Regular Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, August 25, 2020 Page 279 recommendations and advise the Council and Mayor regarding waste reduction and recycling." He asked how committees are supposed to advise the Council and Mayor if they are left in the dark. This is not the first time he has heard of this Administration using committees as a rubber stamp at best and, at worst, completely ignoring their recmmnendations and removing members who do not tell them exactly what they want to hear. He again asked that the City use its committees wisely or stop pretending they have any real purpose in this form of government. He then noted that in the last two weeks he has had to call 911 twice to report very large asphalt and concrete chunks on the 24 th Street viaduct that have been lifted out of the roadway by vehicles. Last he heard, the Utah Department ofTranspmtation (UDOT) would be doing $8.5 million in repairs on the viaduct in 2020, but it is ahnost September and he sees no indication that those repairs have been started. The bridge is becoming very dangerous and he is concerned that someone could be hurt or killed if it continues to deteriorate at this rate. He knows this is a UDOT issue, but he hopes that someone on the Council can push this recommendation to the right people.

column3: stated that COVID-19 has made so many things more challenging than in the past and it takes people longer to do things n
column4: Angel Castillo stated that COVID-19 has made so many things more challenging than in the past and it takes people longer to do things now than in the past. However, she fmds it unacceptable that Council members Hyer and Stephens, and Vice Chair Blair could not respond to an email she sent to them on September 18, 2020 to schedule a Zoom meeting to discuss the ordinances addressing multi-family development in the City's commercial zones. The rest of the City Council did their job; they took their paid obligation to the citizens seriously enough to respond and schedule a time to meet with her. It seems pretty straight forward and common courtesy to respond to an email, especially if it is one's job. Nineteen days with no response is not only professionally unacceptable, it is flat out rude and she is very disappointed.

column3: stated he was glad to hear the discussion during the work session regarding housing needs in the community and he is hop
column4: Heath Satow stated he was glad to hear the discussion during the work session regarding housing needs in the community and he is hopeful that dialogue will continue. He then stated that his comments today are with regard to the ordinance adopted to limit residential development in the commercial zones of the City. He read a quote from a former Planning Commissioner: "as a member of Ogden's Planning Commission, I have learned that we are not prepared for Ogden's expanding housing needs. There are growth issues on the horizon and if these problems are not addressed and planned for, they will profoundly impact our quality oflife. My concern for our amazing City is that we retain what makes it special; I want Ogden to look and feel like Ogden as we grow, and not model it to mimic another city, like Denver, Colorado." These statements were included on the website of Mayor Caldwell's challenger in April of 2019. While that person was serving as a Planning Commission, she saw these problems on the horizon, long before the City took action. This leads him to believe that the City's Planning Division also saw these problems on the horizon. This individual was removed from the Planning Commission by Mayor Caldwell and that is the only removal he has pursued in his entire tenure as Mayor. If that Planning Commissioner saw this issue happening 19 months ago, he wondered why City Administration only started looking at the issue six months ago. Because this process had to be fast tracked, everyone on the Planning Commission and City Council has admitted it was necessary to consider the ordinance limiting residential development in commercial zones too quickly. He wondered why that was necessary; there is absolutely no reason that this had to be a 'rushed job' that the City will need to revisit later. This type of action makes it hard for developers to consider Ogden as a place to invest. Additionally, it is a waste of taxpayer dollars to enact code that must be continually updated. column3: thanked Chair Choberka for her response to an email she sent to the Council and Mayor last week; he has sent several ema
column4: Heath Satow thanked Chair Choberka for her response to an email she sent to the Council and Mayor last week; he has sent several emails to the Mayor over the past several weeks but has not received a response. He has yet to hear the Mayor's plans for dealing with skyrocketing housing processes, or ifhe has any plans. He has only heard complaints from the Mayor about him being called out for his lack of vision and action. He thanked the City Council for listening to his concerns about the COVID-19 pandemic months ago and having the courage to do as much as they could by formally encouraging all citizens of Ogden to wear masks in public places. Sadly, government leadership - from the President to the Governor to the Mayor - have not felt a similar urge to protect lives by doing whatever they could until the Governor finally ignored political pressure and did the right thing this week. Infection rates are spiking as winter approaches and that is because so many acted like the virus would go away if almost nothing was done about it. Even though the deaths in this community are tragic, there is a wider issue of lingering health issues resulting from COVID. Every case that is prevented now will reduce the burden on the health care system down the road. He referenced a peer review study in a medical journal indicating that 20 percent of people who contracted COVID-19 and survive are experiencing mental illness issues; that is one in five people. With Utah's case numbers hovering near 3,000 new cases per day, that is potentially 600 more people experiencing mental illness every day. Utah is a state that suffers from the fifth highest suicide rate in the nation. Considering rising homelessness, skyrocketing housing prices, and potentially soaring mental illness, it does not take much to imagine that the City may be entering a situation that will be much, much worse ifnothing is done. While the Governor finally took action about the pandemic, he is not doing enough to address housing costs and he wondered ifit will be necessary to wait for a true crisis before state leadership takes action. More could have done about the pandemic and citizens may be paying the price for poor choices for a generation or more.

column3: thanked the City Council for taking a mask mandate seriously and speaking openly about it. He thanked Council member Whi
column4: Heath Satow thanked the City Council for taking a mask mandate seriously and speaking openly about it. He thanked Council member White for pointing out how masks reduce transmission and Council member Hyer for pointing out that masks are not difficult to wear and it is important to follow the Governor's mandate. He thanked Council member Nadolski for reinforcing the call to wear a mask, Chair Choberka for bringing attention to this life saving discussion, and Council member Lopez for being the first to stand up about this issue months ago. He noted that Mayor Caldwell was silent on the issue. Since the last City Council meeting, the transmission rates in the State of Utah have increased. Citizens need their leaders to lead and speak up about the fact that it is patriotic to care about fellow Americans and that can be done by wearing a mask. He stated he read an article over the weekend that indicated COVID-19 is accelerating the migration from metro areas to states like Utah and to towns like Ogden. He sent the article to the Mayor and Council earlier and asked them to be aware of the potential impact Ogden could experience. He speaks about housing often and has emailed the Mayor multiple times without receiving a response about how or ifhe wants to work on ways to keep the middle and lower-income work force in Ogden. He does not find the idea of gentrifying lower income Minutes of Regular Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, November 17, 2020 Page 349 households to be acceptable and feels that approach would lead to a very boring and dead City in the future. It is shmt sighted at \ best and does not consider the need to preserve the diversity that makes Ogden the unique place it is. He has heard Council y members worry about these issues openly in work session meetings, but he has no indication that the Mayor is listening or leading on this important issue. He concluded the City's website is inadequate in terms ofCOVID-19 information for the public. There is a link on the front page that takes the viewer to several PDFs that can be gathered on other sites on the web, but there is nothing about how Ogden citizens can do better.

column4: Nick Zimmennan stated he is also interested in the clean renewable energy act created by HB 411. He was happy to work on collaborative efforts regarding this issue a year ago, but he is disappointed now to read that the Mayor and Chief

column4: Heath Satow stated that someone in the City has been vandalizing vehicles with a high-powered pellet gun; he experienced $1,000 in damage to his vehicle, two friends have had the same experience, and a window at The Monarch was shot out. He then stated that along 25 th Street there was a great deal of broken glass so the individual likely struck that area as well. He then stated that he was unable to listen to the entire discussion tonight regarding recycling, but he wondered what exactly the City is waiting for in terms of evaluating new technology for recycling. He does not understand why the City cannot participate in a virtual meeting to get information about that technology rather than wait to travel to another state to receive a demonstration of the technology. It is very upsetting to him that recyclables are still being delivered to the landfill and he would prefer for the City to move in the direction of reinstating a recycling program. Council member Hyer addressed Mr. Satow's comments about recycling; he noted that the City has not had the ability to vet the new technology due to the COVID-19 pandemic. However, there are two companies that have made a proposal to Weber County to accept the City's recyclables and other waste; the materials will be converted to fuel sources or recycled in the traditional manner, but the City is responsible to get the materials to the company that is selected. He stated that it is appropriate to vet those proposals as it would be irresponsible to proceed without enough information and assurances of protection. If the program is viable, it would be a great thing for the entire County as it would not be necessary for residents to sort their waste into two different cans and all waste would be dive1ted and reused. Chair Choberka agreed but acknowledged Mr. Satow's frustration about the amount of time it has taken to address the issue. She stated she feels that valuable work is being done to consider programs that will benefit all residents in the community, and she hopes to have more information soon to report back to residents.

column3: stated that he addressed the Council last week and asked for an update regarding the City's recycling program; he commen
column4: Heath Satow stated that he addressed the Council last week and asked for an update regarding the City's recycling program; he commented on his concern about recyclable materials being dumped in the landfill and he feels that everyone should be upset about that. He also asked for clarification of any plans to resume the recycling program. He thanked Council member Hyer for his comments and response providing the information he had about optional recycling programs, but the Mayor was defensive and suggested that he had accused him of not caring. He stated that he honestly does not know if Mayor Caldwell cares or not, and he never said that, but he does believe he clearly does not care about informing anyone of the recycling situation because he emailed the entire City Council and Mayor three weeks ago about the misinformation and broken links on the City's website regarding recycling. Apparently, the City's website still has a page indicating the recycling program is on hold and provides a link to 'read more', but when he clicks on that link, it takes him to a page saying that the desired destination could not be reached. He stated that he would not be talking about this issue if it had been fixed several weeks ago when he emailed about it. Not one person from the City responded to his email and the Mayor has never responded to a single email he sent, except for acknow!edging receipt of one of the emails by way of sending a received receipt. He stated that if any elected official wants to give people the impression that they actually care, they should respond to emails from the constituents who pay their salaries with tax dollars. He stated that if nothing has been done about a broken link for several weeks, he cannot believe someone when they say they care. He asked that the Mayor spend less time complaining about being held accountable and more time earning his salary.

column3: stated his comments are in relation to the dispersal of homeless individuals in the City. He was disappointed to hear th
column4: Adam Toby stated his comments are in relation to the dispersal of homeless individuals in the City. He was disappointed to hear that people were forced to leave their shelters and that their belongings were thrown into a truck with other garbage from the area. The efforts of the City seem sneaky and unhelpful. There seems to be a lack ofrecognition that people are not taking advantage of the services at the Lantern House for particular reasons. The City should learn what those reasons are, which may include a litany of bad experiences at other shelters or the fact that there are COVID-19 positive individuals in the building. These homeless people were dispersed on the coldest night of the year by police officers and their actions did not take into consideration the dignity of the individuals living outside the shelter. Additionally, this action has resulted in the staff of the shelter losing contact with the individuals, which limits their access to food, water, healthcare, and psychiatric resources. It is shameful that the City does not value this community enough to listen to their needs and serve them with dignity. Rather, the City has chosen to remove them from their living space because it does not look good or is not safe. This traumatized community has been further traumatized and taught once again that they do not matter to the City. He said Ogden needs to do better and he is calling upon the City Council to hold Mayor Caldwell and other City leaders accountable for their actions.

column3: stated that according to the National Law Center on Homelessness and Poverty and the United States Conference of Mayors,
column4: Angel Castillo stated that according to the National Law Center on Homelessness and Poverty and the United States Conference of Mayors, the top causes of homelessness among families are lack of affordable housing, unemployment, poverty, and low wages - in that order. The top causes ofhomelessness among unaccompanied individuals are lack of affordable housing, unemployment, poverty, mental illness and the lack of needed services, and substance abuse. The top three causes for families and individuals are the same, with the top cause being lack of affordable housing. She said that is why she is always talking about the community's lack of affordable housing. The City's challenges with homelessness are not going to go away or get any better until the City prioritizes planning to encourage the development of all levels of housing in Ogden. At least two people have died from COVID-19 in the Lantern House and over 60 have contracted it while staying there. The Lantern House is not a hospital, nor are they equipped or staffed to be one and people are choosing not to seek shelter because they are afraid. Since the City cannot magically conjure housing at the encampment location, it is necessary to move them to a temporary solution for the next 60 days to get them through the toughest part of winter and help them survive the pandemic. This is the right and humane thing to do, and those that call themselves Christians should understand it is the Christian thing to do. She understands the major issues with the encampment near the Lantern House are excessive trash, human waste, fires, and crime; all of these are serious issues that need to be handled.
