column3: stated he could hear the anger in Mr. Van Wagoner’s voice tonight; he stated he has also spoken very angrily in the past
column4: Heath Satow stated he could hear the anger in Mr. Van Wagoner’s voice tonight; he stated he has also spoken very angrily in the past and that anger comes from the fact that citizens often feel their representatives are more concerned about getting along with City Administration and getting their pet projects taken care of than they are with being an actual representative of the people who voted for them. He agreed with Mr. Jones about the unique nature of Ogden City and the need to preserve that nature; residents do not want the City to be developed in a way that makes it reflect Salt Lake or even Denver. The Mayor has not connected with the people of Ogden in any meaningful way since he last campaigned. He only saw one elected official, Chair Nadolski, in attendance at the WonderBlock open house held at the Union Station and he thanked him for showing up. He is tired of hearing the Mayor and Chief Administrative Officer of the City redirecting concerns as some sort of attack on the staff that work under them. Citizens know that staff works hard and that is not the issue they are concerned about; the ‘buck stops with leadership’ and he asked that those leaders genuinely listen to the people they represent. Finally hearing some recognition that the Council is not being given all the information they need in a timely fashion was very pleasing to him; the Council has been rushed into rubber stamping decisions due to this behavior. There is a division of government for a reason and the Council is not expected to merely work together, but to balance one another and push back when it is obvious that the people who elected them do not feel they are being represented. All Council members are good people that all want to do what is best for Ogden, but that should mean not acting as a rubber stamp and, instead, listening to constituents.

column3: stated he listened for the past couple of hours and was inspired by the comments made during the work session; he has on
column4: Jim Greer stated he listened for the past couple of hours and was inspired by the comments made during the work session; he has one comment specific to the WonderBlock project that he wished to share. He is personally very excited about the project and redevelopment efforts in Ogden’s downtown. He attended the open house workshop a few night ago and was very impressed by all the work that has gone into the project and the future of the area. He has an interest in history as well and has written a paper about the history of the owner and entrepreneur of the Brown’s Ice Cream Building and he thinks it would be great to build a sculpture or some other form of recognition of the legacy of John and Jane Brown. He will submit his paper to the Redevelopment Agency for consideration so that they can learn more about the Brown family.

column3: stated she and her husband moved to Ogden in the past year; they relocated for employment and had the opportunity to pic
column4: Margaret Bejarski stated she and her husband moved to Ogden in the past year; they relocated for employment and had the opportunity to pick a residence anywhere between Salt Lake and Logan and they chose Ogden because of the incredible community they observed, the unique infrastructure and town, and the passion of the residents. She addressed the paid parking initiative and noted that while she understands the City stands to gain revenue associated with the program, accessibility to the community will be lost. The Council heard from a certain demographic of the community: young families with kids who want access to open space and sports facilities. She is not part of that demographic, but she is part of the demographic that attends many events and venues in Ogden’s downtown; she lives in the area surrounding 25" Street and she loves it, but asking people to pay for parking in downtown Ogden will reduce accessibility for the demographic she is part of. She stated she understands that foregoing the program will result in a potential loss of revenue, but it is important to value the City’s culture and understand the potential costs of implementing the program.

column3: stated he and his wife, Tina, are the directors of the Ogden FamilySearch Center in Ogden; he has concerns about the pai
column4: Scott Richards stated he and his wife, Tina, are the directors of the Ogden FamilySearch Center in Ogden; he has concerns about the paid parking initiative and how it will impact his business. They have a small parking lot with 13 spaces and they routinely run into problems with people parking in his lot though he has erected signage prohibiting parking by those not affiliated with the Center. When there is an event in downtown Ogden, many people use his parking spaces and he worries that problem will only worsen when other facilitates become part of the paid parking system. All services provided at the Center are free of charge and handled by volunteers, all of which park in public parking areas rather than the lot so that spaces are reserved for patrons. He asked if provisions can be made to protect his small parking lot and he asked that the Council consider this issue as discussion of the paid parking system moves forward. Angel Castillo also spoke to the difficulty of the job performed by City Council members; she thanked them for their service and noted that it must be more difficult to perform that service when the body is dealing with a lack of community trust. She applauded the Council for having difficult conversations and for being transparent. She then referenced tonight’s Council discussion regarding the proposed conversion of certain hotel and motel properties to multi-family units and suggested that any decision on that issue be based on a valid market study. She ran into situations as a Planning Commissioner where proposals were not based upon market studies, but it is important to understand that market studies should be relied upon to make such important decisions. She stated that the same is true for the WonderBlock project; the City should not give away tax increment financing (TIF) so easily without a valid market study supporting it.

column3: stated she grew up in Ogden and she and her husband bought their first home here; when she observes the new development
column4: Stephanie Vaughan stated she grew up in Ogden and she and her husband bought their first home here; when she observes the new development occurring in the area, she becomes concerned about future planning of the City and whether future generations of Ogden residents are being thought of in those planning efforts. She cares deeply about sustainable urban growth and mixed-use walkable growth. She stated that for the WonderBlock project she would love to see economic development that offers opportunities for people to gather and enjoy the space in a ‘third space’, such as a coffee shop, bakery, or bookstore. She stated that ‘third spaces’ have been lost over the last several decades resulting in society becoming more isolated from one another and creating opportunities for people to come together is very important. Walkability is also very important because it supports the health of the community and decreases traffic congestion. There is already a problem with too many cars in the City and increasing walkability will reduce the parking problems in the future. She knows that there is a study that advocates for mixed-use development, but she wished to express her support for ensuring walkability of those mixed-use developments.

column3: stated that he has been meeting with Ogden City and the Ogden School District regarding vacant land and surplus property
column4: Steven Van Wagoner stated that he has been meeting with Ogden City and the Ogden School District regarding vacant land and surplus property since April of 2022; he is disappointed there was not more leadership from City Administration earlier in the year, which resulted in a rushed decision on the part of the City Council and little opportunity for public input. The City Council just saved the City from a result in which some of the property offered for sale by the School District would have been developed for residential use. If the Council had not acted, the Grandview property would have been purchased by a developer who would have built a subdivision with the maximum density allowed by Ogden City Code. With all the plans identifying the Minutes of Special Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, December 13, 2022 need for park expansion dating back 12 years, he asked how park lands were not part of the discussion had by City Administration. Any plan by the City to justify building on vacant school land or facilitating other development of the land should have been considered off limits. City staff should be actively collaborating with the Ogden School District to utilize any land being surplussed as open park space first before considering subdivision. It seems there is no one negotiating on behalf of the residents of the City; otherwise, reasonable negotiation could have saved taxpayers millions of dollars associated with the purchase of the same property two times. He stated he feels the need to set the record straight in terms of information spread about him directly from City Administration; he noted that he does not make any money to lead Ogden Soccer. The program is managed by more than one person, all of whom share the same vision for the program and the community. Ogden Soccer is owned by the youth and all coaches work for them for free, but this summer Ogden City demanded Ogden Soccer pay increased fees to use field space. This demand was communicated to Ogden Soccer just days before the soccer season started; Ogden Soccer was asked to pay a fee for each participant of visiting teams. The Ogden City staff is fearful of being fired by Administration and he asked for formal oversight by the City Council to look into Administration’s abuse of power in an attempt to crush local volunteer organizations with ambiguous interpretations of the ordinances that they are entrusted to carry out. He asked who is protecting the little people from the executive branch of Ogden’s form of government. He stated that he has often been asked to run for Mayor and was even offered substantial funding to explore a bid for the office, but he is not interested in running for that position. He asked that City officials stop spreading that rumor and cease undermining his motives and his integrity.

column3: stated she has been attending City Council meetings for the last several weeks to plead for her private property rights
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she has been attending City Council meetings for the last several weeks to plead for her private property rights to be upheld; she began telling the Council the story of the history of her property in the December 6 meeting and she continued that story tonight. Her family’s farm became the ugliest fourplexes ever built in the history of the world; Ogden City facilitated that project, and it would have never happened if the developer had not been handed her family’s property on a silver platter. The City’s Code Enforcement Division was heavily involved in the transaction and their efforts started with citations regarding the illegal keeping of horses on the property. The City demanded that her family sell their horses and their rabbits and remove outbuildings from their property. Eventually they were told that they had not obtained a permit to enclose their front porch and they were required to remove those improvements. She concluded that her family was harassed by Code Enforcement, which ultimately led to the property being acquired by a developer; essentially, her family’s property was taken by force and sold to a developer who built fourplexes. Minutes of Special Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, December 13, 2022

column3: stated that tonight’s discussion about the Ogden School District properties is a clear example of the many proposals and
column4: Travis Pate stated that tonight’s discussion about the Ogden School District properties is a clear example of the many proposals and recommendations that are made to the City Council without the presence of a valid argument. The same is true for the recent action taken regarding the acquisition of Union Station property. Many other properties in the City have been gifted to developers with no competition; he suggested the City utilize the request for qualifications (RFQ) or request for proposals (RFP) processes to ensure qualified developers are selected for redevelopment projects in the community. He discussed the Redevelopment Agency’s history of property acquisition and noted that they have a poor track record of redevelopment success. This causes lack of trust in the community.

column3: stated she is a business and property owner on 25" Street and she is also very concerned about the WonderBlock project;
column4: Amelia Jones stated she is a business and property owner on 25" Street and she is also very concerned about the WonderBlock project; businesses that have been on 25" Street for over 25 years have made significant investments in the City and they are very concerned about the project. She does not feel that chain businesses should be allowed in the WonderBlock project, and she is also concerned about transitioning from unmonitored parking to paid parking in the area. It is important to consider the best use of Business Depot Ogden (BDO) lease revenues to ensure the greatest benefit for the most residents. She likes the idea of pausing the project and she feels it is necessary to continue to examine whether the project can be phased.

column3: expressed her sympathy to Ms. Bramwell; she noted she has always advocated for properly funded public : safety in the Ci
column4: Angel Castillo expressed her sympathy to Ms. Bramwell; she noted she has always advocated for properly funded public : safety in the City. The City is contemplating a $52 million Municipal Building Authority (MBA) bond, which would equate to $100,000 per week for an entire year. She asked the Council to consider how many new police officers they could fund with that amount of money. The City’s public safety departments are challenged with a lack of funding; the Police Department has 147 sworn officers, but it is rare for all of those positions to be filled. The number of employment positions has not increased at the same pace as growth over the last 20 years. She then stated that being a Council member is a very hard job and she appreciates those members who have accepted leadership positions. She thanked Council member Choberka for her idea of a joint proclamation regarding the Union Station in order to communicate the City’s ideas and plans to the community in order to address rumors. She then echoed the sentiments expressed by others about the need to take additional time to consider the WonderBlock project; the WonderBlock is part of the Continental Community Redevelopment Area (CRA), which expires in 2042 and will need to be extended by 10 years to accommodate this project. If the City extends the CRA, there will be 13 properties for which the City and other taxing entities will be unable to collect tax increment for 30 years. She encouraged the Council to reach out to the Weber County Commissioners or their staff to understand their feelings about giving up tax increment for the WonderBlock project; they should be asked if they feel there are appropriate studies and analyses to support the tax increment funding (TIF). Additionally, the project will increase the population in downtown Ogden, which will further burden the City’s utility infrastructure. She asked where the City will get money to pay for needed maintenance and improvement of those systems until the CRA expires in 2052. \ Steven Van Wagoner thanked each Council member for their attention and response to his concerns about the lack of } adequate park space and recreational programming in the community; without the Council’s involvement, the City would not be : considering the acquisition of surplus properties from the Ogden School District. The leadership that Council members have displayed is pleasing to him and he thanked them for their representation.

column3: thanked the Council for their service on behalf of the community but reminded them that they serve the people rather tha
column4: Carolyn Lietuvininkas thanked the Council for their service on behalf of the community but reminded them that they serve the people rather than the people serving them. She stated that the citizens do not beg for approval of the Council or more evidence to express their thoughts, but they do pay taxes that fund City facilities and the salaries of all who work in them. She stated that the Council should not limit a resident’s speaking time, because they realize that time is money. They should be allowed to get their thoughts out and only someone who is rambling should be cut off. She stated that three minutes is too short of atime frame when lobbyists are allowed to talk for periods of 10 minutes. She attended a Utah Legislature session last year and witnessed residents being cut off, while lobbyists were allowed to speak for upwards of 15 minutes. She noted an individual named Mike Brown was ‘hauled out’ of the session by police officers because he was wearing a ‘we the people’ tee shirt; she declared ‘we the people’ have ‘had enough of that’. She stated that elected officials work for their constituents; it is obvious that constituents should be respectful when addressing their elected officials, but there is a time and place for emotion. United States Constitution Article Eight clearly defines the limits of legislative authority and when investments are approved that exceed those limitations, the people are being stolen from. Last year in Weber County, all property values were increased, resulting in increased . tax revenue for the County and other taxing entities. This included the Weber School District, but in the same year the District increased their tax rate in the face of opposition from over 100 people in attendance at their Board meeting. There are many \ people living ‘in the bubble’ right now and they are struggling to pay their taxes and other bills and a tax increase could be enough to push people out of their home. The sentiment in support of the tax increase was that the increased revenue would benefit students in the school system, but if students are forced to live in their car, they will not be benefitted. It is time for local government to start asking if the initiatives they are considering are constitutional. bn _______t A] Jones thanked Chair Nadolski for his leadership over the past year and he hopes that Council member Choberka will be able to ‘fill his shoes’. He also addressed the WonderBlock project and indicated he is also a proponent for ‘pausing’ the } decision-making process in order to consider all of the concerns that have been raised and to determine progress that is being made on other projects being handled by the same development partner. He is worried about the developer and thinks the City should have a clear understanding of who they are doing business with and what will happen if the project is not a success. Also, given that the City is investing in the project, it should be possible to secure subsidized rent and an affordable housing component. He concluded the Union Station facility should be the top priority for the City.

column3: thanked Council members Nadolski and Lopez for their service as Chair and Vice Chair in 2022; he also indicated he looks
column4: Heath Satow thanked Council members Nadolski and Lopez for their service as Chair and Vice Chair in 2022; he also indicated he looks forward to 2023 with Council members Choberka and Richey in leadership roles. He then addressed the priorities of the City, namely the WonderBlock project. He feels that more time is needed to review agreements and financing plans for the project; he has focused on the parking arrangements for the project and determined there will be a daytime parking deficit of approximately 300 spaces. It is important for the Council to have a clear understanding of what the City will be paying for and the benefit that will be realized by those investments; if the project is going to make things harder on the businesses that have already made a significant investment in downtown Ogden, that should be taken into consideration. He knows it is not possible to fully understand all implications of the project, but there is much more that needs to be discussed to avoid an outcome similar to what occurred with The Junction project. Dave Timmerman echoed the gratitude to Council members who have served and will serve in leadership positions. He then noted that he shares some of the concerns expressed by Mr. Satow regarding the WonderBlock project; he also feels like more time is needed, perhaps three months to give the Council and residents additional time to ‘flesh-out’ the details of the project. He has reviewed the website of the City’s partner in the project, JF Capital, and noted that he would like more information about them. Their website boasts of the projects they have completed, with over $800 million in real estate acquisitions and development; the revenue listed is $16.4 million, but they only have 32 employees. He stated that something is missing, and he is not sure what it is, but he feels the Council should be asking for more information. He cannot find solid information on projects that the firm has completed and some of those involved with the firm appear to have dubious backgrounds; he advised the Council to seek more transparency and to take more time to evaluate the project.

column3: asked the Council to pay close attention to the recurring themes that have been expressed tonight about many different p
column4: Laura Lewis asked the Council to pay close attention to the recurring themes that have been expressed tonight about many different projects and priorities in the community. She asked that the Council listen to the residents of the community. Travis Pate also thanked the Council for their efforts to ensure the City has the ability to acquire surplus properties from the Ogden School District in order to build upon the City’s open space and park offerings. He has spent hundreds of hours of his own time to assemble information that he has submitted to the Council for them to understand concerns of many in the community and he asked the Council to review that information and consider it carefully. He stated that there seems to be a great focus on specific areas of the community, but he feels that the City must take a thoughtful approach to strengthening the entire community | and responding to needs in all neighborhoods. He stated he has had a street light burned out for many years and he has asked repeatedly for the City to respond, to no avail.

column3: thanked Council members Nadolski and Lopez for their leadership in 2022 and congratulated Council members Choberka and R
column4: Sebastian Benitez thanked Council members Nadolski and Lopez for their leadership in 2022 and congratulated Council members Choberka and Richey on their election to leadership positions in 2023. He then echoed the concerns expressed regarding the WonderBlock project and noted he is also supportive of taking time to further evaluate the proposal and the long-term implications of participating in funding of the project. Adrienne (last name inaudible) spoke of her love for Ogden City and its history; she understands that the WonderBlock project is desirable to some, but it sounds to her as if the City is only interested in increasing the amount of parking spaces in downtown Ogden. More important than that would be to preserve the history of the City and she feels that Union Station is the most valuable asset in the community.

column3: stated he is also concerned about WonderBlock; he is disconcerted by the speed with which the Council is being charged t
column4: Vince Proctor stated he is also concerned about WonderBlock; he is disconcerted by the speed with which the Council is being charged to determine the viability of the bonds to fund the development. It must be daunting to try to digest all pertinent financial information about the subject before being asked to vote next week. He has repeatedly heard of the positives related to WonderBlock, but he has not heard a discussion of the financial risks, a developer vetting process, and any protected backstops for the project. He offered suggestions of development projects that have occurred in other areas of the country for the Council to research to understand possible outcomes the City could experience with WonderBlock project. ) Mia Smith echoed the sentiments regarding the speed with which the WonderBlock project is proceeding. She noted she lives near the old Rite Aid property, which is being redeveloped by the same developer, but there has been little movement in that project for the past four years. She suggested that the Council carefully examine their priorities, which should include the Marshall White Center (MWC), Union Station, and existing businesses in downtown Ogden. She is concerned about how the WonderBlock Minutes of Reqular Meeting of Council of Ogden City, Utah, January 3, 2023 Se ; project will impact parking options for business owners and their patrons. She emphasized the community would like the Council ™~ to slow down the WonderBlock project in order to vet the project and the chosen partner correctly. ‘ J Teresa Bramwell thanked Council members Nadolski and Lopez for their service in leadership positions. She noted her é concern tonight is crime in the community; her property at 25" Street and Monroe Boulevard was burglarized three times on i December 17, 22, and 24, 2022. On Christmas Eve she had to cover the windows and doors of her business after the burglaries; there is a Police Department substation just 70 steps from her property, but there is no police presence at that facility. Criminals in the City are not afraid of the Police Department, and she is now in the position of having to spend hundreds of thousands of ; dollars to fix the damage caused by the crimes that have been committed there, but the crime has not stopped. The City needs to properly fund the Police Department and she and other residents and property owners need the City’s help to combat crime and the destitute conditions in the area of the City surrounding her business.

column3: stated she agrees that public communication could be improved relative to many different types of issues > the Council d
column4: Angel Castillo stated she agrees that public communication could be improved relative to many different types of issues > the Council deals with; the Council needs to be more intentional when talking about projects like the WonderBlock project and / access to documents related to such project also needs to be improved because people are interested in looking at that information. i

column3: asked if the Council listening to advice from its bond counsel about the legality of submitting bond issues to the publi
column4: Carolyn Lietuvininkas asked if the Council listening to advice from its bond counsel about the legality of submitting bond issues to the public; the Council has discretionary spending authority for revenue bonds, which means the Council can essentially bankrupt the City through arisky investment without any input from ‘we the people’. It is her position that the Council does not have the authority to proceed with the project without having first request input from their constituents. The residents have elected the Council and the Council has hired people to which they delegate these types of decisions. The Council does not own the people, but they do serve them; all political power is inherent with the people. There is no valid contract whereby taxpayers have ceded their rights to the Council to give them authorization to impose tyrannical, confiscatory taxes for a pet project that the people do not agree with. This form of taxation is against the constitution and a significant number of people have expressed a good case to wait on making a decision for this project based upon ill timing and incomplete City projects. The massive scale of this project can bankrupt Ogden, which is a violation of the taxpayers’ natural rights, and the Council has completely violated their oath of office to defend the constitution, which specifically declares that all political power is inherent in taxpayers. The vote to proceed results in violation of the oath of office and the people have work to do to ensure that the Council understands they have exceeded the constraints placed upon them by the constitution.

column3: stated he wished to offer a clarification to his comments made during the public hearing regarding the ‘ : WonderBlock p
column4: Cullen Chapman stated he wished to offer a clarification to his comments made during the public hearing regarding the ‘ : WonderBlock project; he suggested a vote of the citizens to give them the opportunity to express whether they feel the City should proceed with the project and use money for that purpose rather than for other priorities in the community. Additionally, residents should be asked if they want to enter into an agreement with a developer whereby the developer ends up ‘holding all the cards’. This is necessary because the City belongs to the citizens and it is their taxes that pay for these projects; once the citizens decide whether the project should move forward, the Council can issue the bonds and decided upon the best financing mechanisms for the project. He added that the project will do nothing to address parking issues for businesses on Washington Boulevard or 25" Street; rather, they are being ignored and the paid parking will keep people from coming to Ogden.

column3: stated that now that the City is moving forward with the WonderBlock project, it is necessary to consider offering suppo
column4: Heath Satow stated that now that the City is moving forward with the WonderBlock project, it is necessary to consider offering support to small businesses that will struggle as a result and also offer support for the Union Station.

column3: stated she is disappointed in the decision made by the Council tonight in the fact of the opposition that was expressed
column4: Laura Lewis stated she is disappointed in the decision made by the Council tonight in the fact of the opposition that was expressed by so many residents tonight. She is upset that some Council members have indicated that they voted in favor because they have faith in the project; rather than faith, the Council should be relying upon hard data and figures. She stated that there may have been transparency between the Administration and Council or even the businesses involved in this project, but she asked | | where the public involvement occurred; she has asked to see a development process to understand the point at which the public should be involved. She suspects the majority of Ogden residents do not even know about this project and that is problematic; the Council needs the support of the public and she asked that the City involve the public in the future. Documentation about these types of issues is very hard to find and the Council needs to address that.

column4: Paul Cleeman asked if he will be required to pay for parking on 25" Street, where he is employed. Chair Choberka stated that all parking spaces on 25% Street will be paid parking spots.

column3: thanked Council members Lopez, Nadolski, and Chair Choberka for voting in opposition to the project. He asked those that
column4: Sebastian Benitez thanked Council members Lopez, Nadolski, and Chair Choberka for voting in opposition to the project.
