He cited quotes from the news article about revenue being the driving force behind the duties of OPD employees and concluded that if City Administration and the City Council try to pretend this is not a problem, he has lost confidence in them and the City Attorney’s Office. He stated this will be his priority in the coming months. ~ 3 Angel Castillo also referenced the article cited by Mr. Dayo; those that spoke to the news station indicated that the number of tickets they write is a metric of their performance. She noted that tickets and warning should be weighted equally for Police Officers, and she encouraged the Council to look into this matter. She also referenced the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and noted she understands that the matter is not currently under the Council’s purview. She noted this is due to a loophole in the City Code and she suggested that the Council close that loophole to keep the Mayor from selling or conveying any Ogden City property without their input. She recommended that any property that is valued at greater than $50,000 be subject to a process that would require the Mayor to solicit input and approval from the Council before selling it. The Council was elected to be a guardian of the budget, and this is part of that role. Laticia Garfield also commented on the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and asked that they be given more than six months to find a new location; the decision that has been made by the Mayor is very unpopular; there is sufficient parking in the area and : removing the Center to provide more parking will be a blight on the history of the City. |

column3: addressed the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and asked why the Council cannot assist the Center or the members of the pu
column4: Teresa Holmes addressed the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and asked why the Council cannot assist the Center or the members of the public who are interested in saving it. As of May 15, the Center can no longer accept animals and they will be forced to euthanize animals in their possession that may not be healed by the time the Center is forced out of their location. She , asked if there is any way to extend the contract to give the Center more time to find a new location. The Center is a necessity in the Ogden community, and it must be saved. She encouraged the Council to do better. Heath Satow also referenced the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center, which is a 12,000 square foot building that should be worth about $2 or $3 million; he asked if the Mayor has the sole discretion to destroy any City building without Council approval. He also referenced the discussion of the use of Swift property for a new fire training facility during tonight’s work session; he asked if the City has any plans to recover any of the money spent to acquire the property, destroy the building, and rehabilitate the : property. He asked if the City is aware of the previous owners of the property and if there is any opportunity to pursue collection of costs associated with environmental remediation of that property from them.

column3: stated he has written to the Mayor about problems the residents on 1200 West in Marriott-Slaterville are experiencing wi
column4: Kerry Wayne stated he has written to the Mayor about problems the residents on 1200 West in Marriott-Slaterville are experiencing with Business Depot Ogden (BDO) and he asked for Council assistance. He then expressed his concern about the eviction of the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and urged the Council to address the issue by extending the lease for the Center. It is an important use in the community and there is room for both the Center and Dinosaur Park, or there may be another location that the City could relocate the Center to.

column3: addressed discussion during the work session tonight about the idea of removing benches from parks to prevent them from
column4: Steven Van Wagoner addressed discussion during the work session tonight about the idea of removing benches from parks to prevent them from being used by the unhoused population of the community. He noted that the taxpaying residents of the community are being punished for the actions of others and he urged the City to replace the benches that have already been removed. Angel Castillo echoed Mr. Van Wagoner’s suggestion to replace park benches. She then addressed the topic of employee wages; she noted that money is not the only thing that keeps an employee in their current position, and she acknowledged that the City offers good benefits, but money is the largest factor, and the Council needs to improve salaries offered to employees, especially first responders. She then noted the Council has received an email from O2 Utah, anonprofit entity addressing clean air , issues in the State of Utah; they are pledging to help find money to supplement low-income residents to take advantage of clean _” — energy solutions. Travis Pate highlighted the importance of the Airport Advisory Committee and suggested that the Council utilize them in evaluating matters at the Airport before taking permanent actions. He then noted that the Council should expect accurate and complete information from City staff relative to the applications the Council is considering before taking action on any matter. He Eee noted that the information presented to the Council regarding the boundary adjustment with South Ogden is not accurate and the Council needs to reexamine the issue to determine that the City is taking full advantage of important opportunities. ( }

column3: addressed Council member Hyer’s comments about the ‘pinky swear’ vote; the Council asked nicely for . the developer to d
column4: Angel Castillo addressed Council member Hyer’s comments about the ‘pinky swear’ vote; the Council asked nicely for . the developer to do something, and they agreed and that is essentially a ‘pinky swear’ and that is what makes her nervous. She has mentioned the concept of restrictive covenants in different situations in the City, such as for the property at 550 24" Street. There are three Utah court cases dealing with restrictive covenants; there is a very well-established legal principle that property owners can attach conditions to how a property is used after it is sold. The Council can ask a property owner if they are willing to voluntarily provide a restrictive lease covenant to fit the Council’s desired use of the property. There is precedence for this in the State of Utah. She noted that last week, and the week before that she asked for an update on the City’s participation in the Community Renewable Energy Act Program (CREP) and she has not received a response; there has been no public statement regarding the City’s position, but she has heard Chair Choberka is exploring whether the City can reenter the Program in the future, but if that is what the City chooses to do, any active involvement in the negotiation process will be lost. She has heard members of the Council make comments about needing to continue with certain projects because so much money has already been invested and she stated she would use that sunk cost fallacy for the CREP. The City paid for one of the most comprehensive studies ever completed in Ogden regarding the CREP and found people are willing to pay for additional energy; a nonprofit entity has even offered to provide funding to cover participation for low to middle-income households. She encouraged the Council to do whatever they can to ensure that future generations of Ogden residents can breathe clean air.

column3: thanked the Council for their support and for considering the ordinance that would allow him to use a number of the unit
column4: Ben Roam thanked the Council for their support and for considering the ordinance that would allow him to use a number of the units at the Bristol Manor as short-term rental units. He stated he is not completely clear on the implications of the action that was taken, but he looks forward to continuing to work with the Council to reach a favorable conclusion. He added that he and his partners are willing to provide tours to anyone interested in seeing the inside of the home. He apologized for some of the misunderstandings relating to parking at the property. Heath Satow also referenced Council member Hyer’s comments about the ‘pinky-swear’ deal made with another developer; he noted it was actually him who first made that statement and he believed everyone knew what the term meant. He does not think development deals should be made on promises. He then noted he was a bit disappointed in Council member White earlier in the meeting and hopes that she was not trying to deprecate the value of the Diversity Commission by stating that they are not elected officials like she is. It is true that they are not elected and that they are volunteering their time, but every single one of the members is vetted and approved by the Mayor, who is an elected official. Just because they work for free, their role should not be viewed as being ‘less than’; they are experts that the City should turn to for advice just as the Council does for staffthat are | experts in their role. He also referenced the City’s participation in the CREP and does not want the Mayor or the Council to let the matter die silently. The City has invested tens of thousands of dollars into the project by now and should not silently make the decision to not move forward with environmental protection measures. He encouraged the Council to speak up and make their feelings known about the issue. He concluded by referenced the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center; the Council was ‘promised more information from the Mayor a few weeks ago, but that has not happened, and this seems to be another issue that is dying silently in the background because no one has the courage to say what they actually think or plan on doing. He stated the public should be allowed to judge their elected leaders based upon their intentions rather than being left to guess what is happening.

column3: stated that at the beginning of every semester, he teaches a class at Weber State University (WSU) called Leadership in
column4: Bob Hunter stated that at the beginning of every semester, he teaches a class at Weber State University (WSU) called Leadership in Political Life; on the first day of class, he gives every student a coin and one side has a quote from Mark Twain that says “kindness — the language the deaf can hear and the blind can see.” This is a good reminder in this current political environment. He remembered years ago when the realization was made that the Salt Lake homeless shelter could not house all the homeless individuals in the area and none of the 15 cities surrounding Salt Lake offered to help, except for Midvale, the Mayor of \ which offered to take care of the homeless overflow. That Mayor is a political hero to him, and she also went on to become the ’ President of the Utah League of Cities and Towns and served two additional terms. He stated he feels Ogden City is also very courageous; he recalled a time when the City’s homeless shelter had to be rebuilt and it was located in an area near public transit and other services. Ogden City is the only city in northern Utah that houses homeless individuals and that is important. Ogden is | also home to many nonprofit organizations that serve the area and that is commendable as well. The accommodation that the City has made for the Seager Memorial Clinic is one that will bless the lives of many people in this community. ( |

column3: stated she is the Executive Director for the Seager Memorial Clinic, and she learned a concern was expressed about the C
column4: Jerika Mays stated she is the Executive Director for the Seager Memorial Clinic, and she learned a concern was expressed about the Clinic last week and she wished to address that concern. She had many conversations with the Planning Commission last fall and was granted a legal non-conforming use to operate in the City’s C-9 zone under the new Make Ogden Plan; the building will become a new, modern clinic for the uninsured or underinsured in the community. It will not be a homeless shelter or place of loitering and she has worked closely with the Police Department to ensure no homeless camps are established on the property. There are over 200 volunteers who provide services at the Clinic, and it is a wonderful way for the medical community to give back to the public and to be a light for people who find themselves in a difficult place and unable to access traditional healthcare support. She is currently using the clinic for a monthly adult eye clinic where people can get an eye exam for free and a free pair of eyeglasses. Also, Ogden Schoo! District nurses provide eye exams for students who can also get a free pair of eyeglasses. She looks forward to a bright future in Ogden and to continuing to help people who are struggling.

column3: asked for clarification on what the City just approved for the Bristol Mansion property; it sounds very much like spot z
column4: Laura Lewis asked for clarification on what the City just approved for the Bristol Mansion property; it sounds very much like spot zoning, though the claim was made that was not the case. What the Council has done will apply to any eligible property in the City and it could lead to bad outcomes. There will not always be as positive outcome as there may be for the Bristol Mansion. Chris Africa referenced the Ogden Bike Park at the top of 9" Street; there are no bathroom facilities at the park, and he wondered why. The speed on the hill is also not being controlled and people coming out of the park have a tendency to speed. He also asked why manholes in the streets are recessed so that drivers hit bumps wherever they go; this has a tendency to throw out a vehicles alignment and tires from being balanced. He noted that Ms. Little indicated the area near the Dinosaur Park is a riparian area, but it is not designed for public access and there will be an issue when the private property along the trail and river are vandalized.

column3: stated she needs the Council’s help; she owns a property in Ogden Canyon that is historically marginalized, and Ogden Ci
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she needs the Council’s help; she owns a property in Ogden Canyon that is historically marginalized, and Ogden City is the only entity that can help her. The properties in Ogden Canyon are served by Ogden City’s water utility. Her home was built in 1924 and it is 99 years old; she does not have water from Ogden City, though there was intention to provide water to the property in 2014 when Ogden City replaced the water main down Canyon Road. She has correspondence from Vince Ramos of Ogden City stating that the City would install a water meter on the property when the project was completed, but the City failed to do that for the people who owned the property at the time. They were told they were on their own and they would need to find a contractor to do the work. When she purchased the property in 2021, she got permission from the City to attach to the water line at three different places, but that she would need to hire a contractor and work ; with the Utah Department of Transportation to complete the project; she has contacted nearly 50 different contractors and found just two who could do the job, one of which is currently doing a project for Ogden City in the same spot that she was told she could connect. At this moment, there is a hole in the road related to that project and she asked that she be granted the ability to install the water meter at this time while the road is open. Otherwise, she will have a permanently disabled property. Natalie Little referenced a news article in the Standard-Examiner related to the expansion of the Dinosaur Park and she has serious concerns about the project. First relates to public input and influence and she asked the Council to allow the public to learn of the details of the project and give input. She is also concerned that the plan will eliminate the shade in the area and the natural habitat for many animals and humans in the area. She is concerned about river encroachment by the parking lot that will be built; there is currently overflow parking across the street from the Dinosaur Park that is substantially underutilized, and she is not , Sure why anew parking lot is needed. Additionally, the project includes two new bridges across the river; these are very expensive "and will reroute people across a very busy section of 12" Street.

column3: stated that over the last few weeks she has attended political debates in the community; there may often be different op
column4: Adrienne Zubiller stated that over the last few weeks she has attended political debates in the community; there may often be different opinions and views, but she really appreciates what all of Ogden’s elected officials have done for the City. She then asked that all candidates stay involved in the City even if they do not win their race. Everyone should work together and make Ogden the City that others want to emulate. Eric Jacobson also referenced the CREA Program; the Legislature passed the Act in 2019 and shortly after that, PacifiCorp changed their long-term plan to include more renewable energy. He does not think this is a coincidence. By 2040, PacifiCorp will be almost entirely renewable energy. They had other plans that would have resulted in renewable energy by 2032, but they were not being pushed hard enough to implement that plan. He discussed the health risks of pollution and asked that the Council consider the points that have been raised tonight. Chair Choberka invited City Administration to respond to questions asked during the public comment period. Community and Economic Development Department Director Cooper addressed Mr. Satow’s comments about the Brown Ice Cream building; the original purchase agreement for that property provided a two-year occupancy deadline with a one- year extension and that deadline is approaching. He stated that the City is working with the developer because the redevelopment of the Ice Cream building was always intended to correspond with the development of the Wonder Block due to shared access and other factors. The delays to the Wonder Block project have delayed the Brown Ice Cream building redevelopment and he will keep the Council updated on any changes to the status of that building. | : Council member Nadolski asked that someone send him documentation of the facts that were stated during the public comment period about 45 percent reduction in emissions associated with the CREA Program. He then stated that he is not 100 percent supportive or opposed to the CREA Program, but he does want to have 100 percent of the pertinent information before making a final decision. en ee eee ee ee Ee ~ Chair Choberka asked if Administration has a response to questions about the Dinosaur Park expansion; she inquired as \ to the difference between their agreement with the City and the agreement that the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center ’ had with the City. Chief Administrative Officer Brown stated that the City has an operating and management agreement with the i Dinosaur Park Foundation for the Dinosaur Park, while the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center simply had a lease agreement. : Proposed Ordinance 2023-49 amending the Ogden Municipal Code to remove newspaper noticing requirements aligning with state notification laws A memo from the Community and Economic Development Department regarding proposed amendments to notification requirements came before the Council for consideration. The memo stated based on recent state law changes, cities are no longer required to provide public notice using the newspaper for land use applications. Instead, State law generally requires posting . notices on the City’s website, on the Utah Public Notice website, posting in at least three public places, and, ifapplicable, mailing to affected entities as required by both state and city code. As such, the proposed amendments remove the newspaper noticing requirements for subdivision code section changes, street and alley vacations, zoning ordinance changes and rezones, general plan amendments, and designations to the local historic register. The Council extended consideration of the proposed amendments at the March 21, 2023 meeting. Council members voted to extend consideration with the direction that information regarding noticing costs and newspaper subscribership and circulation be presented. City staff presented the information requested by the Council at the work session on July 11, 2023. : Deputy Planning Manager Simpson summarized the memo and used the aid of a PowerPoint presentation to summarize the proposed amendments to notification requirements. Senate Bill 201 eliminates the requirements to post notices in newspapers but does require notices be posted on the Utah Public Notice Website and the City website. The proposed ordinance amendment addresses notices for the following types of applications: e Street name changes e Subdivision ordinance amendments e Street and alley vacations e Zone changes e Zoning ordinance amendments \ e General plan amendments / e Historic resource designations If the proposed amendment is approved, the requirement to publish notices in the newspaper will be replaced with a requirement to post the notice on the State Public Notice Website. During the March 21, 2023 meeting, the Council asked questions about newspaper circulation in the area and staff found that subscription to the paper has decreased by over 30,000 in the last 30 years; current circulation is just 22,000. Since the Council tabled the proposed ordinance on March 21, Planning staff has conducted their own survey to determine how people who attended Planning Commission meetings had learned of certain agenda items; they found that just one person out of the 40 polled learned of an application through the newspaper, but they had read a headline and article about the application, not the actual legal notice. The Council also asked about the cost associated with newspaper noticing; each notice has a cost of approximately $200, for an annual average cost of $2,400. Mr. Simpson concluded the Planning Commission has recommended that the Council adopt the proposed ordinance amendments to replace the requirement for posting notices in the newspaper with a requirement to post it on the State Public Notice Website. Vice Chair Richey asked if residents could sign up for notifications on the City’s website and the Utah Public Notice Website. Council Executive Director Eller-Smith answered yes; residents can subscribe to a specific public body. Council member Hyer stated his remaining concern is historical preservation of notices; he asked if the Utah Public Notice Website retains or archives notices to be able to determine the date that certain notices were posted. Mr. Simpson stated he imagines the State of Utah does archive public notices, but he cannot say for certain. Council member White stated that she had that same question the first time the Council discussed this issue; she is concerned that the questions that were initially asked by the Council have not been answered and that it is not possible for City staff to fully explain the current noticing process or the process that will be in place when the amendments are approved. Mr. Simpson stated the only change is advertising on the Utah Public Meeting Notice website versus the newspaper, and he is not sure if the newspaper archives their public notices. Council member White stated she understands the proposal and does not fault Mr. Simpson for not being able to address the Council’s questions tonight; however, if the matter is voted on tonight, she will vote in opposition. Chair Choberka stated that she is worried that not all residents have digital capabilities to search and find notices they may be interested in. Mr. Simpson stated he understands that concern, but noted staff has weighed whether the small number of people who obtain notices via the newspaper warrants the City’s annual expense on hard copy notices. Council member Blair asked when the changes would go into effect if approved. Mr. Simpson stated that it would be ) — effective based upon the effective date of the ordinance; however, staff is willing to work to phase out the current practice and - transition to the new practice and will work with the City Council to spread the word about updated noticing procedures. Council member Hyer stated he is not as concerned about reducing access to notices by eliminating newspaper notices, but he is not sure that the Utah Public Notice Website is being fully used by public bodies, not just Ogden City; he has searched for notices from several entities and has been unable to find them. He stated he would recommend a three-month transition period a and work to make changes to the City’s website to provide an archiving mechanism. Additionally, newspaper notices should . include language informing the reader that the City will cease providing newspaper notifications and will eventually be providing } all notices on the City website and Utah Public Notice website. The Council engaged in discussion about Council member Hyer’s recommendation, after which Council Executive Director Eller-Smith suggested that the Council table this item until the August 29 meeting to give Planning staff time to address the concerns expressed by the Council. She would also recommend that the transition period be six months rather than three months, which will give the Council staff sufficient time to activate a communications plan regarding the matter. Chair Choberka introduced in writing proposed Ordinance 2023-49, entitled: “An ordinance of Ogden City Utah, amending the Ogden Municipal Code by amending section 14-1-8; amending Section 14-7-7; amending Section 15-1-4; amending Subsection 15-1-19.B; amending Subsection 172-2.E to remove newspaper noticing requirements aligning with State notification laws; and providing that this ordinance shall become effective immediately upon posting after final passage.” A copy of the proposed ordinance was deposited with the Deputy City Recorder and ordered that the City Recorder have at least one copy available for public inspection in her office during all business hours. Chair Choberka then called for public input regarding the proposed ordinance.

column3: stated there are still many people who receive the newspaper; additionally, senior citizens who frequent local senior ce
column4: Angel Castillo stated there are still many people who receive the newspaper; additionally, senior citizens who frequent local senior centers often obtain a newspaper while there and read through it. She was recently at the Golden Hours Center where there were three editions of the newspaper, but at least 12 people read them in the short time she was there. There is a small part of the population for which the newspaper is still their primary source of news and information. She agreed with Mr. Pate’s concerns about the importance of being able to archive notices and information provided in the newspaper; the same benefit is not available for electronic notices. She finds it hard to believe that the City would not want to be intentional when trying to reach out to all residents of the community. She agreed that it is necessary for the Council to be able to evaluate all the unintended consequences of this proposal. Providing adequate notice is worth the $2,400 spent by the City each year. Council member White stated it is important to point out that this is not just a $2,400 hard expense, but also a significant amount of staff time and resources on current noticing practices. Council member Nadolski agreed and stated that the workload imbalance is an issue that he is considering. COUNCIL MEMBER HYER MOVED TO TABLE PROPOSED ORDINANCE 2023-49 UNTIL AUGUST 29, 2023. COUNCIL MEMBER WHITE SECONDED THE MOTION, ALL VOTED AYE.

column3: discussed recent actions taken regarding redevelopment of the property at the Ogden Airport; she had an interesting conv
column4: Teresa Bramwell discussed recent actions taken regarding redevelopment of the property at the Ogden Airport; she had an interesting conversation with someone last week who owns property on the new Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) line in Ogden. The individual is looking to pursue a conversion of an office building to residential or mixed-use development. She noted that she offered to sell her property, which is also on the BRT line, to the individual and his response was that he would only pay 60 ) percent of what it is worth. She believes that to be true because developers are in the business to make money. This will be the ~~ same for redevelopment of properties at the airport; the landowners there have no intent to sell their property, but if the City authorizes developers to proceed with the acquisition of property at 60 percent of its value, she is not sure what options the landowners will have. EEE ss - Ira Macner stated she received an email from the Sierra Club about a letter drafted by Mayor Caldwell to revoke Ogden’s participation in the Utah Community Renewable Energy Act (CREA) Program. If the Program were to be implemented, emissions { ) could be reduced by 45 percent by the year 2030, with the goal of 100 percent clean energy by that year. She is not sure how serious the letter is, but she wished to voice her support for staying in the program, execution of the utility agreement, and proceeding to the regulatory process in order to obtain costs about electricity rates. The Program is wonderful, and the City should continue to be a leader in the transition for renewable energy. Angel Castillo echoed the sentiments expressed by Ms. Macner. She also restated comments she made in the last Council meeting regarding programs available to low to middle income households to participate in the CREP. She also addressed the item on tonight’s Redevelopment Agency (RDA) agenda regarding a policy governing the acquisition and conveyance of real property; she is excited to see the Board moving forward and defining parameters that the Agency must abide by related to property transactions. She asked that the policy include a requirement for an appraisal signed by an official independent agent as opposed to a broker’s estimate of a property value. This will help to ensure the City receives the highest and best value for any property that is sold. Heath Satow also referenced the RDA policy regarding the acquisition and conveyance of real property; he has discussed the Brown Ice Cream building in the past and asked what the status of that project is, but it appears that the developer is allowing the building to rot though it is the last bit of remaining history on the Wonder Block. He spoke to the importance of using actual appraisals as mentioned by Ms. Castillo; for the Brown Ice Cream building, the City relied upon a broker’s estimate and the developer that acquired the property did so at a very low price. He also asked if the Mayor has obtained a timeline for the Dinosaur Park’s expansion and the need to evict the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center from the property that is needed for the Dinosaur Park expansion. Travis Pate referenced the agenda item dealing with proposed amendments to the City’s notification requirements; he cited a situation in the past where the City was considering the declaration of surplus property and he learned of the situation because ofa public notice. A few of the things that were part of the list of surplus property should not have been disposed of and if he had not seen that notice and had been unable to provide important input to keep the City from doing something they should not have done; the outcome would have been dire. He stated that the new noticing requirements are not sufficient for communicating potential actions of the Council to the public and he encouraged the Council to first research the past errors of noticing electronically and ask themselves if they are willing to sacrifice history for convenience. Mark Stevenson echoed the comments made by Ms. Macner, encouraging Ogden City to stay involved in the CREA Program; he suggested the Council approve the execution of the utility agreement at the soonest opportunity. The Mayor is unable to explain why he would send a letter withdrawing the City from the program and this action is contrary to votes that have previously been taken by the Council. Ogden would be the only city of 18 to withdraw before final details are known and this makes no sense. It would also be difficult for the City to reengage in the future and the City will have essentially wasted the $70,000 that has been spent to get to this point. He provided facts about current energy offerings in the community, emphasizing there are no other options for achieving reduced emissions and clean energy. He noted the people of Ogden deserve to have a choice in energy production. David Timmerman also echoed the comments made by Ms. Macner and Mr. Stevenson; he urged them to ‘finish the job’ in terms of staying engaged in the CREA Program. There are no other options available to the City and he asked each Council member to think through the implications of withdrawing at this point in time. This matters to many residents that live in this community; Ogden does care and is willing to try to solve the problem of ongoing carbon production and fossil fuel consumption.

column3: stated she does not trust government; she has been taken advantage of several times in her life specifically by Ogden Ci
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she does not trust government; she has been taken advantage of several times in her life specifically by Ogden City and she does not like anything that makes it easier for the government to manipulate taxpayers. If passing the proposed ordinance only means that it will be convenient for City staff to post and find notices, but not necessarily convenient for a resident to find, she does not trust the position and feels that the City is trying to undermine the people. Dave Timmerman agreed with Mr. Pate’s assessment that the $2,400 spent on public notices is a very small portion of the City’s budget. i

column3: stated that it may be that just one person sees a newspaper notice, but in his case, he has informed up to 30 people of
column4: Travis Pate stated that it may be that just one person sees a newspaper notice, but in his case, he has informed up to 30 people of a notice that he has read. He stated the input of these residents matters. He then noted that it may be possible to view an archive of notices that have been posted on the Utah Public Meeting Notice Website, but it is not possible to know how many notices were not posted on the website, even if there was a requirement for them to be posted. The accuracy of the noticing is difficult to determine. He added that the $2,400 spent on noticing is a tiny fraction of the City’s total budget. Also, it would be difficult to manipulate the records of an independent source — the newspaper; the same cannot be said for the two websites that are managed by government entities. He emphasized the historic value and independent source value of newspaper noticing is immeasurable.

column3: thanked the Council for their action on the proposed ordinance to change noticing requirements; she agreed with Chair Ch
column4: Angel Castillo thanked the Council for their action on the proposed ordinance to change noticing requirements; she agreed with Chair Choberka that the City does have issues accessing a portion of the population, namely those that do not have internet access. She agreed with the suggestion to submit a thorough survey, but to gather census tract info as part of the survey to determine the validity of the response. Access to quality programming and resources is vital for many residents in the community, this starts with quality communication. The communication channels that the City is developing need to have the same type of integrity and intention as the survey that the City paid for regarding the Utah Community Renewable Energy Act (CREA) Program. Weber State University is a Carnegie Institute and they have pledged to use their services to connect with the community. Their data plan was used to conduct the CREA survey and the City should use their expertise to guide the outreach process.

column3: thanked the Council for their thoughtful deliberation of the topic of public noticing. However, it causes him to pause w
column4: Heath Satow thanked the Council for their thoughtful deliberation of the topic of public noticing. However, it causes him to pause when considering the amount of time, the Council spent on adopting a $20 million buffer on a $50 million budget to | j contribute to a paid parking program in downtown Ogden. This means citizens parking on the street in downtown Ogden, and specifically 25" Street, will be paying for parking twice over through fees and taxes. This equates to 8,000 years of the $2,400 amount dedicated to noticing in the newspaper. He concluded by stating he is glad to hear of movement on the negotiations of an extension of the lease for the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center, but he asked that the City consider waiving the $7,000 per month that RR Re ee ———————————————————————————E _ the Center will pay in rent; if the City believes the building they are in is not worth saving and will eventually be torn down, it : ) does not make sense to charge them $7,000 a month for a few months. They should be allowed to put that money into a new ae facility. i

column3: addressed the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center; he encouraged the Council to pressure the i} Mayor to extend
column4: Kerry Wayne addressed the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center; he encouraged the Council to pressure the i} Mayor to extend the lease agreement so that they are not forced to shut down. Their new facility is not yet ready for them to move into, and they need an extension. He then requested dialogue with the Mayor and Council to consider working with local non- profit organizations to secure housing for the unhoused population of the community. This type of program has been undertaken by other communities and it has been very successful. Chair Choberka asked Administration to provide an update on their negotiations with the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center. City Attorney Williams stated that Administration has been working with the Center for the last few weeks and they have addressed the requirements placed upon them in order to receive an extension of their lease. Therefore, an extension will be granted once all pertinent documentation is executed and delivered to the City. John Thompson referenced the official City magazine, which discusses revitalization and redevelopment, and he asked the difference between the two. He added there are no authors listed for the articles in the magazine and he has contacted the publisher and the City and been unable to get that information. He asked that Ogden be prioritized and highlighted in the magazine. He then also referenced the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center; he is not sure why they were evicted from their current location after being there 12 years with no mention of any problems. He also feels they are being treated unfairly in terms of zoning restrictions for their new location. He stated that Ogden’s logo is ‘still untamed’ and that means wild.

column3: thanked the Council for listening to the input of the public regarding the public noticing ordinance; the E public wants
column4: Linda Sanchez thanked the Council for listening to the input of the public regarding the public noticing ordinance; the E public wants the City Council to be transparent and the action taken tonight is a step in that direction. She also referenced tonight’s work session meeting and the discussion of elected officials’ salaries. She stated she is employed as a nurse and nurses must take a test to prove their competence. They also must take tests every year. She suggested elected officials also take a test every year regarding their Oath of Office to uphold the Constitution. The test could show competency and annual training on the Constitution could be offered as well. The community wants to get behind their elected leaders and being transparent will help in many ways. Alexander Costanio suggested that the City create a bulk waste program; once or twice a year, residents could place bulk . waste on the curb in front of their home and the City or a contracted hauler could pick it up. This would help many residents who do not have trucks to move large items or yard waste to the dump. It would also help clean up the City and increase community pride. Council member Hyer mentioned the dial a dumpster program in response to Mr. Costanio’s suggestion. He noted the’ City tried a bulk waste program several years ago, but the amount of debris that sat at the curbside for several months was overwhelming and it took too long for it to be collected. The City looked very trashy during that time. He noted that aresident and four of their neighbors can work together to schedule a dumpster to be delivered to their street free of charge and they can place ; their waste in the dumpster over a three-day period. Chair Choberka stated she is also very concerned about the unhoused population of the community and appreciates the City’s homeless advocates and the many volunteers in the community who are working to provide aid. She then suggested that Mr. Thompson contact City Administration with his concerns about the magazine and they can provide answers. She addressed the comments about the Union Station Framework Plan and noted that it only addresses the infrastructure and architectural standards for the campus, but not the end users. There is a great deal of community engagement to take place before the Master Plan for the Union Station Campus is developed and finalized. She then asked City Administration to respond to Mr. Satow’s comments about the $7,000 month rent being charged to the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center. City Attorney Williams stated that is the City’s default rent amount, but not the monthly rent that will be charged to the Center. Chair Choberka concluded by thanking . Mr. Benitez for his suggestion to pay property taxes for police officers and school teachers. ) Council member White addressed the comments made about the proposed changes to noticing requirements. She stated - she knows there is a certain population of the community that does not use the internet to find information, but she does not believe that the population is as high as has been portrayed. There have been recent efforts to extend internet service to as many people as possible in the State. Chair Choberka agreed; access to the internet is available to anyone, but some may not be able to take advantage of that access for a variety of reasons.

column3: stated that he is concerned about the retention of police officers and school teachers. In Ogden, there are 34,251 homes
column4: Sebastian Benitez stated that he is concerned about the retention of police officers and school teachers. In Ogden, there are 34,251 homes paying taxes, but there are many issues with retaining officers and teachers. He is asking City Administration and the City Council to consider having the City pay the property taxes for all police officers and teachers; this would be less than 3,000 homes and the average annual property tax is approximately $3,000. This would equate to $900,000 per year and this would help these valuable residents of the community. He would recommend making the same proposal to the Ogden School District Board. Travis Pate also referenced the development of the Union Station Campus; the Union Station will turn 100 years old next year and celebration of this important asset of Ogden City is much needed. The history and heritage associated with the Union Station is so meaningful and celebrating it may help to address the concerns raised by the many individuals who have volunteered at Union Station. It is important for the Council to meet the people where they are, and this could occur at Union Station.

column3: discussed homelessness in Ogden and the concentration of poverty in the East Central neighborhoods of Ogden. She referen
column4: Teresa Bramwell discussed homelessness in Ogden and the concentration of poverty in the East Central neighborhoods of Ogden. She referenced an affordable housing gap estimate published by the Utah League of Cities and Towns in 2019 and she believes it is the most current document; in 2019, Ogden had 2,313 too many units classified as very low-income housing, which is 30 to 50 percent of the median income. Ogden has 1,801 too many housing units. In the extremely low-income category, which is below 30 percent of the median income, Ogden has a deficit of 117 units. She does not believe that is true because she heard in — the last meeting that the homeless shelters in Ogden have never been full. This tells her thatthe homeless people thatareinOgden § * will not stay in a homeless shelter. She does not believe a lot of high-income housing has been built in Ogden in the last three years, but there have been many new low-income housing units added. This massive surplus of low-income housing is creating a massive amount of crime and destitution; it is making real estate less valuable because people do not want to own and invest in real estate where crime and destitution is high. She asked that the Council consider the City’s housing situation in a more realistic manner in the future.

column3: discussed her volunteer service at Union Station and noted that all that time she never had anyone ask her where the ret
column4: Teresa Holmes discussed her volunteer service at Union Station and noted that all that time she never had anyone ask her where the retail centers were. That is because people visiting Union Station are interested in history and not chain retail outlets. There are many rare artifacts at Union Station, and she was a fantastic tour guide, but the City has ruined it. Steve Jones also discussed the Union Station; he attended the work session earlier tonight and listened to the presentation about the Union Station Framework Plan and he was appalled. This plan does not take into account any of the recommendations from the residents or those that have been involved at Union Station. He asked the Council to take a closer look at the plan and consider if the citizens’ input has been adhered to in the development of the proposal.

column3: stated that the action just taken by the Council about the Union Station Campus Master Plan Development - Framework is a
column4: Adrian Zubler stated that the action just taken by the Council about the Union Station Campus Master Plan Development - Framework is a travesty; the Council had a discussion, invited input from the public, had another discussion, and then refused to . let people respond to that discussion. That seems to be unfair, and it seems there are not enough people speaking. The Council is supposed to represent the citizens of Ogden, not just themselves, but that is what seems to be happening. This whole project is being rushed through. She addressed Council member White’s comments about the requirement for moderate income housing around transit stations and asked the deadline for complying with that legislation. The City has time and people should not be pushed to make premature decisions. The matter should be tabled; a scaled model of the potential buildout of the Campus is : needed. The people who designed it have a clear understanding of it, but the rest of those interested do not have that same luxury. : Laura Lewis also addressed Council member White, noting this is the second time she can recall her citing House Bill (HB) 462 and the requirement to create low-income housing near a transit hub. She stated she has reviewed the legislation and cannot find that specific requirement. She asked that Council member White point out the requirement for her specifically as she wants to be able to understand the requirements of the legislation.

column3: stated that Ms. Sanchez may be confusing the work that Council member White does with the Wasatch Front Regional Council
column4: Angel Castillo stated that Ms. Sanchez may be confusing the work that Council member White does with the Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC) as employment with the State; WFRC is not a State agency. She also noted she has provided Ms. Lewis with the information she asked for regarding HB462. She then noted that what is happening tonight is evidence of the reasons the reasons the City needs to invest money and time into holding town hall meetings. The Council’s regular meeting format is not conducive to the type of dialogue the Council says they want to have with their constituents. She then thanked the Council for tabling the Framework matter; it is imperative to put guardrails on the City’s intention for future use of the Union Station Campus and surrounding areas. There is a difference between planning for growth and paying for growth; the City has a tendency to utilize the Redevelopment Agency (RDA) to pay for growth at the expense of infrastructure needs in the community. Travis Pate cited the Council and Mayor’s failure to follow-up on information and requests that are made during these meetings; the City has done a lot of great things, but they have done bad things as well, such as supporting developing on the west side of Business Depot Ogden (BDO) to the detriment of residents living across the street in Marriott-Slaterville.

column3: discussed the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and noted he is so pleased the City has granted them an exten
column4: Heath Satow discussed the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and noted he is so pleased the City has granted them an extension of their lease and that the terms of the extension are favorable. He wished that the process had not been so painful and costly, but he is happy with the outcome. He then stated tonight during the work session, a really good developer spoke about a project they are pursuing on Washington Boulevard; they are funding the project on their own, with the exception of receiving a few small pieces of land from the City and the Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT). They are securing their own funding and developing quality building plans and he really appreciates developers like that. More of those types of projects could be achieved if the City would work with other developers rather than just a ‘group of insiders’ that get things for free.

column3: stated she has been trying to get people to come to City Council meetings to express themselves, but many people are not
column4: Linda Sanchez stated she has been trying to get people to come to City Council meetings to express themselves, but many people are not heard by the City Council. She reminded the Council that the public does not serve them, but the Council does serve the public. It is important for the Council to get input. What was concerning to her is that during tonight’s work session meeting, the Council indicated that if they accepted public input tonight, they would not need to accept public input during the September 26 meeting when the matter is discussed again. She stated that should not be the case; there may be things that change, and people may have a different opinion and they should be able to speak about that. It is important for the Council to listen. She )} noted she is concerned after having heard Council member White state several times that the City is doing what the State wants ° them to do. She understands Council member White works for the State of Utah. Council member White stated that is incorrect.

column3: stated she found that on an internet search; she advised Council member White to work for the City and to get her consti
column4: Ms. Sanchez stated she found that on an internet search; she advised Council member White to work for the City and to get her constituents involved. Ifthe State is requiring something her constituents do not want, it is her obligation to listen to and help her constituents. She then thanked the Council for the wonderful presentation this evening in recognition of Constitution Month and Constitution Day.

column3: reiterated her comments about the upcoming 100" anniversary of the Union Station. She asked if the campus would be torn
column4: Teresa Holmes reiterated her comments about the upcoming 100" anniversary of the Union Station. She asked if the campus would be torn up in advance of that event. The City does not realize that Union Station is a goldmine for the City, and she \ thinks that the City could do better. She wants a spectacular party for the Station’s hundredth birthday. She suggested that a development be focused on Washington Boulevard rather than around Union Station, or the other development that is aging be improved and brought up to date. She is not thrilled with the Framework plan, and much more should be considered.

column3: addressed the conversation that took place in tonight’s work session regarding proposed amendments to the City’s manufac
column4: Angel Castillo addressed the conversation that took place in tonight’s work session regarding proposed amendments to the City’s manufacturing zones; as a former Planning Commissioner, she understands how important land use regulations are and former Planning Manager Montgomery once told her to think of a use change as a ‘forever change’ because once a use is allowed, it will remain in place for at least 30 to 50 years. She stated that there were some matters presented to the Council tonight that deserve more time and consideration; she is concerned that these types of recommendations are made by City Administration at the last minute with a sense of urgency. She agreed with many of the comments made by the Council during the work session about the need to preserve private property rights and she was crushed that during the discussion, the Community and Economic Development staff never mentioned local/existing businesses and that is because their focus is on bringing in outside businesses and industry, which will stress the City’s natural resources and challenge its housing needs. There are already many small businesses in the community that could use the kind of support Community and Economic Development is offering to outsiders.

column3: stated tonight’s work session was great and she appreciated the Council standing up for their constituents and local bus
column4: Linda Sanchez stated tonight’s work session was great and she appreciated the Council standing up for their constituents and local businesses. It was the best work session that she has listened to, and she thanked the Council for keeping checks and balances in mind. She looks forward to hearing the next discussion of the issue. She also congratulated those individuals who were successful in the recent Primary Election.

column3: inquired about plans of the City Council to meet with people where they are in terms of the Union Station; this would in
column4: Angel Castillo inquired about plans of the City Council to meet with people where they are in terms of the Union Station; this would include holding meetings outside of normal business hours and even on the weekend. She suggested that the consultant working on the Union Station project do the same.

column3: stated progress implies a goal towards something and he asked what exactly the City’s end goal is; growth for the sake o
column4: D.S. Anderson stated progress implies a goal towards something and he asked what exactly the City’s end goal is; growth for the sake of growth is not progress and it is possible for a community or an area of a community to be too dense. He noted some ; actions cannot be undone and they should be very carefully considered.

column3: stated he also appreciates the thoughtful discussion tonight about the zone change of the property on Washington Bouleva
column4: Heath Satow stated he also appreciates the thoughtful discussion tonight about the zone change of the property on Washington Boulevard; he was pleased to learn that the developer bought all of the property on their own and that the City asked them to include a commercial element, which led to tonight’s discussion. He wondered if the developer does not know that Ogden City willingly gives other developers property or other incentives. He stated this is evidence of the fact that developers will work in Ogden on their own dime if it is not so hard to get things done in the City. He concluded that during the last meeting, the Mayor ‘and Council member White got very ‘worked up’ about the arrangement with the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center, -” — which included them using a City property free of charge for several years; he asked if they are only concerned about giving things away for non-profits, but not for developers. It seems private developers are the only entity worthy of the transfer of public land for a private development. a Council member White clarified that her comments last week were based upon the fact that the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center had received a space free of rent for 12 years, but other non-profit organizations have not been given that same to! consideration. -

column3: stated for the second week in arow she has appreciated the Council’s discussions and actions during their work session a
column4: Linda Sanchez stated for the second week in arow she has appreciated the Council’s discussions and actions during their work session and meeting. She thanked them for their interaction with the public.

column3: thanked the Council for delaying any consideration of the Union Station Campus Master Plan, further consideration will b
column4: Steve Jones thanked the Council for delaying any consideration of the Union Station Campus Master Plan, further consideration will be beneficial to the City as it is important to develop a solid plan that can be lived with for many years into the _ future. ? Al Jones stated he is a huge supporter of the museums at Union Station as well and the Campus Plan will impact the future of Ogden forever; he urged extreme conservativism in the planning process to make sure it is done right. He then noted that he drove down Harrison Boulevard the other day and he is not a fan of the new OGX Bus Rapid Transit line; he is not sure why the City allowed the Utah Transit Authority (UTA) to install a barrier down the middle of the road. He acknowledged the need to improve the public transportation system, but he does not like the project. He then echoed the comments made by Council member Lopez earlier in the meeting about the need to provide opportunities for residents to build equity in the City through home ownership; proper planning to determine where owner-occupancy is required is essential.

column3: addressed the Union Station Campus Master Plan and wondered if the parking lots will be large enough to accommodate all
column4: Teresa Holmes addressed the Union Station Campus Master Plan and wondered if the parking lots will be large enough to accommodate all of the vehicles that will be visiting the area and to hold the equipment needed at the Station. She then noted that the museum collections housed at the Union Station are what make Ogden and should be preserved. The Union Station is the Utah State Railroad Museum and that is very important and one of the things that draws visitors to the community.

column3: addressed concerns he has raised previously regarding the Jefferson Historic District; he encouraged the City to give mo
column4: Travis Pate addressed concerns he has raised previously regarding the Jefferson Historic District; he encouraged the City to give more care to that neighborhood that was so passionately supported by both the Mayor and City Council in the past. Care is not displayed when decorative concrete is replaced with standards concrete or when streetlights remain burned out for months on end. He then suggested that a protection area be placed around Union Station to prevent development in certain areas of the Campus that would block the Station. He then asked what the City is doing to celebrate the 125" anniversary of Utah’s statehood; he suggested that Council member Lopez be invited to remain involved in that matter in representation of the City.

column3: thanked the Council for taking the amendments to the M-1 and M-2 zones under consideration; he addressed ordinance 2023-
column4: Alex Maurer thanked the Council for taking the amendments to the M-1 and M-2 zones under consideration; he addressed ordinance 2023-55 and noted that it is his understanding that the Planning staff and Planning Commission are concerned about the environmental impacts of salvage yards and the amount of space the uses take up. However, he wondered about the difference between towing yards being allowed and given an amount of space for outside storage of vehicles when the same practice is being outlawed by banning future salvage yards. Mr. Maurer asked the Council to consider the improvements that salvage yards have made to their operations to help address concerns about environmental issues.

column3: stated that last year a retired schoolteacher was evicted from her hangar at the Ogden Airport and was given 14 days to
column4: Ed McKenney stated that last year a retired schoolteacher was evicted from her hangar at the Ogden Airport and was given 14 days to vacate; a legal challenge ensued and due to a mistake made by Ogden City, a judge dismissed the case and awarded the individual $17,000 in attorney’s fees. Ogden City continued to pursue the eviction and the individual ultimately decided to turn over the keys to the hangar when she was told that she would be required to pay Ogden City three times their attorney’s fees if she lost her fight against the City. This is a hangar she has invested in and improved based upon requirements imposed by Ogden City. The hangar was part of her planned retirement, and she has never received a penny from Ogden City following the judge’s ruling. This past week, Ogden City and City Attorney Williams filed for a summary adjustment against the individual, Ms. Wendy Williams; he asked why that was done given that the City already has Ms. Williams’ hangar. He asked why she is being asked to incur more legal fees to defend against summary judgement. He is concerned about Ogden City making such a heartless move and he asked if this is how the City Council wants a retired schoolteacher treated after being a stakeholder and investor in the Ogden Airport.

column3: addressed Ms. Bramwell’s comments about the Justice Center bond; he is supportive of the bond as he feels that it will u
column4: Heath Satow addressed Ms. Bramwell’s comments about the Justice Center bond; he is supportive of the bond as he feels that it will ultimately save residents money in the long run by helping to reduce recidivism, which will reduce crime in the long run. Crime is very costly to a community.

column3: stated he was happy to witness the Governing Body make good decisions tonight on the matters relating to amendments to t
column4: Steven Van Wagoner stated he was happy to witness the Governing Body make good decisions tonight on the matters relating to amendments to the M-1 and M-2 zones; he does not believe the Council got the answers to all the questions they asked of Administration over the past several weeks, but they did a good job of coming together and finding compromise under a great deal of pressure. He is thankful to Council staff and Mr. Brierley for helping to clarify the processes, which enabled the Council to make wise decisions tonight.

column3: stated she just came from the Weber County Commission meeting where there was a discussion regarding the proposed Justic
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she just came from the Weber County Commission meeting where there was a discussion regarding the proposed Justice Center bond that will be on the upcoming General Election ballot; she addressed the Commission and told them she is one of Weber County’s largest crime victims and anything that could be done to address the crime in the community will be supported by her. She stated the bond will cost the average household $4.50 per month and businesses $8.50 per month, but it will make it possible to build a mental health facility near the existing jail and fund programs aimed at reducing recidivism. She stated that 70 percent of the population of the jail is either mentally ill or on drugs. She then thanked everyone | who is running for office in Ogden City and for their willingness to help improve the community. _” Laura Lewis stated she is still concerned about the City’s attempt to control how private property owners are using their property; she does not believe manufacturing facilities are any cleaner than storage units or other uses that are being prohibited in the M-1 and M-2 zones. She knows that the Council is trying to implement broader plans for the community, but it is also important to listen to the input of the public and business owners. She agreed with a point made by Acting Chair Richey that these nnn nnn nnn ______________ matters should be market driven. She then noted that she learned this week that former Chief Administrative Officer Johnson has been hired by the City as a consultant at a very significant salary. She asked if the Council was aware of that and if they approved } it. Teresa Holmes agreed with Council member Nadolski about the need to protect the Ogden River corridor in order to preserve the habitat of the many wildlife that live along there. She then reiterated her comments made during the last City Council meeting about the need to retain ownership of the Union Station land in order to make it possible for the museums housed there to become accredited.

column3: addressed Union Station and suggested that the City retain ownership of the property rather than sell or trade it as par
column4: Travis Pate addressed Union Station and suggested that the City retain ownership of the property rather than sell or trade it as part of a larger development project. The City has relied upon Business Depot Ogden (BDO) as a funding source formany = projects and that has only been possible because the City retained ownership of the land. He advised the Council against doing something different for another huge asset of the community. He suggested a thorough assessment of the manner in which Redevelopment Agency (RDA) funding has been used and whether the use of that funding has created success and improvement in various neighborhoods of the community.

column3: stated she is thrilled that Council member Hyer is researching and reviewing articles that have suggestions for addressi
column4: Angel Castillo stated she is thrilled that Council member Hyer is researching and reviewing articles that have suggestions for addressing the housing problems in the community; many other communities have experienced housing problems, and the City should consider what they have done to pursue solutions. She addressed Ms. Fuentes’ earlier comments about the Annual Action Plan (AAP) being a five-year plan; she emphasized that the AAP can be changed, though such a change would be cumbersome and lengthy. She challenged the City to evaluate its own processes to see why developers are not bring affordable housing projects to the community; much of that is due to the City’s processes and ‘red tape’; the minute someone purchases property in Ogden, they start losing value on it because it takes so long for the developer to get through the development approval process. Uncertainty prevents developers from participating in Ogden City and the Council needs to remove barriers to participation.

column3: stated he has called the City’s Police Department dispatch asking for help at his property and he cannot get anyone to c
column4: David Crosby stated he has called the City’s Police Department dispatch asking for help at his property and he cannot get anyone to come to his house to take his complaint; he is getting no respect from the Police Department. When he makes a complaint, he wants it to be taken seriously and he should not be asked to wait for hours to hear back from the police. He added that the street he lives on, Grant Avenue, is falling apart and the City is not fixing it or repairing any burned out streetlights. He is tired of being treated as an idiot by the Police Department and the City in general. He would like some feedback and comments from the Council. , Chair Choberka expressed a willingness to speak with Mr. Crosby after the meeting about the areas of Grant Avenue that | ; need attention. Mr. Crosby stated he lives at 550 Grant Avenue and the street is falling apart and the lights are burned out and no one is fixing it.

column3: addressed Mr. Timmerman’s comments and asked if a dollar amount has been identified for a household to participate in th
column4: Emily Beally addressed Mr. Timmerman’s comments and asked if a dollar amount has been identified for a household to participate in the program. Chair Choberka answered no. Ms. Beally asked if the Council is expecting to identify a dollar amount before singing the agreement; she does not believe the City should agree to participate in a program before fully understanding the financial implications. Chair Choberka stated that the way the program is structured, the City would sign the agreement to participate in the program, but costs will not be known until later. Signing the agreement does not commit the City to participate in the project indefinitely. Ms. Beally stated that fiscal responsibility is very important; from what she understands, she is concerned about the non-renewable energy that will be needed to create renewable energy. She recently heard that the City could ; own its own nuclear plant to create clean energy and she will research the matter further and provide her findings to the Council.

column3: stated he was frustrated when a Council member chose her time to make a disingenuous remark about something Ms. Castillo
column4: Heath Satow stated he was frustrated when a Council member chose her time to make a disingenuous remark about something Ms. Castillo said about the City’s housing issues. Ms. Castillo was not implying that the projects that have been completed or the loans that have been made are meaningless, only that she wishes that the City could do more. He agreed with Council member Hyer’s comments that it may be possible for the City to do more to push for change at the State level and even look outside of the State for solutions that have not yet been considered in terms of housing.

column3: thanked the Council for their consideration of the AAP and funding that will provide residents with down payment assista
column4: Linda Sanchez thanked the Council for their consideration of the AAP and funding that will provide residents with down payment assistance and purchasing their own home in the community. She is concerned by the increase in high density housing in the community and would rather see the City pursue single-family housing projects. She then reported a situation that occurred recently on the City’s trail system; someone using the trail was approached by someone with a large knife and dog and told to leave the trail. She is not sure if the trail is not appropriately marked to identify public and private property. She stated that the | | police were called, and a police report was filed, but the individual did not hear anything from the police as a follow up. This is , concerning to her, and she hopes the City will take it seriously and try to address something that could become a dangerous situation. EEE ~, David Timmerman referenced the City’s participation in the Community Renewable Energy Act (CREA) and signing an agreement to remain in the program; he knows Mayor Caldwell is not running for reelection, but he hopes a majority of the ~ Council and the Mayor will sign onto the agreement, which is critical for the community. There are no other alternatives for E producing energy for Ogden in the future and he asked the Council to work to finalize the City’s participation in the program. He : asked the Mayor to do the right thing, which he believes is to sign the agreement.

column3: emphasized the need to pursue accreditation of museums at the Union Station; if Ogden City is not paying attention, many
column4: Teresa Holmes emphasized the need to pursue accreditation of museums at the Union Station; if Ogden City is not paying attention, many of the Union Station artifacts will be shipped to Salt Lake City. She also wondered where the State Legislature is on this matter; she asked why they are not paying attention to the need to save one of the most historic places in Utah, and even in the western United States. The Union Station is very important, and she will continue to bring it to the Council’s attention. After 21 years as a docent in Union Station and its museums, she has a right to speak up and she will not be quieted by the treatment she has received from City Administration.

column3: reiterated her earlier comments about the adjustments to HUD funding in the City’s budget; she does not believe the expl
column4: Angel Castillo reiterated her earlier comments about the adjustments to HUD funding in the City’s budget; she does not believe the explanations that were provided are acceptable. She then agreed with Council member Hyer that it is necessary to review the City’s noise ordinance. Another option would be to remove carwashes as a permitted use in the C-2 and CP-2 zones, rather than all high impact uses. With regards to the winter parking discussion during tonight’s work session, she also appreciated Council member Lopez’s comments. She suggested the Council carefully consider that certain populations should be protected from these types of regulations.

column3: addressed the WonderBlock project; the City has been sitting on the property for many years and it would typically gener
column4: Heath Satow addressed the WonderBlock project; the City has been sitting on the property for many years and it would typically generate a great deal of tax revenue for the taxing entities. However, the City is covering taxes for developers so they can make more money, which is harming taxpayers who are on fixed income. He does not see the sense in any of this and the Council is proceeding through a tunnel with no light at the end; he is ashamed that they continue to proceed in this direction. _

column3: stated that she appreciated Council member Lopez’s comments during the work session tonight in response to Administratio
column4: Linda Sanchez stated that she appreciated Council member Lopez’s comments during the work session tonight in response to Administration’s recommended amendments to winter parking regulations. She is not convinced that the proposal will [ not negatively impact those with lesser economic means. She is astonished that the City can tell private residents where they can 7 park on their own properties or require them to move their vehicle during a snowstorm. This is America, and the City should not be dictating how people should be using their properties. The City Council members have been elected to stand up for residents,

column3: discussed the history of her property on Monroe Boulevard; she purchased it in 1997 and got a letter from the Mayor in 2
column4: Teresa Bramwell discussed the history of her property on Monroe Boulevard; she purchased it in 1997 and got a letter from the Mayor in 2001 with an offer to buy the property. She indicated the property was not for sale but wondered why he wanted to purchase it. The Mayor told him that another investor owned the rest of the block and was going to develop it ina way that would be detrimental to her property value. She offered to sell it for $250,000, but the City got an appraisal and found the value to be $200,000. The City did not purchase her property but did pursue other projects in the area surrounding her property. She felt good about keeping the property because she believed these other projects would ultimately increase the value of her property. She later learned of the Ogden on Board plan and it showed a high-rise development on her property; however, she has never had a seat at the table to provide input on what she feels is the best way for her neighborhood to develop or how her property should be used in the future.

column3: discussed the change in the City’s structure to assign the Union Station to the Community and Economic Development Depar
column4: Teresa Holmes discussed the change in the City’s structure to assign the Union Station to the Community and Economic Development Department; the Museum Foundation was devalued, and the museums disbanded, resulting in a loss of years of expertise. This is one of the biggest losses in the City of Ogden and decisions were made by people with no experience in museums and artifact preservation. Caren Warner publicly thanked the City Council and Ogden City staff for their support and facilitating the clean-up of the hoard around the exterior of her neighbor’s home; it took 75 volunteers several hours to get the cleanup done. This shows the power of the community when working toward a conumon goal. For several years, the home has been packed with debris, junk, and nonpermitted structures. She has tried to solve the problem with little success until she reached out to Chair Choberka who facilitated a meeting with Code Services and the Ogden Community Action Network (CAN). She is relieved by the change; the clean up has lifted her spirits and given her hope that things can and will improve. She is grateful for the partnership that Ogden has made with My Hometown, an organization that has worked tirelessly to improve the property; their efforts will continue to make the community better. Steve Jones also referenced the Union Station; he listened to the conversation about the Centennial Celebration during the work session tonight and he thanked City Administration for their efforts to commemorate the 100" birthday of Union Station. The following individuals addressed the Council, thanking them for their action to remain in the Community Renewable Energy Act (CREA) Program: David Timmerman, Heath Satow, Angel Castillo, Linda Carroll. Tiana Tonga stated she disagrees , with the decision to remain in the program, based upon the fact that the survey that was conducted regarding participationinthe | ! program only considered the input of 669 residents in the community. Linda Sanchez stated she does not believe an opt-out program is appropriate and, for that reason, she is concerned about the City’s participation in the CREA program. She suggested the City perform an audit to determine abuse of public funds. Laura Lewis stated she is concerned about the City participating in the CREA Program because it is poorly defined; she does not think an opt-out program is good for residents.

column3: stated he graduated from WSU in 1972. He then referenced the agenda item to appoint a new Public
