This has been the case ever since redevelopment activities have been underway in the area. Many property owners in the area feel the same as him; they feel preference is being given to big developers at the detriment of longtime residents and property owners in the area. He has not been adequately informed of these changes. Chris Barrigan echoed Mr. Richey’s comments about the proposed closure of Taylor Avenue near WSU. His neighborhood has been greatly inconvenienced and Mr. Richey has done a great deal of research into the matter. He asked that the Council take his comments and the requested closure under advisement and approve the road closure because it is the right thing to do for the community. Tim Nestoriak also echoed the request for the closure of Taylor Avenue south of the WSU campus; he discussed the increased traffic over the years and the impact that it is having on the safety of residents living on the street. Other roads have been closed and this has forced traffic onto Taylor Avenue, which is unfair to residents living there. He appreciates the radar signs but agreed they will only be effective in the short term. A gate would not be too expensive and there are other options for routing traffic through the area as desired by WSU. Stuart Richards also echoed the comments made regarding the requested closure of Taylor Avenue; he also does not believe the radar signs will have a long-term impact on the traffic and rates of speed on the road.

column3: commented on the changes to the Ogden Bend Mixed Use Zone; she was not involved in Ogden when the taking of the land occ
column4: Teresa Bramwell commented on the changes to the Ogden Bend Mixed Use Zone; she was not involved in Ogden when the taking of the land occurred to make up the Ogden Bend Plan area, but she has researched the current ownership of the land and found it has been sitting vacant in its current state since 2014 with no action. She noted the mailing address for the landowner is a vacant building in Provo City and she still does not have answers about the current owner. She understands the frustration of the long-time landowners and residents of Ogden City who are frustrated by this situation and by being harassed by Code Enforcement. Brooke Barrigan echoed the sentiments expressed by her neighbors regarding the requested closure of Taylor Avenue. She relayed personal experiences that she and other residents have had due to increased traffic on Taylor Avenue; there are several children, some of them disabled, who live on Taylor Avenue, and they are not being cared for and protected by the City.

column3: asked for an update on Dinosaur Park.
column4: Heath Satow asked for an update on Dinosaur Park.

column3: stated he previously made comments that may have been upsetting to some Council members; he addressed the Council’s rece
column4: Pieder Beeli stated he previously made comments that may have been upsetting to some Council members; he addressed the Council’s recent action to increase the City’s property tax rate and the Council’s prioritization of City employees. He tried to express his concern about that prioritization and indicated he feels the City Council’s greatest concern should be for the Ogden taxpayer. He stated that many people enjoy benefits that can be afforded to them in the free market, but Ogden City uses its authority to enforce property maintenance codes against City property owners and their threats of enforcement are ‘backed up by the guns of Ogden’ and the judicial system. This means there is no longer a free enterprise system in Ogden City. Wealth is not created by the government, but by the private sector and he is very offended that the City of Ogden is in the business of operating a golf course and imposing regulations on property owners that are contrary to free enterprise. He invited any member of the Council to meet with him to discuss his concerns and he suggested they read the book entitled “Our Enemy the State”.

column3: addressed the Council’s approval of a code of conduct and Rules and Norms; she follows federal legislation on a regular
column4: Tiana Tua addressed the Council’s approval of a code of conduct and Rules and Norms; she follows federal legislation on a regular basis but is fairly new to City legislation. She has read the Rules and Norms document and did not understand what changes are being made and she asked for clarification or insight into what the language relative to Council member conduct includes.

column3: stated tonight’s work session was very informative. Additionally, she discovered a link on the City Council page of the
column4: Emily Beeli stated tonight’s work session was very informative. Additionally, she discovered a link on the City Council page of the City’s website entitled ‘citizen information packet’. She clicked on the link and found a great deal of information. She believes the link should be on the homepage of ogdencity.com because it is fantastic. She then discussed upcoming community events, including a townhall event for Senator Johnson, who represents much of Ogden City, at the Huntsville Library on September 12, and a meeting with local and State school board members at the Roy Library on September 18. These are opportunities for residents to interact with their elected officials on issues that are important to them. She would like something similar in Ogden soon so that residents can meet with City leaders about issues, such as the City’s budget and the benefits residents can expect following the recent property tax increase. Marcus Carr agreed with Mayor Nadolski about the divisive issues currently plaguing the State and the nation; however, based upon statistics and real-life events, it is necessary to combat political warfare and be better with one another. It is necessary to improve communication and agree to do what is right for all residents. Political divides are hurting children and all citizens, and he wants to work to unite everyone, even though it will never be possible to get everyone to agree about everything.

column3: expressed her gratitude to the Council members and the Mayor for their efforts to bring a new lens and perspective to th
column4: Tea Nutonga expressed her gratitude to the Council members and the Mayor for their efforts to bring a new lens and perspective to the Lester Park amenity in the City; she worked at the branch of the library near Lester Park for nearly four years and the park was a great concern to the function of the library for many reasons. She stated that she appreciated Council member Graf’s renewed focus on the park and looks forward to further discussion of improving the park. She also noted her goal is to strengthen civic engagement in Ogden, but she is very new to this area. She believes the majority of Ogden residents are uniformed and do not know how to get involved and participate in the City’s business and she asked for guidance and ideas on how an ordinary citizen can be better engaged. She thanked the Council’s staff, especially the individual who provides information on social media, for the videos they make to inform residents. She thanked Mayor Nadolski for his comments about the need for everyone to come together for the betterment of the community.

column3: stated she wished to echo the encouragement that has been offered to the Council to proceed with an improvement project
column4: Andrea Bell stated she wished to echo the encouragement that has been offered to the Council to proceed with an improvement project at Lester Park; she currently chooses to use parks that are not as close to her home as Lester Park because of the safety concerns, lack of amenities, and illegal activities occurring at the Park. She referenced an apartment project that has been approved in close proximity to Lester Park and she is hopeful that the people who occupy that complex will make a positive impact on Ogden in general. She encouraged the Council to consider the many opportunities Lester Park presents in terms of strengthening the neighborhood. Sam Barnett echoed the comments made about the need to improve Lester Park in an effort to unite the surrounding community and enhance the library and other surrounding uses.

column3: stated he wished to revisit the petition that was submitted on June 18, 2024 to add a gate to the north end of Taylor Av
column4: Blaine Richey stated he wished to revisit the petition that was submitted on June 18, 2024 to add a gate to the north end of Taylor Avenue where it meets Village Drive on the WSU campus. There was some traffic enforcement at the start of the college’s school year, but it has since waned. Residents have concerns all day and all year round, not just during the fall and winter semesters. Somehow this issue has been framed as only dealing with speed of the vehicles driving on the road. That is one issue, but the greater issue is with the volume of traffic on the residential road. The City’s spokesperson has responded to a request from a local television station and stated that if the street was blocked, certain services would be crippled. He stated that it is interesting to him that the same argument was not made when the City considered the closure of Birch Avenue; he was told the gate at the end of Birch Avenue could be opened in the case of an emergency and the same could be true for Taylor Avenue. At present, when there is an emergency in the area, emergency vehicles use County Hills Drive and Taylor Avenue rather than driving through the WSU campus. Garbage collection trucks are forced to make a turnaround at the end of Taylor Avenue to complete their route on the west side of Taylor Avenue. Adding a gate would not impact service provision any more than it did on Birch Avenue. He stated there is some misinformation regarding the proposed location of the gate; the petition asked for the gate to be located at the intersection of Taylor Avenue and Birch Avenue. He has driven the routes that motorists would be forced to take if the gate were installed and has found that commute times would only be increased by 12 seconds. Based upon these points, he is renewing his request for the gate to be installed.

column3: stated he lives near Lester Park and asked that the Council consider some very important issues before moving forward wi
column4: Brian Van Vliet stated he lives near Lester Park and asked that the Council consider some very important issues before moving forward with any plans to change the park: first is inclusivity and the fact that parks should be accessible for anyone and everyone rather than a certain type of user or demographic; preservation of the mature trees at the park; and safety as the top priority for the park and its surroundings.

column3: stated she lives at 25th Street and Monroe Boulevard and is the president of the neighborhood group called “Thrive at Le
column4: Eva Barnett stated she lives at 25th Street and Monroe Boulevard and is the president of the neighborhood group called “Thrive at Lester Park”. After Council member Graf’s proposal discussed in last week’s work session meeting for funding at Lester Park – also known as ‘molester park’ – she paid extra attention to the sirens she hears in her neighborhood. Over the course of five days, she could hear or see sirens in very close proximity to her home on seven occasions. It is the norm for her kids to see a police vehicle on her street. However, they choose to live where they do because they love the community and believe they are here to create and shape the community. They believe good people are needed in every neighborhood no matter the average income and education level. There are hundreds of invested, law-following, friendly residents in the neighborhood; for every police vehicle they see, they know that someone who cares called for their support. She has gathered and participated in events of the park regardless of who is sleeping there; she has collaborated with the City to secure funding for a crosswalk for safer accessibility to the park; and she has helped to secure more trashcans at the park to help improve cleanliness. Soccer goals have been placed at the park and sports equipment has been donated to the library for check-out for park users. She wants to teach her kids to use the closest park to them, even though there are sometimes dangerous conditions present. However, she and her neighbors are tired. They keep gathering because they are tough and invested and tonight, she is asking that the City also be invested. For the first time, she knows there are funds available for Lester Park; she has waited eight years for this day. Crime has actually worsened in her neighborhood, which is not the case in other neighborhoods in the City. It is evident that new parks, like Liberty Park on Monroe Boulevard, can help to improve and strengthen a neighborhood and she wants that within walking distance of the homes in her neighborhood. This is what she has envisioned and has been working towards; she and many others have donated time to the development of plans, and she asked that the City trusts this group and proceeds with improving Lester Park.

column3: stated he wished to offer his support for the paid parking program in downtown Ogden; people coming from out of town sho
column4: Jake Bruin stated he wished to offer his support for the paid parking program in downtown Ogden; people coming from out of town should not be surprised when being asked to pay for parking. He suggested the revenue generated by the program be used for bicycle and pedestrian improvements in Ogden’s downtown.

column3: thanked the Council for commemorating Constitution Day. She stated that she feels blessed to live in this nation and esp
column4: Linda Sanchez thanked the Council for commemorating Constitution Day. She stated that she feels blessed to live in this nation and especially in Ogden, Utah. She stated she appreciates the elected leaders of Ogden City and their preservation of freedoms in the community. She also encouraged the Council to be frugal in their use of taxpayer dollars.

column3: addressed recent public concerns surrounding trail access near and within the Mt. Ogden Golf Course. He stated he is a m
column4: Shane Storey addressed recent public concerns surrounding trail access near and within the Mt. Ogden Golf Course. He stated he is a member of the City’s trails committee and indicated he believes there are opportunities to accommodate both trail users and the golfers that use the golf course; there is an easement that predates the golf course that runs along the canal road from 23rd Street past Weber State University (WSU) and trail users wish to continue to be able to use the trail. He has sent correspondence to the Mayor and Council and thanked those that have responded to him and have met with him near the golf course to gain their own understanding of the conditions. He provided examples of signage that is used in other cities for similar situations where a trail runs near or onto a golf course and feels that something similar could be used in Ogden for the section of the trail that interacts with Mt. Ogden Golf Course.

column3: thanked the Council for recognizing Constitution Day. She also thanked many of her neighbors for their efforts to improv
column4: Teresa Bramwell thanked the Council for recognizing Constitution Day. She also thanked many of her neighbors for their efforts to improve Lester Park and the surrounding areas. She then noted her great-great-great-great grandfather, Thomas McBride, fought in the Revolutionary War and died in a very interesting way. He became a Mormon later in his life and lived in Missouri; on October 27, 1838, the Missouri Governor issued an extermination order for the Mormons. Her grandfather was the Justice of the Peace for the County he lived in, and he owned a home there. When he learned of the order, he did not believe it would impact him because of his position and his status as a homeowner and taxpayer. However, on October 30, 1838, he and 17 other Mormons in his town were killed by a militia. He was dismembered with his own farm tools and thrown down a well. The rest of the Mormons left and escaped to Utah. The next generation of his family made it to Utah and are still here today and they believe in the Constitution and in freedom.

column3: stated she has not found a single business owner on 25th Street that supports the paid parking program. She believes the
column4: Amy Wicks stated she has not found a single business owner on 25th Street that supports the paid parking program. She believes the program will have a detrimental impact on many businesses in downtown Ogden because many customers will choose to shop elsewhere. It seems the only impetus for the program is to be able to finance a parking garage for J. Fisher as part of their WonderBlock project. There must a more sensible solution and the Council has ‘missed the mark’ in rolling the program out. Staff may have told the Council that they have talked to the businesses on 25th Street, but they haven’t; public engagement is missing in this process and for the Council to implement the program without engaging the businesses or residents on their own is irresponsible. Deann Arms also discussed the paid parking program; she works on 25th Street all week and patronizes businesses there on the weekend; she rarely has trouble finding a parking spot and she hopes the Council will consider alternate solutions as suggested by Ms. Wilkerson and Ms. Wicks. Chair Richey acknowledged the concerns expressed by the public regarding the paid parking program; he invited Mayor Nadolski to respond. Mayor Nadolski thanked those who provided input regarding the paid parking program and acknowledged the frustration in the community. He took accountability for the manner in which the program is being implemented. He respects those who have made such an investment in Ogden’s downtown, and he has instructed staff to delay further implementation of the program responsive to the feedback he has received. He will not proceed further until some level of comfort can be achieved. A public engagement/outreach process will be launched to involve all stakeholders in the process before the paid parking program moves forward. He believes that there was some effort in the past to engage the business owners in the process, but it clearly was not enough, and he wishes to receive their input. He stated something similar occurred at the Ogden Airport and he will use the model he employed to engage the stakeholders there as he proceeds with further examination of the paid parking program. He will move forward in good faith, and he truly wants the businesses in downtown Ogden to succeed. Chair Richey stated there has been a great deal of investment in downtown Ogden in the recent past and it is necessary to find a solution that will benefit all stakeholders in the community. Council member Choberka agreed and thanked Mayor Nadolski for his response to those that have asked for assistance from the City. Council member White stated she supports the decision to pause implementation of the paid parking program, but also noted that what has been proposed for Ogden City is not unique and many other communities have a paid parking program, and she thinks it will be possible to move forward in a way that benefits all parties. She then acknowledged Ms. Morelli’s comments about speeding in the community and she believes that something must be done to evaluate and address the problem. There being no further business to come before the Council, COUNCIL MEMBER MYERS MOVED THE MEETING ADJOURN AT 7:37 P.M. MOTION WAS SECONDED BY COUNCIL MEMBER HYER, ALL VOTING AYE. ________________________________________ TRACY HANSEN, MMC/CRA CITY RECORDER ________________________________________ KEN RICHEY, CHAIR APPROVED: November 12, 2024

column3: stated it was great to hear from the Youth Council tonight and she stated it would be great for their events to be inclu
column4: Emily Beeli stated it was great to hear from the Youth Council tonight and she stated it would be great for their events to be included on the City’s calendar. She also discussed upcoming events that the Youth Council could benefit from attending. She thanked Mayor Nadolski and Chair Richey for agreeing to an upcoming meeting with Ogden residents to discuss the City’s annual budget process and the laws regulating taxation in the State of Utah; she is hopeful this meeting will encourage residents to get involved in the annual budget process in the future.

column3: discussed citizenship classes offered in the community; it is her opinion that someone who is not a patriot is selfish.
column4: Linda Sanchez discussed citizenship classes offered in the community; it is her opinion that someone who is not a patriot is selfish. It is everyone’s duty to defend the Constitution, assert their rights, and recognize when their or another individual’s rights are violated. She has met with some who do not truly know the rights preserved by the First Amendment. She loves and appreciates all elected leaders of the community, but feels it is her duty to remind them of their responsibilities in service to the community.

column3: discussed concerns with speeding on 29th Steet between Tyler Avenue and Waterfall Canyon; she has circulated a petition
column4: Sarge Morelli discussed concerns with speeding on 29th Steet between Tyler Avenue and Waterfall Canyon; she has circulated a petition gathering signatures of residents who share her concerns, and she has purchased two poles, and two four-way stop signs that could be installed to help improve safety in the area. Ogden City needs to address the issue in an effort to preserve safety of residents living around Ogden High School. Thaine Fisher referenced the comments made by Thomas and Weston Hardy regarding the paid parking program; one option for employees who are parking in a parking garage located a few blocks from 25th Street is to utilize the trolley system that operates on nights and weekends.

column3: stated that she has owned two businesses on 25th Street and she is deeply concerned that the City has not adequately tho
column4: Sue Wilkerson stated that she has owned two businesses on 25th Street and she is deeply concerned that the City has not adequately thought through the implementations of the paid parking program. Her employees often do not end their shift until 2:00 or 3:00 a.m. and requiring them to walk to the parking garage is ‘asking for trouble’. She stated she hears regularly that Ogden is a walkable city, but that is only true in the times of year when the weather is pleasant. There are months each year when people will avoid patronizing a business if they have to walk a distance to get there or to pay for parking. She urged the Council to rethink the program or – at a minimum – delay it until the WonderBlock project is completed. She also suggested offering two hours of free parking before a charge is imposed.

column3: shared his thoughts about the paid parking program in downtown Ogden; he has owned a business in downtown Ogden for over
column4: Thomas Hardy shared his thoughts about the paid parking program in downtown Ogden; he has owned a business in downtown Ogden for over 40 years and he is grateful for the efforts of the City to improve 25th Street, but he is concerned about the impact the paid parking program could have on businesses. He employs 16 stylists in his salon and if they and their customers are required to pay to park, they may choose to move to another salon. There are many other business owners on 25th Street that share his concerns. Weston Hardy echoed his father’s comments about the paid parking program; business owners and their employees should not be required to pay for parking, but they should also not be forced to park up to two blocks away in a parking garage in order to receive free parking. Many workers on 25th Street start their day before 5:00 a.m. or end their day after 12:00 midnight and it is unsafe for them to be walking a distance to and from their vehicles. He stated that business owners have not been engaged in the development of this program and many of them do not live in Ogden City, so they do not have the ability to vote for elected leaders in the community. He loves Ogden and wants to continue to work here, but he is very concerned about the implementation of the program. He suggested other free parking options for businesses and their employees on 25th Street and he is hopeful the Council will take these recommendations under advisement.

column3: stated she owns a business and other commercial property in Ogden; while addressing the General Plan, she would like the
column4: Annie Dunnaway stated she owns a business and other commercial property in Ogden; while addressing the General Plan, she would like the Council to take time to consider the City’s business licensing procedures. Before purchasing property, she reached out to the business licensing division to learn of her obligations and responsibilities, and it was very difficult to get clear guidance on how to make the building she purchased occupiable. It took her 10 weeks to get an answer, and this had a significant impact on the costs associated with improvements to her property. It also delayed her business production, costing her $8,600 per week in revenue since May of 2024. She stated this is the burden a low-income, single mother in Ogden is expected to carry.

column3: stated Ms. Dunnaway is not alone in her frustrations and many small business owners are facing the same issues. He then
column4: Heath Satow stated Ms. Dunnaway is not alone in her frustrations and many small business owners are facing the same issues. He then stated that he has input regarding campaign finance rules for the City, but he will save those comments until the matter is included on a future agenda. He then noted that over the course of a several year period, the Council heard from someone who repeatedly told them that the City’s General Plan was woefully outdated, and the Council seemed to ignore her; however, it is a positive move for the City to be taking action to update the General Plan now. He stated that he understands that less affordable housing means that impoverished people may be pushed out of the community, but he is not in favor of raising the average wealth of the community by pushing out the poorest residents. The City must do better. He discussed impediments to homeownership in the Ogden community and asked what the City Council is doing to work with other cities to try to collectively address housing concerns in all of Weber County.

column3: stated that housetops are needed to help support commercial development; if the number of housing units are decreased in
column4: Keith Warburton stated that housetops are needed to help support commercial development; if the number of housing units are decreased in one area, the value of that are is decreased and property rights are reduced. He addressed Vice Chair White’s comments about the need for other communities to share in the burden of providing affordable housing and noted that he built an affordable housing project in West Haven and 80 percent of the tenants in that project came from Ogden. The number one need for most communities is affordable housing and he believes that the City’s action on Ordinance 2024-28 was improper because it does not address affordable housing. The only fall back for the Council was that housing should be in the right place and it would have been best for the Council to table the ordinance and take the next 30 days to address the issues that have been raised. He feels he has been intentionally misled about the implications of the ordinance.

column3: asked the Council to consider what they are doing each day to protect the liberty of citizens. Government’s role is to p
column4: Linda Sanchez asked the Council to consider what they are doing each day to protect the liberty of citizens. Government’s role is to protect rights, not provide things. She encouraged the Mayor and Council to ask themselves what they have done to earn freedom and if they are not thinking about that every day, they are not involved. She is growing a deeper love and respect for the nation’s founding fathers. They believed they faced a death sentence for the decisions they made and the documents they created. She listened to a recent work session meeting where there was a focus on commercial and housing needs in the community; if commercial development is needed, she wondered what the City is doing to help businesses thrive. She heard during tonight’s work session that the City Council is possibly taking a trip to Germany next summer and that they may be paid $1,500 per day for that travel. She asked why tax dollars are being used in that way.

column3: stated she grew up in Ogden and has owned real estate here her entire life; she has witnessed a lot of changes in the co
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she grew up in Ogden and has owned real estate here her entire life; she has witnessed a lot of changes in the community as many single-family homes have been demolished to make way for multi family development and high-density housing. This has changed the demographic of Ogden dramatically, reducing homeownership from 70 percent of residents to below 40 percent – the lowest in the entire State of Utah. This creates a community of poverty, and it is difficult for people to invest in and do business in certain areas. Ogden needs to focus on creating housing that can be purchased by initial homeowners to create a balance in the community; this will also lead to renewed investment in the community. She added she agrees with Ms. Beverly that the City’s rules and regulations for business licensure are too stringent and result in great expense to the applicant; she suggested adjustment to these policies. Council member Hyer addressed Mr. Satow’s comments, noting that he was member of the Weber Area Council of Governments (WACOG), and members of that group voted on a County-wide Housing Master Plan, which designated individuals in each city that would work together to identify housing needs and opportunities in each community. That Plan is still in effect, but no Ogden City official has the power to require any other community to do something. Vice Chair White agreed that the Plan is still in effect and some communities are doing more than others; however, some of the smaller cities do not have the staff to work on these types of issues and projects and it will take time to make some progress. Mayor Nadolski thanked Mr. Pate for his comments and indicated a willingness to visit with him further about his concerns. He also noted he is aware of Ms. Dunnaway’s concerns and frustrations, and he is not surprised that she addressed the Council tonight. Administration has been working to address the process that caused issues for Ms. Dunnaway in her licensure application process; City staff is working to identify solutions and improve processes as well. He again addressed the housing discussion and emphasized his earlier comments about the need to plan for the future to ensure proper and viable development; he is committed to be a collaborative Mayor and will work with his counterparts in other communities to help achieve meaningful change. He then addressed Mr. Satow’s comments about campaign finance regulations and indicated he does not support doubling the maximum contribution amount, but he would like to revisit the topic and work to eliminate any unfair advantages for one candidate over another. Most cities operate in accordance with State Election Laws, but Ogden has had some variances to those laws. He would prefer to follow State Election Laws and wants to operate transparently and consistently. Finally, he addressed the paid parking program for downtown Ogden; he has scheduled a stakeholder meeting and will use an independent facilitator to conduct the meeting to provide for a clear and robust decision-making process. He will report back when he has new information. Council member Graf stated that he made a joke during the work session meeting that the Council should receive a $1,500 per day stipend during their trip to Germany. He stated he will think carefully about making such comments in the future. He noted Ogden City has a 75-year sister city relationship with Hof, Germany and it is Ogden’s turn to visit Hof, Germany; the 2020 trip was cancelled, and this was the next scheduled trip for Ogden officials. Chair Richey stated Council members will receive a stipend, similar to what employees receive when travelling for work. However, each individual Council member will pay a large portion of the travel expenses. Council member Blair referenced Ms. Dunnaway’s comments and stated he is hopeful that Administration will make meaningful changes to processes that have such an impact on many business owners in the community. Vice Chair White stated she attended a concert in Salt Lake City over the weekend and ate at a restaurant while there; she parked in the designated area for the restaurant and paid $20 for 1.5 hours. She feels a new slogan could be created to encourage people to stop eating in Salt Lake and come to Ogden and pay just $2 per hour for parking. There being no further business to come before the Council, COUNCIL MEMBER HYER MOVED THE MEETING

column3: stated he attended the Weber County Commission meeting this morning and there was an agreement for the purchase of right
column4: Travis Pate stated he attended the Weber County Commission meeting this morning and there was an agreement for the purchase of right-of-way along 2550 South for corridor preservation using Weber Area Council of Governments (WACOG) funds. If these funds are being used for corridor preservation, they should also be used for historical preservation, housing, and other aspects in the General Plan that have not been addressed. He asked if the Council is familiar with and has read the General Plan or other guiding documents that they rely upon when making vital decisions for the community. There is a significant lack of citizen participation in many processes in the community, specifically related to historical preservation.

column3: addressed the discussions during tonight’s work session; the Land Exchange Agreement (LEA) involving Lotus is a positive
column4: Heath Satow addressed the discussions during tonight’s work session; the Land Exchange Agreement (LEA) involving Lotus is a positive improvement for the City, but he is disappointed there is a rush to proceed to approval of the transaction even when there is some hesitation on the part of the Council. He asked who performed the appraisal for the land involved in that LEA. In 2018, a Standard-Examiner article included comments from the City’s former Community and Economic Development Director regarding the plans to relocate the Beehive Storage facility to the property. He asked if there has been any movement on that matter since 2018. He then noted that he has emailed the Mayor and Council in recent weeks regarding a push to increase donation limits for those seeking election to a public office; in his research he found that higher donation limits only benefit the incumbent in a race and not the general welfare of a community. He added that the developer that is party to the Lotus LEA donated the maximum amount to the Mayor’s campaign last year, though he is not saying there is a direct connection between that donation and the current proposal. However, large donations do erode trust in government, and he hopes the Council will maintain current donation limits. Laura Lewis referenced the transfer of property near 18th Street and Washington Boulevard near the river bridge; the appraisal amount cited for the property was near $200,000. Several months ago, she asked who performed the appraisal and if more than one appraisal was performed; if the property were appraised when the building was still located on it, it would have been much higher. She feels the appraised value is low. She understands the City took payment of $250,000 for the property but used $190,000 to purchased Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT) property. She stated the City’s appraisal process is undefined and vague and she is interested in a documented process the City must follow for future transactions. She then noted that about a year ago there was a lot of discussion about the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center of Northern Utah and there was a push to get them to move out of a City-owned building they occupied near Dinosaur Park. As of today, nothing has happened with that property, and she asked why nothing is moving forward. She inquired as to plans and a timeline for the reuse of the property. Most of the public felt the non-profit entity should have been allowed to stay in the building. Adam Jensen also expressed concern about the speed at which the Lotus LEA is moving; he asked why there is a rush and asked that the matter we slowed down. He encouraged the Council to solicit input from the public regarding the matter. Scott Jensen echoed Adam Jensen’s comments and asked that the City respond to the concerns from the public. He stated ever since a decision was made to proceed with the LEA with Lotus, his business has dealt with harassment from the City. He has received notices of violations, though no violation exists. His business license was reclassified without his knowledge and when he approached the Business Licensing Division of the City, they could not tell him why. They also do not have the history of his business license past 2019. The reclassification has resulted in the code enforcement actions because City staff believes that he cannot use his property as he is using it due to the change in his business license. He stated this activity is highly coincidental given the acceleration of the Lotus development and he asked if the City is helping the developer to push him out of his property. He has tried to make a deal for his property in the past and the City has never entertained them; now, even if he wanted to move, he could not. Chair Richey asked Mr. Jensen the name if his business, to which Mr. Jensen answered Creative Welding.

column3: stated she also shares concerns about the Lotus project. A few months ago, she attempted to research the properties alon
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she also shares concerns about the Lotus project. A few months ago, she attempted to research the properties along the river and could not find anything owned by a company called Lotus; she found some properties were owned by a company that has not paid their property taxes, LLC renewals fees, and they seem to be defunct. They purchased the property from Ogden City in 2014 for a very low price, something close to $2.6 million. She would like to know the history of the property, how Lotus acquired it, and the price they acquired it for because she would like to learn how much it has appreciated, and the exact number of years Lotus has owned it. Her concern about them trading for property on Wall Avenue is that they will build apartment units rather than housing for sale. She referenced the rezone of the rezone of the property near 2nd Street and Wall Avenue near the Fenway Fields project and stated the public was initially informed that the units built there would be for sale rather than rent, but the applicant tonight expressed his intent to maintain ownership of the properties and rent the units. If Ogden City is going to have any say in development of property, they must be sure that the units being built are for sale so that young people can invest in their community and ensure their own future wealth. She stated that she is also concerned about building housing for homeless people in the community and she would like to know the developer that is pursuing that type of development and if they have some sort of a land swap agreement with the City to give them access to cheap property, but rights to other property where they can build high priced units. Chair Richey stated the majority of the questions raised during the public comment period were Administrative in nature and he asked Chief Administrative Officer Brown to respond. Ms. Brown stated that relative to the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center matter, she is willing to perform research and report back to the Council in a future work session. She offered the same response for the questions regarding the Lotus LEA. Chair Richey addressed the public and stated the Council shares some of the concerns that were communicated tonight; the Council is trying to gather additional information and will evaluate it before taking action on the current proposals.

column3: expressed frustration with the 20th Street construction project between Brinker Avenue and Harrison Boulevard, particula
column4: Andrea Baltazar expressed frustration with the 20th Street construction project between Brinker Avenue and Harrison Boulevard, particularly regarding a general lack of communication from the City to residents. She came home recently to find the curb in front of her home painted red, including the driveway approach to her home. All homes on half of the block she lives on experienced the same. This has created a lack of trust, and she is concerned about the lack of transparency on the City’s part. Residents were told one thing, but something entirely different happened and it is now too late for residents to intervene. She invited the Mayor and Council to drive by her home and consider if they would have approved the project if they had known this would be the outcome. She and her neighbors have been told that the project is now done, and nothing can be done to change it. The project managers refused to meet with her and her neighbors, and she is deeply disappointed. This situation impacts her property value, and she does not have sufficient parking space for herself and her guests. She asked that the Council do something to resolve the problem that has been created. Marie Hogge echoed Ms. Baltazar’s comments; she also lives on 20th Street and is very negatively impacted by the situation Ms. Baltazar addressed.

column3: stated he also lives on 20th Street, and he echoed Ms. Baltazar’s comments; he implored the Mayor and Council to visit h
column4: Brody Smith stated he also lives on 20th Street, and he echoed Ms. Baltazar’s comments; he implored the Mayor and Council to visit his home to understand the true impact this project is having on the daily lives of the citizens living on that block of 20th Street.

column3: thanked Council member Graf for responding to his email regarding the ongoing discussion of campaign donation limits. He
column4: Heath Satow thanked Council member Graf for responding to his email regarding the ongoing discussion of campaign donation limits. He thought tonight’s discussion about the matter was great, but he still believes the campaign donation maximums should be reduced as Ogden’s limits are much higher than surrounding cities in Utah and in other states. Higher limits allow for more influence from donors. He would also suggest a cap on anonymous contributions as this would help to avoid large sums being hidden as untraceable donations listed as $50 anonymous donations. He added he also appreciated hearing a discussion about the status of the Brown Ice Cream building, but he wished to remind everyone that the building sold at such a low price without going through a public bidding process in order to remedy the blight quickly. The original deadline for occupancy was November of 2023, but after a one-year extension the deadline has passed. He hopes this expedience will be used to strengthen future contracts similar to this one and to protect Ogden taxpayers. Teresa Bramwell referenced the transfer of land on 18th Street and Wall Avenue involving the Lotus company; she raised concerns about the land adjacent to this property last week. The land she is concerned about is on Grant Avenue between the Ogden River and 20th Street and it was sold to another developer by Ogden City. Ther are many lots on the property, which was formerly home to single family homes. She has researched the property ownership records and found that the taxes for these properties have not been paid for three years and the LLC that owns them is not active with the State of Utah. This is a dire situation, and the properties could be sold at a tax sale in the near future. It is her understanding that the City wants this area to become a park, and her suggestion would be to use eminent domain to take other land from Lotus to use as the City sees fit, especially if Lotus is not willing to develop as the City desires. The City is doing a huge favor for Lotus in the form of land trades and financial incentives, and these are benefits that no other property owner in the City receives. She then concluded that she opposes the homeless housing project planned for Madison Avenue and 23rd Street; Ogden City does not need more homeless people in the neighborhood, especially since Lester Park is being improved so that it is safer for children.

column3: stated he owns property in Ogden and over the past three to five years he has found difficulty in getting aid from law e
column4: James Edwards stated he owns property in Ogden and over the past three to five years he has found difficulty in getting aid from law enforcement or the Mayor. He has reached out to the Mayor’s assistant and asked to schedule a meeting with him, but that request has been refused. The Mayor has sent officers as a way to communicate with him; Officer Jared Nelson visited his home two years ago when he was renovating the home that was formerly used as a drug house. He has invested over $150,000 into the community and planned to invest even more, but he was treated very disrespectfully by Officer Nelson while he was responding to a wildfire situation near his property. The lack of response and professionalism from the City has left him with no other option than to take matters into his own hands multiple times, but he has been called a criminal as a result for protecting his neighborhood and himself. He is not a violent person, but acts of violence have been committed against him and threats made as well. However, the City’s police officers do not agree and have not supported him.

column3: addressed the ongoing issues with the 20th Street construction project; arbitrarily painting the curb for an entire bloc
column4: Andrea Baltazar addressed the ongoing issues with the 20th Street construction project; arbitrarily painting the curb for an entire block to prevent on-street parking without explicitly informing residents is wrong. Saying information is available about the project is not the same as clearly informing residents who would be impacted; homeowners should not have to sift through public documents to learn that their parking areas will be taken away. Good intentions on paper do not always translate to practical solutions and taking a simple drive down 20th Street will help anyone understand that the changes are not reasonable. The street is and will always be a high traffic road and adding a bike lane has increased safety concerns for bicyclists; she asked what biker will use a bike lane to cross Harrison Boulevard on 20th Steet. She encouraged all Council members to visit 20th Street for themselves; residents will be impacted due to the neighborhood being less valuable, less welcoming, and less accessible and she wondered how this can be defined as progress. The elimination of on-street parking on 20th Street will create a ripple effect throughout adjacent neighborhoods. She asked the City to review the red curbed zone along the street and consider other solutions. She also asked the Council and Administration to rethink how the City is communicating with residents regarding projects that will impact them.

column3: stated it means a lot that Wayne Niederhauser attended tonight’s meeting to discuss the proposal from the Weber Housing
column4: Heath Satow stated it means a lot that Wayne Niederhauser attended tonight’s meeting to discuss the proposal from the Weber Housing Authority (WHA). He stated he appreciates the Council’s action to table the proposed resolution to take more time to study the matter. He noted that it has been his own experience that communities that do not deal with housing for vulnerable populations end up in worse situations. Ogden City has the ability to be a leader in terms of supporting permanent housing options for individuals in need in the community.

column3: stated she was not able to listen to tonight’s work session, but she did notice an agenda item dealing with increases to
column4: Linda Sanchez stated she was not able to listen to tonight’s work session, but she did notice an agenda item dealing with increases to fees charged by the Police Department; she is not in favor of any increases given that the City Council recently voted to increase the Police Department budget and salaries for employees of that Department while residents have not been experiencing similar wage increases. The public will be paying these fees, and she is not in favor of any increases. She then noted she appreciates the Council will take time to listen to the issues surrounding the WHA housing proposal and she encouraged Council members to reach out to their constituents to hear their thoughts on the matter; she feels a win-win solution can be achieved and the City can work towards breaking the cycle of homelessness.

column3: stated Christmas Village is phenomenal again this year. He then stated his family had a challenging week and their spiri
column4: Travis Pate stated Christmas Village is phenomenal again this year. He then stated his family had a challenging week and their spirits were lifted by the lighting of the Christmas Village; he appreciates the love and strength it has provided to him and his family. He stated that the same thing can be done for the chronically homeless in the community and he looks forward to continued discussion of the issue with the Council. Chair Richey advised Ms. Sanchez to listen to the recording of tonight’s work session meeting; the proposal regarding Police fees includes elimination of seven different fees and one or two additional fees intended to cover the cost of work that is being done in the Department. He then deferred to City Administration to respond to Ms. Baltazar’s comments about 20 th Street. Chief Administrative Officer Brown stated the City utilized a third-party consultant to perform public outreach regarding the 20th Street construction project, but she acknowledged that outreach can always be better. City Administration has discussed the shortfalls with the consultant and will identify opportunities for improving that process in the future. The road was designed with safety in mind and there are a few complex issues on 20th Street, but City Administration has asked the Engineering Division to revisit the project to determine if there are other options for the bike lane and red curbing. No immediate answers are available at this time, but Administration will report back to the Council and the public in the future. Chair Richey asked if all red paint on the street is new or if there were previously some pockets of red paint. Ms. Brown stated there were some sections of red paint, though it was very worn and old. Council member Myers stated he met with Ms. Baltazar and other residents on 20th Street, and he sympathizes with their concerns; the residences on that street have single-car driveways and there is not adequate on-site parking for the people living there. He thanked Administration for taking the time to review the project.

column3: thanked the Board for discussing the average median income (AMI) in the area as they were considering action on the acqu
column4: Heath Satow thanked the Board for discussing the average median income (AMI) in the area as they were considering action on the acquisition of the Forest Service Building (FSB). He then stated that he still has concerns about the risks the City has taken with the WonderBlock project but hopes the project will ultimately be successful. He reiterated his support for the selection of the Giv Group for the redevelopment of the FSB and stated he is happy to have the project move forward.

column3: stated he believes the Board is ruminating on the tradeoffs of the free market and private enterprise versus government
column4: Pieder Beeli stated he believes the Board is ruminating on the tradeoffs of the free market and private enterprise versus government aspirations. He believes the vote to purchase the FSB is being subsidized by the taxpayer and he feels that is immoral. elected officials do not have the right to impose sentimentality on taxpayers; taxpayers will not spend the time to investigate all actions that are being taken by elected officials that will ultimately impact their wallets. He concluded that a good government is a small government. It is immoral for any government to push away the free market when there is a solution in the free market. Executive Director comments Executive Director Nadolski again addressed the action taken to authorize the acquisition of the Forest Service Building (FSB); one positive aspect of the project is that it will result in the creation of an environment where people will have access to opportunity to make themselves better. He wants to be part of a community that prioritizes those types of projects. He then acknowledged the Parks and Recreation Division of the City for partnering with the Government Employees Health Association to provide swim lessons to youth in Ogden that cannot afford to pay for this activity. Board member Comments There were no Board member comments. There being no further business to come before the Agency, BOARD MEMBER HYER MOVED THE MEETING

column3: addressed the Council’s work session tonight and discussion of the completion of a townhome project on 24th Street by J.
column4: Heath Satow addressed the Council’s work session tonight and discussion of the completion of a townhome project on 24th Street by J. Fisher Company. He is concerned about the subsidy the developer received from the City, which guaranteed them an 11 percent profit on the project. The Council’s vote on the project last year was split, and today the Council learned that the homes in the project area were sold above market prices and those that had been presented to the City when the agreement was initially approved. He asked if the development contract included a provision for profit sharing between the developer and the City. He requested the City prepare a publicly available report detailing the profit margins for the project and how much of that profit will be returned to the City. The City needs to examine past projects and patterns and make contractual adjustments for future project in order to ensure the City realizes the best possible return on investment.

column3: stated she attended a meeting regarding the 24th Street interchange project with Intersate-15 but found that most of the
column4: Laura Lewis stated she attended a meeting regarding the 24th Street interchange project with Intersate-15 but found that most of the discussion was about development of West Ogden near the interchange. She would like to know when there will be more discussion about the actual interchange project. She added that she learned of plans for a roundabout in the middle of West Ogden, but it goes nowhere. However, it will eliminate four homes, and she would like an explanation of that element of the project. She then referenced the Council’s discussion of the paid parking program during tonight’s work session. She asked if residents planning to attend future City Council meetings will be charged to park downtown. She concluded by addressing the relocation of the Northern Utah Wildlife Rehabilitation Center and asked for an update on the status of building and the property that was vacated.

column3: addressed the 20th Street construction project; the residents were sold on a nice, wider road but residents are now deal
column4: Marie Hogge addressed the 20th Street construction project; the residents were sold on a nice, wider road but residents are now dealing with negative consequences associated with elimination of their on-street parking spots in front of their homes. She does not have adequate space for off-street parking for more than one vehicle on her property. The residents were not properly informed of this element of the project. She cannot find another street throughout the City that is wide as 20th Street where on- street parking has been eliminated. She invited the Council to visit her street and see what residents are experiencing and then get to work to fix the problem.

column3: commented on plans for a homeless shelter on 23rd Street and Madison avenue; there were many people in attendance at the
column4: Teresa Bramwell commented on plans for a homeless shelter on 23rd Street and Madison avenue; there were many people in attendance at the December 3 meeting to comment on their support for the project, but many of those people stand to benefit financially due to the project. She has learned that ‘the wool has been pulled over her eyes’ for the last several years as she has contacted so many different people throughout the City and State due to her being the victim of crime nearly every day. She has had an idea of where the criminals were coming from, and she attempted to find out who was responsible for putting them there. She approached Weber Housing Authority and asked if they were housing people in her neighborhood and they claimed they were not. She also scheduled an appointment with Mr. Niederhauser regarding the homeless population in the community and he seemed to be completely baffled as to why there could be crime occurring in her neighborhood. No one admitted that homeless people were being housed in her neighborhood, but she has since discovered that is not true and the Housing Authority now wants to put more homeless people in her neighborhood. She asked if this would add to the crime problem in her neighborhood. Chair Richey noted that the Council will meet in a work session on January 7 to research and discuss the Weber Housing Authority project further, with possible action on their proposal scheduled for January 14. He also addressed Ms. Lewis’s question about the Wildlife Rehabilitation Center; the building they formerly occupied was demolished within two weeks of them vacating the building. Walls are being constructed for the new hatchery building and that project will continue to move forward. He deferred to the Mayor to address Ms. Lewis’s question regarding the paid parking program. Council member Choberka referenced Ms. Lewis’s questions about the meeting to discuss the 24th Street interchange project; the project is being managed by the Utah Department of Transportation (UDOT) and any feedback they received during that meeting will be used to inform the design process of the project. She added there will be another meeting in January to discuss the project further. Many residents indicated they were not supportive of the roundabout element of the project. Chair Richey then addressed Mr. Satow’s comments about the 24th Street townhome project; he noted that Administration did not report the sales prices of those homes, but they did discuss prices for units in other project areas. He stated that the Council can ask for sales prices for the 24th Street project specifically. He then addressed Ms. Hogge’s comments about the 20th Street project and noted Administration has assigned the Engineering Division to research the matter and provide a detailed report back to the Council.

column3: shared her personal experience with homelessness and noted she is dismayed by the opinion that people have about disable
column4: Adrienne Zubler shared her personal experience with homelessness and noted she is dismayed by the opinion that people have about disabled and vulnerable individuals. She learned the hard way that anyone can experience homelessness; there are not enough homes for the population in the community, and not enough shelter space for homeless individuals. Sean Bishop echoed Mr. Barragan’s suggestion that the Council advertise when they will be discussing the WHA matter again and when they plan to make a decision. He reminded everyone that the people that will live in the housing project are already Ogden residents, but this project will give them a place to stay off the streets. People want to live in the housing project and will not abuse that privilege. This is a unique opportunity to Ogden City, and he asked the Council to make the humane decision. He concluded by reading a text from someone he loves that is unhoused. He stated he lives in the neighborhood where the subject property is located, and he supports the housing project in his backyard.

column3: shared her personal story of temporary disability and the importance of supporting individuals with disabilities. She al
column4: Angel Castillo shared her personal story of temporary disability and the importance of supporting individuals with disabilities. She also urged the Council to consider the long-term benefits of the WHA permanent housing project. The proposed project is not a detox facility but is a housing project for people with many different types of disabilities that limits them from fully functioning them on their own and need some level of support. There are 25 people in need of this housing, and they may ultimately end up homeless, which costs the City much more money than this project would.

column3: thanked the Council for their consideration of the WHA project this evening, but echoed Mr. Satow’s comments about the n
column4: Chris Barragan thanked the Council for their consideration of the WHA project this evening, but echoed Mr. Satow’s comments about the need to make a quick decision. He suggested that everyone consider whether they would be willing to sleep outdoors until a decision is made on the housing project so that they understand the true impact their inaction is having on people in the community. He stated that the WHA project is well thought out and the Council needs to move in the direction of uplifting and caring for the people in the community. He asked that the Council communicate the date that they plan to make a decision on the proposal.

column3: stated that she has lived in the neighborhood surrounding the proposed site of the WHA project for over a decade and she
column4: Debra Barrington stated that she has lived in the neighborhood surrounding the proposed site of the WHA project for over a decade and she does have some concerns about some conditions in the neighborhood that may make it difficult for those struggling with drug and alcohol abuse issues to stay away from their vices. She has personally been approached by people attempting to sell her drugs. She knows there are many people struggling with disabilities and other vulnerabilities, and she wants everyone to have access to housing and other opportunities, but if the housing project is located in the wrong place where there is already high crime and drug use, it may make impact the success of the individuals who would be living in the project. She appreciates the Council’s time and willingness to take a step back and evaluate the project from a very high level.

column3: stated that one of the previous speakers discussed her encounters with crime but noted that there are many individuals i
column4: George Barragan stated that one of the previous speakers discussed her encounters with crime but noted that there are many individuals in the community that are suffering much more than her. Additionally, that individual has indicated she lives in Salt Lake City but also owns a home in Ogden, but there are many residents who do not have one place to stay. He called for consideration of the needs of those without homes, emphasizing the importance of providing resources and support.

column3: reiterated his support for the Weber Housing Authority (WHA) permanent housing project and asked that the Mayor carefull
column4: Heath Satow reiterated his support for the Weber Housing Authority (WHA) permanent housing project and asked that the Mayor carefully consider his position on the matter. He stated that he feels the project is great and the way that the people who will live in the housing units have been spoken about is unacceptable. He emphasized the need for immediate solutions in terms of housing for homeless individuals.

column3: questioned the Council's familiarity with the WHA housing program and called for clear communication and informed discus
column4: Jackie Kent questioned the Council's familiarity with the WHA housing program and called for clear communication and informed discussions on those programs as well as the current proposal. She stated that she found documents regarding the WHA programs that answered many of the questions that the Council was asking during the last work session meeting and that left her wondering whether they had read the meeting materials prior to attending the work session.

column3: raised concerns regarding access to resources for Ogden residents, including transportation and medical services. It is
column4: Jordan Scott raised concerns regarding access to resources for Ogden residents, including transportation and medical services. It is important to locate a permanent housing project in an area where residents can easily access the services they need.

column3: emphasized the importance of addressing the fears some in the community have regarding homelessness; she also emphasized
column4: Lucy Barragan emphasized the importance of addressing the fears some in the community have regarding homelessness; she also emphasized the need for the City to provide support to those in need.

column3: stated he does not question the compassion of the City Council and Mayor, but he wished to remind them that there are hu
column4: Robert Hunter stated he does not question the compassion of the City Council and Mayor, but he wished to remind them that there are hundreds of thousands of dollars on the line and there is a very important timeline that must be followed for this project. He feels the Council has heard a great deal of misinformation and hopes that will be resolved to give the Council the ability to make a quick decision on this proposal.

column3: expressed disappointment in the Council's antagonism towards community members supporting the housing project and called
column4: Shelby Hornbeck expressed disappointment in the Council's antagonism towards community members supporting the housing project and called for education on the matters of homelessness and the lack of housing, as well as community engagement. She stated that the desire to put the City’s homelessness issue out of sight and mind is not a valid reason to reject the WHA project.

column3: shared her positive experiences with affordable housing and the impact access to a two-bed room unit in Ogden had on her
column4: Stacy Bernal shared her positive experiences with affordable housing and the impact access to a two-bed room unit in Ogden had on her quality of life. She urged the Council to approve the project and support vulnerable residents in the community.

column3: addressed the Council regarding their rules and norms as well as their meeting procedures. The published rules document
column4: Taylor Knuth addressed the Council regarding their rules and norms as well as their meeting procedures. The published rules document indicates that members of the public addressing the Council during public comment will have up to three minutes to provide comment. He criticized the Council for not following their own rules and procedures. He then asked Mayor Nadolski to clarify the statements that include the word ‘we’; he asked Mayor Nadolski to defined who ‘we’ is. He also referenced past actions and discussions in regard to housing in Ogden; in 2019 the Council was presented with a housing needs assessment for central Ogden. This assessment was written by a renowned economist and expert in housing and the assessment has been ignored by the Council. He stressed the importance of trusting subject matter experts on topics such as homelessness and housing needs; there is a local Homeless Coordinating Council, which holds public meetings, and no member of the Council nor the Mayor has engaged with that Council in the past 15 years. He concluded the Ogden Housing Authority (OHA) has already approved the WHA housing project. Linda Sanchez announced an upcoming Ogden City Town Hall meeting with Mayor Nadolski and Chair Richey on January 20, 2025, at 6:00 p.m. at the main library on Jefferson Avenue. This will be an open discussion format, and the public will have the ability to ask questions of the participants.

column3: shared her experiences with crime and the need for solutions to prevent individuals from repeatedly being a crime victim
column4: Teresa Bramwell shared her experiences with crime and the need for solutions to prevent individuals from repeatedly being a crime victim; she urged the Council to focus on practical solutions for the entire community.

column3: stated that he does not feel the Council has ‘missed the mark’ on the issue of the WHA project; he discussed past missed
column4: Travis Pate stated that he does not feel the Council has ‘missed the mark’ on the issue of the WHA project; he discussed past missed opportunities in the community and encouraged the Council and Administration to continue to work as a team and involve the public as much as possible in their efforts.

column3: commented on his participation in the Citizens Police Academy, which was incredible. He then thanked Fire Chie Mathieu f
column4: Heath Satow commented on his participation in the Citizens Police Academy, which was incredible. He then thanked Fire Chie Mathieu for the information he provided tonight regarding preparedness efforts of the City and Council member Graf for raising questions about fireworks in Ogden’s foothills. He then stated his main point is a serious concern about a pattern he has seen in recent comments from the Mayor and Council members dealing with removal of transparency; he does not support that sentiment and other in the public share his concerns. Public debate is a cornerstone of American democracy; it is not about persuading elected officials but showing others that they are not alone in their concerns. More than one person sharing the same opinion is not redundant, but powerful and he encouraged the Mayor and Council to listen and allow that discourse to occur in public rather than in private.

column3: shared concerns about development on 18th Street; apartments are consuming commercial properties and existing commercial
column4: Scott Jensen shared concerns about development on 18th Street; apartments are consuming commercial properties and existing commercial businesses feel they are being forced out of the community. He also referenced the devastating fire in Ogden’s downtown recently and expressed his concern about proper protection of existing structures in the Ogden community. He stated there is limited commercial space in Ogden and the space that is available is overpriced. Many business owners are fed up and feel they do not have a voice about the future of downtown Ogden. He asked the Council to consider if there are too many apartments due to recent increases in the development of that type of project. Council member Hyer addressed Ms. Bramwell’s comments and noted that the Good Landlord Program has changed significantly; he believes the limitations on who landlords can rent to may have been removed from the program. However, those that complete the program get a discount on their business license. He does not disagree that some landlords may not be following the guidelines of the Good Landlord Program. Chair Richey referenced Mr. Pate’s suggestion to advertise previous discussions of an item; he referred him to the hyperlinks on each Council meeting agenda, which point to a staff report regarding the item and provide all dates that the issue was previously discussed by the Council or any advisory body. He also addressed Mr. Jensen’s comments about development on 18th Street and noted that the Council adopted an ordinance last year that prevents commercial property from being used for apartment projects. He also referred Mr. Jensen to the recording of tonight’s work session meeting, during which Fire Chief Mathieu discussed efforts to mitigate fire risks and respond to fires in the community. Council member Graf also referenced Mr. Jensen’s comments and acknowledged an action taken by the Council to shift the zoning of a property on Grant Avenue from commercial to residential; he noted that given the character of the area surrounding that property, the applicant and Planning staff felt that shift was appropriate, though it would allow a multi-family development in a commercial area.

column3: thanked outgoing Chair Richey for his service in the role of Chair. She then shared her personal experiences with the Ci
column4: Teresa Bramwell thanked outgoing Chair Richey for his service in the role of Chair. She then shared her personal experiences with the City’s Good Landlord Program; she felt the program was removing some responsibilities from the Police Department and placing them on individual landlords and that was difficult. However, most recently, she has noticed that landlords in her area are not complying with the same rules she agreed to follow after graduating from the Good Landlord Program. She wondered where the disconnect is and she feels that the permanent housing project being pursued by the Weber Housing Authority also ‘flies in the face’ of the Good Landlord Program.

column3: thanked Chair Richey and Vice Chair White for their leadership in 2024 and noted he looks forward to the leadership of V
column4: Travis Pate thanked Chair Richey and Vice Chair White for their leadership in 2024 and noted he looks forward to the leadership of Vice Chair White and Council member Hyer in 2025. He also encouraged the entire Council to listen to their constituents and respond to them when they are active in discussions of public issues. He concluded by recommending that the Council share as much information about the timing of discussions that will eventually end with a public hearing; if an issue scheduled for public hearing has also been discussed in work sessions or by other advisory bodies, it would be helpful if the public had access to an advertisement that included the dates of those previous discussions.

column3: stated she has opened several businesses in Ogden and would like to open more, but one of her concerns about being a res
column4: Debra Darrington stated she has opened several businesses in Ogden and would like to open more, but one of her concerns about being a resident of Ogden is that she does not have access to a local store that offers quality clothing for men, women, and children. Most residents are shopping in Riverdale because the retail offers in Ogden are lacking. She opened a pizza restaurant in Ogden, and it was shut down two weeks after it opened because the counter was 38 inches high rather than 36 and it was not compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). These are the types of barriers that are keeping people from investing in Ogden. She relayed a story of another potential business that was never started because the City did not have a mechanism to allow them to sell soap out of a cart. The City needs to pave the way for improving the economic base of Ogden other than beer and tattoos.

column3: thanked Council members Choberka and Graf for the great questions they asked during tonight’s work session meeting; he a
column4: Heath Satow thanked Council members Choberka and Graf for the great questions they asked during tonight’s work session meeting; he agreed that some processes and projects do not feel transparent at this time. He is grateful there was a discussion about the housing data that is used to populate certain reports and agreements coming from the Ogden-Clearfield area, rather than just Ogden. This is important because it impacts housing inventory and the average income of the population of that area. Executive Director Comments Executive Director Nadolski stated he is not sure what else to do or how much harder to try to be transparent; he is tired of the claims of a lack of transparency and is not sure how much more he can do. He asked for suggestions for improving transparency. He then addressed Ms. Darrington’s comments about her pizza restaurant and stated that is the first he has heard of that issue; there is work underway to perform a ‘deep-dive’ of the Business Services division to try to address those types of issues. He stated that he truly believes the City staff ‘hits the mark’ 95 percent of the time but only hears about the few instances that do not go perfectly and that is what he is committed to fixing and changing. Board member comments There were no Board member comments. There being no further business to come before the Agency, BOARD MEMBER RICHEY MOVED THE MEETING

column3: stated that in a prior Council meeting, there was an action prohibiting multi-family development on a main road or on a
column4: Linda Sanchez stated that in a prior Council meeting, there was an action prohibiting multi-family development on a main road or on a commercial property; however, there is an action on tonight’s City Council agenda to allow just that. She then stated her 90-year old mother-in-law lives with her currently and she wanted to share what she currently sees in the City. She noticed there are way too many stores and other buildings that are not open to the public or are boarded up and vacant. These buildings are targets for homelessness and could result in fires or other damage.

column3: stated he recently met with a member of City staff to express the dynamic of his neighborhood and his ideas about its fu
column4: Travis Pate stated he recently met with a member of City staff to express the dynamic of his neighborhood and his ideas about its future; many residents are investing in the area, and it is important to recognize that investment and pursue redevelopment projects that will be the catalyst for continued private investment in the community. He is opposed to wiping out historic buildings and properties in favor of new development.

column3: stated the people of Ogden City are so lucky to have so much to celebrate; tonight, the Council and the public celebrate
column4: Anne Dunaway stated the people of Ogden City are so lucky to have so much to celebrate; tonight, the Council and the public celebrated Ms. Blaisdell’s commitment to the community and that seemed like a perfect gateway for her to hone in on her purpose for attending tonight’s meeting. Ogden City’s pattern of ignorance over community and social development project components leads to eventual lambasting of projects like the WHA project.
