That established pattern of broadsiding community development projects leads to those projects being sunk into the murky waters of the City’s economic opportunities. She urged the City to take a long look at its obligations to let community development leaders do the leading, and for government to stick to what it does best, which is to protect the community’s ability in those pursuits.

column3: with PATH Forward Utah echoed Mr. Thompson’s comments and talked about the tools available to the public from the Utah O
column4: Jaime Wadman with PATH Forward Utah echoed Mr. Thompson’s comments and talked about the tools available to the public from the Utah Office of the State Treasurer. She thanked the Council for their attention and for consideration of adopting the proposed resolution.

column4: Karece Thompson stated he is from the Utah Office of the State Treasurer; he encouraged the Council to consider passing a resolution recognizing April as Financial Literacy Awareness Month. column3: commented on the update provided by Mayor Nadolski regarding the WHA project; he asked if the plan truly is for Ogden Ci
column4: Kevin Lundell commented on the update provided by Mayor Nadolski regarding the WHA project; he asked if the plan truly is for Ogden City to spend millions of dollars of taxpayer money to purchase the WHA property simply to prevent disabled homeless individuals from being housed in permanent supportive housing that the neighborhood actually supports. He stated that it does not seem like a very good plan. City Administration has had an entire month since the last time the topic was discussed to submit a thorough report to the Council, but basically no information was provided. The information that was presented could have easily been sent to the Council in an email so that further action could have been taken tonight. He referenced the funding sources for the project and the possibility of securing additional funding during the 2025 Legislative Session, noting that there are a record number of legislative bills pending and he is doubtful that additional funding bills will be considered this year. He stated that none of the citizens of Ogden know the Council’s position on this project because they have never actually voted on it. He concluded by referencing comments made in a recent meeting regarding the City’s Good Landlord Program and the fact that the City has a policy that a landlord will receive a discount on their business license if they do not rent to anyone with a drug offense. He stated he wants to know if that is indeed a policy of the City. During that same meeting, Council member Hyer and Mayor Nadolski commented that the WHA project flies in the face of the Good Landlord program based on housing those with a past drug offense. He stated he wants to know if the City truly wants to prohibit the housing of recovering addicts either privately or publicly. He has family members who have been impacted by the opioid crisis in the United States; it is not an option to express opposition to opioids but then abandon those that have fallen victim to the drug. A great deal of time and effort has been poured into the WHA project and the residents of the neighborhood surrounding the property deserves to know where the Council stands. Heath Satow also expressed disappointment about the lack of information regarding the WHA project, as well as a lack of leadership on the matter. He noted Mayor Nadolski’s presentation felt like a ‘kid showing up to do a book report’ and asking those he is presenting to to read the book on their own and share their thoughts. He is disappointed about the delay in the project and the lack of communication between the Mayor and Council. He stated the City government has failed on this issue, and it is time to step aside and let the WHA move forward. Brooke Barragan also referenced the information provided tonight and in the Council packet regarding the WHA project; in the January 14 meeting, the Mayor indicated Administrative staff had made some progress in their research of the project but needed additional time. Again, on January 21, Administration agreed to provide a progress report on efforts to find an alternative site for the permanent supportive housing project. The public came to tonight’s meeting expecting a progress report and they got nothing. She cannot believe the public has waited this long for the Mayor to not say anything at all. She asked why the offers that have been made to buy the property from WHA were not discussed tonight in the progress report. She stated that the City is failing; inaction is an action, and the City is actively leaving disabled homeless people out in the cold. Chair White asked Mayor Nadolski to respond to Ms. Morielli’s comments about the need for a 4-way sign on Polk Avenue. Mayor Nadolski stated he and the Public Services Director are aware of the matter and will continue discussions with her after this meeting. Chair White then acknowledged there are a number of old water lines throughout the City and there are capital improvement plan (CIP) projects in place to eventually address those issues. Council member Richey stated that he also discussed Ms. Lewis’s concerns with Public Services Director Anderson who informed him that the City is currently not drawing any water from its wells; all water being supplied comes from the treatment plant and due to temperatures and mineral components, the water may look a bit different, but it is safe and drinkable. Chair White then asked the representatives of the Utah Office of the State Treasurer to submit a sample resolution or proclamation for the Council to consider at a future meeting. Council member Graf stated he also supports action to bring awareness of personal finances to the public. Council member Richey agreed. Chair White then thanked everyone who commented on the WHA project; she acknowledged the concern that the project has been underway for some time but noted that the details of the project were only made available to the Council in recent months. She stated that the Council heard tonight from those in support of the project, but there are just as many people on the other side of the issue that have expressed their concerns and opposition to the project and the Council must listen to both sides and weigh what is best for the community.

column3: discussed water supply lines; her street is constantly dealing with dirty water coming out of their lines and a main lin
column4: Laura Lewis discussed water supply lines; her street is constantly dealing with dirty water coming out of their lines and a main line broke earlier this week and that resulted in the water in her home looking like mud. She spoke with workers in the area and asked them to flush the lines, which they agreed to do, but there is still wastewater in her water lines and that is building up in her water heater, which will cause it to fail prematurely. She inquired as to the City’s plans for replacing older water main lines in the City. Much is being done for new construction, but those that have lived in the City for a long time deserve the same quality of water as new residents and businesses.

column3: stated the timeline that the Mayor and Council discussed earlier this evening regarding the Weber Housing Authority (WHA
column4: Robert Hunter stated the timeline that the Mayor and Council discussed earlier this evening regarding the Weber Housing Authority (WHA) permanent housing project was very concerning; there is not enough time to wait, and WHA is at risk of losing grant funding that was awarded for this project. The Ogden City Council’s job is to enhance the economic viability of Ogden, and the goal of the WHA is to find housing for the homeless population in the community as expeditiously as possible. They will move forward with that goal as quickly as they can.

column3: thanked the Mayor and Council for their service. She then addressed conditions on 29th Street and Polk Avenue; two weeks
column4: Sarge Morielli thanked the Mayor and Council for their service. She then addressed conditions on 29th Street and Polk Avenue; two weeks ago, there was a major accident at an intersection involving two vehicles. There is not a 4-way stop sign at the intersection and the vehicles landed in front yards of residences on Polk Avenue. Conditions are very dangerous, and a 4-way stop is needed. She recommended two 4-way stop signs within two blocks of every school in the community to improve safety for residents, students, and motorists. She has already purchased two stop signs and poles and needs permission to have them installed. Many residents are very upset and need to see something done. She also suggested reducing speed limits on roads throughout the community; there are too many people that do not care about the safety of others. She concluded by urging the City to increase wages and benefits for Police and Fire Department employees in the City.

column4: Laura Lewis addressed the condition of the water in her home; it was very dirty last week but is much clearer this week and she is very happy about that. She wished to compliment City staff on how they handled what was a very difficult situation. Every person she talked to was very helpful and patient. She then referenced the discussion during tonight’s work session regarding wellbeing in the community; her feelings align closely with the findings of the survey, especially pertaining to the loss of green space. She is also concerned about building heights for development projects and that new buildings could block views and shield sunlight. She then discussed the property along the Ogden River that was formerly considered to be green belt in nature; it was agricultural in nature, but that has shifted and commercial development and high-density residential is now allowed along the River. People walking along the trail next to the River used to feel connected to nature, and now they feel like they are walking down a tunnel between all the apartment buildings. Those types of things need to be carefully thought of when projects are being planned.

column4: Steve Jones reported the “Save the Union Station” group has resumed their activities and is holding weekly meetings; their current focus is on how the Union Station impacts 25th Street, downtown Ogden, and the community as a whole and he wanted to be sure the Council and Administration know they are invited to attend those meetings. Some of the ideas that have been proposed as part of the revitalization of the Union Station campus are great, but others are concerning to the group, and he advised the City to continue to research and review all options and provide opportunities for public involvement in the planning stages of the project.

column4: Teresa Bramwell raised some issues that are happening in Ogden as a result of some of the changes that have been made in the federal government that have resulted in the loss of federal jobs. She has seen many rumors about the potential for the federal buildings located in Ogden to be vacated and even sold. Ogden, for many decades, has relied upon federal jobs and money and she has watched the community deteriorate in that same time. She would love for Ogden to focus more on small businesses, or anything that is not being funded by the federal government. If the City government focuses more on its own people, the City will improve.

column3: stated she sent the Council an email and she wished to read the email for the record of tonight’s meeting: “Dear Ogden C
column4: Deanne Chaston stated she sent the Council an email and she wished to read the email for the record of tonight’s meeting: “Dear Ogden City Councilmembers, I am one of the owners of Ogden Brinker Apartments, a 10-unit town home complex near 36th and Harrison Boulevard in the C-2 zone. In December of 2024, we were concerned when Adam & Eve moved into the building that historically housed Family Dollar. At first, we were sure that Ogden City wouldn't let such a business locate within yards of a residential complex and a day care facility. The business is located just 20 yards from the front doorstep of where minor children reside. A preliminary search of their business informed us what kind of a company this was moving in next door. According to their own website at adameve.com, they are "the leading sex toy company in the USA. For more than 50 years, we have built up a reputation as a trusted and reliable adult toy store that takes pleasure & privacy seriously. When you want to shop erotic toys, we have it all" (See website Image 1 below). However, according to Adam & Eve's November 2024 business license application with Ogden City, they are merely a "lingerie clothing retail store." Despite its reputation, a search of Ogden City Municipal Code showed us that Ogden City does NOT consider Adam & Eve a Sexually Oriented Business (SOB) as long as they keep their "sex toys" in an area less than 15% of total floor space and make that area not accessible to minors. This business has already had adverse secondary effects on my business and may contribute to declining property values. Incidentally, soon after Adam & Eve moved in, the day care moved out. Their space is still up for lease, and the landowners have likely suffered from loss of income since December. Interestingly enough, when they marketed this space for lease, their marketing materials indicated they were adjacent to Family Dollar, not Adam & Eve. We ourselves have already had tenants leaving and breaking their leases because of their proximity to this business. Despite how much room these sex toys take up in the store, I would guess that a majority of its sales and revenue come from selling sex toys. Their website has very little reference to "lingerie," and it is clear the reputation they are building their business on is sex toys. However, their business license application didn't even mention sex toys or, more specifically, "instruments, devices or paraphernalia which are designated for use in connection with 'specified sexual activities."' I am also concerned about just how much an average pedestrian, including minors, can see merely by passing in front of this store. (See Images 2-9, all of which were taken from outside the store.) In early communication with City Staff, Adam & Eve assured that their mannequins would be "fully clothed" and "nondescript, meaning there are not any anatomically correct body parts displayed." I will let you decide from the provided images (Images 8-9) if this is the case. I am here to ask Ogden City to change its definition of a Sexually Oriented Business in order to protect land and business owners such as myself. If Adam & Eve were considered an SOB, it would not be allowed in the C-2 zone or near other residential uses. I understand that the City must allow SOBs; however, zoning and appropriate land use planning directs the proper location for such businesses. I ask you to seriously consider if this situation as presently constituted is appropriate. If it were you, would you want to live within 20 yards of such an establishment? I understand that changing the definition of an SOB now likely won't affect my own situation, but I encourage Ogden City to take a close look at other options it may have. Other cities have SOB ordinances that reference a percentage of business income or inventory, not just square footage of retail space. Both Brian Head and Hurricane City. Utah, point to things other than the percentage of floor space when defining an SOB. In those cities, an SOB is defined as "a commercial establishment which has a significant or substantial portion of its stock-in-trade or derives a significant or substantial portion of its revenues" from the sale of "instruments, devices, or paraphernalia which are designed for use or marketed primarily for stimulation of human genital organs." The owner and business license holder of Ogden's Adam & Eve business lives in Idaho, so a review of SOB codes in that state may be appropriate. Rupert, Idaho, has a definition of an SOB that is similar to Hurricane and Brian Head. Closer to home, neighboring Washington Terrace and Marriott-Slaterville's SOB ordinance doesn't refer to floor space, business income, or inventory. There, an SOB is merely a commercial establishment that, as one of its principal business purposes, offers for sale "instruments, devices, or paraphernalia that are designed for use in connection with 'specified sexual activities."' Farr West, Roy. and Uintah City don't refer to floor space, but both mention inventory, revenue, and even advertising. I assume that "principal business purpose" is a matter of interpretation, but who should be doing that interpretation: the applicant or the City? A review of Syracuse's SOB ordinance offers a definition for "principal business" as generating 20 percent or more of the business's income, or accounting for 20 percent or more of inventory. Their code also references "exterior portions of sexually oriented businesses" that are worth noting, specifying what can be "visible from a point outside the establishment." On an unrelated topic, we are concerned with Adam & Eve's exterior lighting that directly affects our tenants' second-story bedroom windows. We had been accustomed to Family Dollar turning off their lights after business hours, but Adam & Eve's remain on at all hours of the day and night. Simply shading their lights to only shine directly downward would help. We believe their lighting is in violation of Ogden City Code 15-13-8: "LIGHTING: A. Exterior Lighting: No spotlight or floodlight shall be installed in any way which will permit the direct rays of such light to penetrate into any residential zone or onto any property used for residential purpose." However, our attempts to mitigate the issue by communicating with store management and Ogden City Code Enforcement have done nothing to change the situation. In conclusion, I would like Ogden City to preserve and promote the health, safety, welfare, peace, quiet, and quality of life of its residents, including my tenants. I hope you agree that we do not want the City to become a place known for locating what should be considered Sexually Oriented Businesses next to residents' homes and day care businesses. This situation already has negatively affected Ogden's reputation, and I hope you can help put a halt to it in the future. If I can be of further assistance, or if you have any questions, please don't hesitate to contact me. Deanne Chaston ogdenbrinkerapts@gmail.com”

column4: Ty Chaston stated he is the other owner of the Ogden Brinker Apartments, and he echoed the comments made by Ms. Chaston. He also has concerns about snow removal practices at the property as well as light pollution that is disturbing his children in the evening hours. He advised the Council to drive by he property and look at the items that are on display in their window; he asked them to consider if they would want the business as their neighbor or as the neighbor of their young children or grandchildren. Recent reconfiguration of the roadways in the area has led to increased traffic on the private lane in front of his home. He has been cited for trying to slow traffic or keeping the snowplow from pushing snow onto his private property. He asked for help from the City because he no longer knows what to do.

column4: Deborah Darrington expressed gratitude for the support received from the Your Community Connection (YCC). She also suggested the City create a program where residents and non-residents can set up a payment plan for memberships at the Marshall N. White Community Center. She concluded by referencing the City’s recent acquisition of property at 2325 Madison Avenue, noting she feels the City’s revitalization of the property would help to benefit the entire neighborhood. column3: spoke in support of the proposed zone change that was reviewed by the Council during tonight’s work session meeting; the
column4: Heath Satow spoke in support of the proposed zone change that was reviewed by the Council during tonight’s work session meeting; the property owner is a longstanding community member whose businesses have strengthened the community. It is a challenging property, but since it is located within walking distance of the heart of downtown Ogden, the proposed use is appropriate as it aligns with the City’s goal of increasing housing density in the area. He would prefer a smaller, self-funded project like this one versus a taxpayer subsidized mega-project completed by outside developers. The City needs to stop getting in the way of good, local developers. He concluded by noting he would like to know the status of the paid parking program for downtown Ogden and whether the City is considering abandoning the system altogether or how it plans to address the significant debt obligation associated with building parking structures as part of the WonderBlock project.

column4: Laura Lewis shared her concerns about the police presence near her neighbor's house, which was one of the individuals referenced by Mr. English as being improperly targeted by the Police Department. She noted she listened to the Mayor’s podcast recently and appreciated the detail with which he discussed some issues the community is facing. She also referenced tonight’s work session discussion regarding fees for the new Marshall N. White facility, noting she feels the proposed fees are too high.

column4: Laura Lewis stated she also understands the concerns expressed this evening, but indicated the City has a large trail network with many other locations to run, walk, or hike; the Mount Ogden Golf Course was not designed to co-exist with an active trail and she supports the City’s decision to close the section of trail that is the subject of tonight’s discussion. She does not think the Mayor did anything wrong by putting the safety of the community as a top priority.

column4: Maurice Barnes expressed an understanding of the City’s decision to close the section of the trail that crosses the golf course; he has worked as a marshal on the course and is an avid golfer and communicated that at the point where trail users cross the course, it is very difficult to see golfers on the tee box and he is concerned about the safety of the trail users; safety is not just an excuse the City is using, but it is a reality. He understands the community’s desire to continue to use the trail, but safety is a real concern.

column4: Oliver Del Carlo stated he also works at the Mount Ogden Golf Course, and he echoed the concerns about safety of trail users that were expressed by Mr. Barnes.

column3: encouraged the City to consider the creation of a communications department; many problems arise in the City due to inad
column4: Travis Pate encouraged the City to consider the creation of a communications department; many problems arise in the City due to inadequate communication about important issues in the community. He also stated that there must be other options for trail users to cross the Mount Ogden Golf Course and the argument that the trail connection has been used for many years and decades is not valid when facing safety issues such as those that are present under the current conditions.

column3: thanked Council Assistant Executive Director Symes for his budget presentation, and he thanked the Council for their eff
column4: Heath Satow thanked Council Assistant Executive Director Symes for his budget presentation, and he thanked the Council for their efforts to provide additional opportunities for public involvement in the budget process. Walt English referenced the City’s Police Department; he is shocked that the City is spending $118 million on the Department. There is an organization called PoliceScorecard.Org and he recommended the Council visit that site to see information they have published about the Department. Citizens have a 97 percent change or greater of being arrested in Ogden than in any other City in Ogden and a 95 percent chance of being shot to death. He is currently dealing with legal proceedings because Ogden City Police officers manhandled him, pulled his pants down and exposed his garments, and falsely arrested him. He is very angry that the City’s police officers are untrained and believe they can do whatever they want. He stated he is a former law enforcement officer, having served as an investigator in the military. The City’s Police Department has a lack of transparency and is rated one of the worst Departments in the State of Utah. The Council is responsible for this problem. He noted he submitted a public records request on May 2 and has not received a reply. He also submitted a complaint over eight months ago and has not received a response. He also referenced recent discussions about the closure of trails through one of the City’s golf courses and noted the City will need to reopen the trails based upon a prescriptive easement described in Utah State Code. He stated he will be suing the City for $40 million.

column3: thanked the City for the help he has received from the City relating to concerns he has had due to poor maintenance of t
column4: Ty Chaston thanked the City for the help he has received from the City relating to concerns he has had due to poor maintenance of the property abutting his, as well as an ongoing construction project that has negatively impacted his property. He is concerned about the lack of sufficient dumpsters on the abutting property, or that the dumpsters that are there are not secured and locked to prevent the homeless people from accessing them and removing items, or from the wind blowing debris onto his property. Many people are dumping trash on the property and many of the items placed in the trash by the sexually oriented business are disturbing to residents and children that stumble across it. He is not sure how the business was approved so close to residential properties, and he encouraged the City to amend its land use code to prevent something similar from happening in the future.

column3: stated that while he disagrees with Ms. Lewis’s position on the golf course, he appreciates her taking the time and effo
column4: Heath Satow stated that while he disagrees with Ms. Lewis’s position on the golf course, he appreciates her taking the time and effort to visit the golf course and speak with people who are familiar with the situation. He then stated that he appreciates Council member Graf’s comments about fireworks and urging caution relative to fire conditions in the coming months. Chair White referenced Mr. Bauman’s comments and stated that the explanation that Mr. Sorensen offered earlier in the meeting regarding the ‘haircut’ line item was an accurate explanation; the rec center is actually the Solomon Center in the Central Business District (CBD), and not the Marshall White Center as she believes Mr. Bauman is assuming.

column3: expressed concerns regarding housing issues in the community; a property two doors to the north of her was for sale rece
column4: Debra Darrington expressed concerns regarding housing issues in the community; a property two doors to the north of her was for sale recently and it was a great opportunity, but she did not purchase the home. She now has regrets because the person who did purchase the property is not a good landlord and does not respond to maintenance requests from tenants, does not perform background checks for residents, and is not a resident of the community and is not aware of the problems occurring at his property. She has made significant investment in the community and her experience when trying to move through the City’s development application process has been that there is ‘a lot of unnecessary red tape’; many other property owners are not following the City’s permitting process, so they likely do not have the same experience as her, but they are conducting business improperly in the community. Many are out-of-state investors, and they have turned the properties into low-income housing that is not well maintained. She asked if the City can require property developers to go through a Good Landlord Program or a specific background check; it is important to ‘get a grasp’ on the community and the people developing here. Theresa Bramwell also discussed housing issues in Ogden; she has experienced similar ‘red tape’, but it appears that big developers are able to bypass those regulations. She attended the auto show over the weekend, and it was great; at the event she learned of a project at the corner of 25th Street and Quincy Avenue, which is less than a block from her own property. It looks like a nice property, so she visited the website for the project to learn about project. The website advertises rental opportunities, but she recalled attending the meetings during which that project was discussed and there were statements made that the income levels for residents who would be living in the project would be 80 percent of the average median income (AMI); this would be tenants that are paying their own rent rather than receiving a subsidy. This would be great for her neighborhood, but that is not what is happening. The website advertises units available to those with an income of 60 percent of AMI. Rent rates are the same price regardless of the size of the unit and every unit can have two pets. There are 176 units in the building, which means there can be 352 dogs at Quincy Avenue and 25th Street. Her concern is that no one will be able to rent the property at the prices listed and the developer will be in a situation where they are ‘going broke’ because they cannot secure tenants and the project will immediately be converted to a Section 8 housing development. This is very concerning to her. Holly, no last name given, stated she lives in Section 8 housing, and she does not appreciate Ms. Bramwell’s comments; she is a functional adult, but she has struggled in her life. She discussed some of the issues she has encountered in the community and encouraged the City Council to work to address the problems that many residents are facing at the Lantern House property. Another resident, no name given, also spoke of her experience at Lantern House; she has experienced seizures while staying at the facility but does not receive the help she needs during these seizure events. People are treated horribly at Lantern House, so much so that they choose to sleep on the street rather than be housed at the facility. Norene Jordan also discussed the problems she has encountered at Lantern House; she stayed at the facility for four months and was treated badly. Her medicine was thrown away and the facility does not have the appropriate equipment to keep and store needed medicines. She asked the Council to explore options for assisting the segment of the population that relies on resources at the Lantern House.

column3: stated that she moved her family to Ogden from rural Syracuse in 2013; unfortunately, all her adult children have moved
column4: Debra Darrington stated that she moved her family to Ogden from rural Syracuse in 2013; unfortunately, all her adult children have moved away from Ogden, and this has caused her to think of some of the things that she was most excited about when she moved to Ogden, but which have never come to fruition in the community. She asked the Council and Administration to be mindful of the residents who have planted roots in Ogden and to not lose sight of the things that have brought them here. This includes promises for improvements to Lester Park, specifically. Mayor’s Comments Mayor Nadolski thanked Administration staff for their efforts to develop the Fiscal Year 2025-2026 budget and Council staff and the Council members for the sincerity with which they review and attempt to understand the budget. The budget process this year was very collaborative and dynamic, and he is grateful for that and the benefits it creates for the residents. He then stated he has been receiving emails about the status of public lands in Utah; Washington, D.C. lobbyists have been engaged to help understand what the Federal Government is proposing in terms of preservation of public lands, and he is happy to report back when he has more clear information. He then echoed Mr. Pate’s appreciation for “My Hometown Ogden” and also agreed with his concerns about impacts business owners in downtown Ogden are feeling as a result of new development in the community. He also thanked Ms. Darrington for her poignant comments and expressed his love for the community as well. He then offered his feelings about immigration enforcement activities that have been spotlighted recently; he summarized the role of Ogden City and the Ogden City Police Department in immigration enforcement, emphasizing that the City does not enforce federal immigration laws. Criminal laws, however, will be enforced and anyone committing crimes in Ogden will face enforcement from the Ogden Police Department, which has his full support. Ogden City is not a sanctuary city for criminals; it is a constitutional city with zero tolerance for crimes against residents. He will not politicize the City’s Police Department and will not ask them to enforce laws they do not have the legal authority to enforce.

column3: stated she is passionate about the historic preservation of Ogden City; she asked each Council member to ask themselves
column4: Debra Darrington stated she is passionate about the historic preservation of Ogden City; she asked each Council member to ask themselves if they truly are about the history of the community. She has encountered some problems related to her efforts to preserve a home she owns in Ogden. She has no business plan whatsoever related to the Leroy Eccles Home. She previously restored the Chantilly Mansion in Ogden City, and she learned a great deal about the history of the original owner of that home. She recently discovered that Leroy Eccles was the president of First National Bank of Ogden, and she has chosen to preserve his home. She discussed the issues she has encountered as she has begun the preservation project and has been required to submit to the Landmarks Commission for their approval of her work. She started the application process and has found that she will be required to spend a considerable amount of money and time before she is even allowed to start actually working on the home. Chair White asked Mayor Nadolski to respond to Mr. Humphries’ question. Mayor Nadolski stated that David Sawyer, Assistant Executive Director of Community and Economic Development is overseeing the community engagement element of the downtown parking program, and he advised Mr. Humphries to meet with Mr. Sawyer after the meeting. He stated Administration is working hard to empower businesses and affected entities to provide input and he wants to hear Mr. Humphries’ input. Mayor Nadolski then referenced Mr. Pate’s comments and noted there are a few individuals that will represent Ogden as part of the America 250 celebration; he will be sending a transmittal to the City Council regarding the efforts currently underway. He concluded that he would look into Ms. Darrington’s concerns and respond to her.

column3: reported he is an artist from Gallery 25, LLC, and once a month the LLC members meet to discuss relevant matters; each m
column4: Nick Humphries reported he is an artist from Gallery 25, LLC, and once a month the LLC members meet to discuss relevant matters; each month, there are more and more concerns about parking conditions on 25th Street and surrounding areas and the potential for the City to impose parking regulations and a paid parking program. He is concerned that a parking program may put the gallery out of business and the artists and other LLC members have not been given the opportunity to provide input to the City regarding the matter. He has heard a survey has been conducted, but no member of the LLC has been provided with a survey to complete. Adjoining business owners have the same concerns.

column3: stated he attended the kickoff event for the America’s 250 celebration; this is a significant milestone for the nation,
column4: Travis Pate stated he attended the kickoff event for the America’s 250 celebration; this is a significant milestone for the nation, and he is excited about the emphasis on the history of the Country, State and each City in the State. He encouraged the City Council to participate in the celebration as there are some tremendous opportunities for shining a spotlight on Ogden’s history.

column3: stated the process to access the Landmarks Commission is very difficult; she and her architect are not sure how detailed
column4: Debra Darrington stated the process to access the Landmarks Commission is very difficult; she and her architect are not sure how detailed project drawings must be in order to appear before the Commission. She has spent upwards of $8,000 on her design but is still not sure if it is sufficient to receive approval from the Commission; however, she cannot afford to wait another month in the event that the documents are rejected or tabled. She asked for a liaison that could help answer those questions. She then stated she loves preserving historic buildings, but some can be very costly and time-consuming as has been proven with the buildings at the old Ogden Stockyards. She relayed her own personal experiences in trying to install landscaping on a historic site and suggested that it would be helpful for the City to waive some permits or costs associated with restoring historic properties. Travis Pate echoed Ms. Darrington’s comments about the importance of providing some flexibility relative to historic preservation; additionally, the timeline for the Landmarks Commission to consider a historic project is too strict and includes several conflicts for applicants and the City. He asked that the Council carefully consider this matter and help to streamline the process and remove conflicts of interest.

column3: inquired as to the status of the renewable energy program the City was pursuing with other cities and Rocky Mountain Pow
column4: Laura Lewis inquired as to the status of the renewable energy program the City was pursuing with other cities and Rocky Mountain Power. She added she visited the City’s water treatment plant recently and was very impressed with the operations and the competency of the staff. She also appreciates the Green Waste facility and the services offered there; the staff is very helpful, and the facility is very clean. She noted she likes the idea of improving Lester Park as discussed during tonight’s work session meeting. The City should focus more on public amenities that are free of charge rather than economic development that will financially burden residents. Quality of life is very important for residents. She asked if the pickleball courts at Lester Park will be lit. She addressed the idea of amending the Rules and Norms to address the amount of time a person can speak during a public meeting; she suggested development of guidelines that will ensure impartiality. She concluded she recently saw a marketing campaign where Ogden City was referred to as a ‘spillover option’ for the Park City market; real estate in Park City is very expensive and Ogden was listed as a more affordable locale for those in the market to purchase a home. This is concerning to her because she is worried about current residents being able to afford homes.

column3: stated she was out of town recently and heard of a fire on the City’s bench; she was reminded of Council member Graf’s c
column4: Linda Sanchez stated she was out of town recently and heard of a fire on the City’s bench; she was reminded of Council member Graf’s comments in a recent meeting about the risk of fire in that area and what the City should be doing to protect residents. She extended her thoughts and prayers to the family that lost their home in the fire and encouraged the City to revisit the issue of fire restrictions. She relayed her own personal experience of living in a town that shot fireworks from an area where the embers would fall into a lake as an effort to mitigate risk of fire. She noted that she appreciates and agrees with Ms. Lewis’s comments.

column3: addressed looming United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in the community. He is present to advoc
column4: Malik Dayo addressed looming United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in the community. He is present to advocate for those at risk of being impacted by the raids; residents fear family separation, arrest, or being forced to leave their homes. This does not only address undocumented immigrants, but documented United States citizens as well given that documented citizens have been arrested in mass raids. He is not asking the City to protect criminals or those in the country illegally, but he is asking for leadership that provides clarity. City Administration should stand against federal overreach and the use of United States military force in Ogden City. He encouraged vocal opposition from the elected leaders of the community to communicate that Ogden prioritizes its residents over federal actions. He asked the City to take immediate action to implementing a “know your rights” campaign; this would include distributing multi-lingual information material giving people information about legal support. He stated ‘the City’s hands are not tied’ and last week he respectfully addressed a point made by the Mayor suggesting that if any rights are violated during federal enforcement, legal action can be taken afterward. While he agrees that people can seek justice after an incident, he believes it is more important to prevent rights violations from occurring in the first place. He suggested proactive measures by the Mayor and City Council. Heath Satow echoed Mr. Dayo’s comments and asked for clarity regarding the role of the Ogden Police Department in the ICE raids or response to those activities. He also addressed the consideration of amending the Council Rules and Norms specific to public comment; this would only be imposed in events when many people are in attendance, but that is problematic because most often when there is a large turnout at a meeting, most of the people in attendance have never attended a meeting and the fact that they are present signals that an issue is very important to them. Limiting their ability to provide input is concerning and will only discourage people from participating in the future. He concluded by addressing the proposed plans for the Lester Park improvements and suggested a different color scheme that is not as bold/bright.

column3: stated that there was previously a police substation in the area of 25th Street and Monroe Boulevard and there was much
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated that there was previously a police substation in the area of 25th Street and Monroe Boulevard and there was much less crime in the area than there is today; it has been well proven that there is an enormous amount of crime in that area and a restored police presence in that area would be helpful. She then noted she recently contacted a commercial real estate agent that claims to be the best in the area, controlling 40 percent of the commercial market in the community. She presented to him the options that she feels she has for her property, but he stated he feels those options are bad and the best option is to demolish the building and sit on vacant land for many years before it is acquired by someone else. She does not agree and thinks that is a terrible idea; she is looking for different uses or tenants for her property. Chair White stated the Council and Council staff will attempt to answer some of the questions asked during the public comment period; she addressed the question about the renewable energy program with Rocky Mountain Power and noted it is her understanding that project has stalled. Council Executive Director Eller-Smith reported Rocky Mountain Power has issued a request for proposals (RFP) seeking a developer to build a solar farm in the State to support the program. There are also some proceedings before the Public Services Commission that should conclude before the end of the year; this includes negotiations of cost to participate in the program. Chair White thanked residents for their input regarding fireworks restrictions and noted the City continues to work with State lawmakers on the issue as local governments have restricted authority in decisions related to fireworks. She thanked Ms. Darrington and Mr. Pate for their input regarding the processes that involve the Landmarks Commission and asked that City Administration take those matters under advisement. She thanked Ms. Bramwell for her input and noted she has forwarded an email from Ms. Bramwell regarding the use of her property on to the Community and Economic Development Department. She commented on the input regarding ICE raids and referred the public to the input provided by Police Chief Sube during the July 1, 2025, work session meeting. She appreciated the suggestion from Mr. Dayo regarding a ‘know your rights’ campaign. She concluded that the real estate campaign referring to Ogden as a ‘spillover option’ did not come from the City, but from a private realtor.

column3: stated he is the founder and owner of Apogee Worx, an aerospace defense firm near the Ogden Airport; he shared his insig
column4: Brian Janroy stated he is the founder and owner of Apogee Worx, an aerospace defense firm near the Ogden Airport; he shared his insights regarding the efforts underway to amend the City’s ordinance governing the Ogden Airport. Three and a half years ago he moved from the Ogden Airport and almost left Ogden City entirely due to the climate at the installation; what has happened over the past year has been very collaborative and positive and there are a lot of very smart people working on improving the Airport. He asked the Council to keep an open mind as they navigate the proposed amendments to the Airport regulations as it is his belief that the consultants and group of stakeholders working on that issue are very qualified, competent, and impressive. He noted he would like to move back onto the Airport in the next several years and build a 150,000 square foot facility there and he needs leases at a minimum standard to make that happen.

column3: addressed the ordinance regulating landscape requirements for new single-family dwellings, expressing concerns from a ho
column4: Jilian Snyder addressed the ordinance regulating landscape requirements for new single-family dwellings, expressing concerns from a homeowner's perspective and the impact the new standards could have on daily life. She thanked Council member Graf for his comments about the matter and stated that she agrees with him for the most part; she understands that the

column3: discussed the importance of addressing climate change and the need for scientific climate research and weather services.
column4: Robert Hunter discussed the importance of addressing climate change and the need for scientific climate research and weather services. The Council is the voice of the Ogden community and should be promoting research into the causes of climate change.

column3: expressed concerns about homelessness and blight in Ogden and noted he is seeking ways to get involved in community impr
column4: Gregory Allen expressed concerns about homelessness and blight in Ogden and noted he is seeking ways to get involved in community improvement. He finds Ogden to be a challenging place to live for a reformed felon or homeless individual; these people cannot even go to a City park and use restroom facilities, and he does not believe that is fair. He is planning to meet with Council member Choberka following tonight’s meeting to discuss his concerns further.

column3: addressed the proposed amendments to Title 8 regarding the Ogden Airport; he is concerned about ceding more authority to
column4: Heath Satow addressed the proposed amendments to Title 8 regarding the Ogden Airport; he is concerned about ceding more authority to the Mayor’s Office and noted that the implications of the proposed amendments have not been discussed enough. He encouraged the Council to work to strength the role of advisory bodies and promote transparency for those groups. The Council must retain meaningful oversight and urged them to discuss the proposal with outside legal counsel. He also expressed concern about the changes to the Rules and Norms document regarding limitations on public input during public meetings. Based on the changes, the Council will only be reducing the amount of time spent on public comments when there are a lot of people at a Council meeting. This is the worst time to impose restrictions because people rarely show up to Council meetings and if they do show up, it means that they care deeply about the issue they are intending to hear or address. It is very important to give these people their full three minutes. If the Council cuts public input time short, residents will feel disregarded. He urged the Council to reconsider this change.

column3: questioned the Ogden Bend land exchange from 2011 and the City's support for Lotus Development. As an Ogden City taxpaye
column4: Kerry Wayne questioned the Ogden Bend land exchange from 2011 and the City's support for Lotus Development. As an Ogden City taxpayer, he cannot understand the City’s willingness to trade land with developers that only benefit the developer and not the City. He suggested that the City’s efforts be redirected to programs that can benefit the youth of Ogden. No-cost leases are not good for Ogden City. Laura Lewis recognized a City employee in the Parks Department for the assistance he offered to her recently. She then criticized the City Council’s handling of public comment time; she asked them to reconsider their action to approve amendments to the Council Rules and Norms document and called for consistency and fairness in public meeting procedures.

column3: voiced concerns about a recent fire on 18th Street; communication between the Fire Department and property owners/reside
column4: Scott Jensen voiced concerns about a recent fire on 18th Street; communication between the Fire Department and property owners/residents living near the property involved in the fire was lacking and this is very concerning to him. He has notified the City of safety issues with the property long before the fire occurred and those issues were not addressed. He is very disappointed; he lost a structure and several pieces of equipment due to the fire, and he is now forced to put his life on hold to address those matters. He asked the Council to explore options for addressing these types of situations in the future.

column3: shared a recent experience with homeless individuals on her property; she was disappointed by the response from 911 Disp
column4: Teresa Bramwell shared a recent experience with homeless individuals on her property; she was disappointed by the response from 911 Dispatch, who dispatched the Fire Department and paramedics. After the paramedics were able to rouse the individuals, they quickly jumped up and left her porch and started walking towards her. They quickly left her property, at which time she called the Police Department again and this time she received a response. However, she is unsure whether the individuals were taken into custody. She felt the Police should have come to her house upon receiving the first call and the initial response was not useful. President Trump signed an Executive Order on July 21 called “Ending Crime and Disorder on America’s Streets” and that order deals with homeless people, drug use, and mental illness and she feels Ogden could use an increased focus on those matters. Chair White referred to the comments made regarding the amendments to the Rules and Norms document and noted the Council has studied this issue at length. Council member Graf agreed and stated he is sympathetic to the concerns that were expressed; the Rules and Norms document is a living document that can be changed in the future if deemed necessary. He also noted that the changes do not prohibit residents from reaching out to Council members directly and he noted he is willing to speak to any resident of the City on the telephone with no time limits. He also answers every email he receives, and he does not feel the public’s access to elected officials is limited. Chair White then addressed Mr. Jensen’s comments about the 18th Street Fire and noted that Chief Slater addressed the Council tonight during their work session regarding the Fire Department’s efforts to address the issue. She also commented on the Police Department’s response to Ms. Bramwell’s situation and deferred to Mayor Nadolski to discuss dispatch protocols. Council member Choberka stated she wished to address Ms. Bramwell’s comments as well; she is assuming that the reason the Fire Department was dispatched is that the dispatcher believed the homeless individuals were in danger or needed medical support. She apologized that Ms. Bramwell had a negative interaction, but feels the response was appropriate. Council member Blair addressed Ms. Lewis’ and Mr. Satow’s comments about public comment rules; he acknowledged that it takes a great deal of courage for residents to attend and speak at a Council meeting, and he does want to hear from them. He believes that the changes to the Rules and Norms are appropriate, and the changes will only be exercised when warranted; the change gives the Chair another tool to effectively manage public meetings of the Council, and he does not believe that it will be abused. Mayor Nadolski stated that Council member Choberka’s assessment of the response to Ms. Bramwell’s call for service was accurate. Chair White recognized Kirk Nigro from Rocky Mountain Power (RMP) and asked him to provide comments regarding a recent increase in power outages in the community. Mr. Nigro stated RMP has implemented enhanced safety settings for areas with elevated fire risks; if there is a trip in an area that is at risk of a fire, the system will shut down to avoid sparking a wildfire. Safety has been prioritized above reliability of power. He knows this can be frustrating and the protocol will be evaluated regularly; efforts are also underway to clear areas where there is an increased risk of wildfire. He apologized that the situation has the potential to impact residences and businesses, but safety is a top priority for RMP. The Council engaged in brief discussion with Mr. Nigro regarding the causes of specific power outages and anything the City can do to assist RMP in their efforts. The Council requested increased and improved communication between RMP and their power customers in the event of an outage. Mr. Nigro briefly summarized the current notification methods employed by RMP and expressed a willingness to participate in public workshops to discuss these issues directly with the public. Council members then discussed options for ensuring backup power generation in the event of a power outage.

column3: stated she can understand the position of those who want the Taylor Canyon property to be purchased by the City and pres
column4: Teresa Bramwell stated she can understand the position of those who want the Taylor Canyon property to be purchased by the City and preserved as open space; however, she has her own personal experience with Lester Park, which the City has promised to develop and improve for several years, but that project has not been a priority and there has been a significant increase in crime and homelessness in the park. The people who have spoken tonight have even talked about the disrepair of the two existing parks in their neighborhood. She noted Ogden City is lacking single family homes and taxpayers and she feels the Taylor Canyon property could be used for that purpose and perhaps it could include a pocket park. There is currently way too much high-density housing in downtown Ogden, especially below Harrison Boulevard, and it is time for the people who live above Harrison Boulevard to take their fair share.

column3: stated he has reviewed the planning documents for the West Ogden improvements associated with the 24th Street interchang
column4: Heath Satow stated he has reviewed the planning documents for the West Ogden improvements associated with the 24th Street interchange project and he feels the signage welcoming people to Ogden is very underwhelming; it is something that is worth putting a lot more thought into and he asked the Mayor to take that under advisement. He stated that the old welcome sign on the south end of Harrison Boulevard has not been replaced, and he asked for a timeframe for that as well.

column3: thanked Vice Chair Hyer and the entire Council for acknowledging Constitution Day; she advised everyone to learn more ab
column4: Linda Sanchez thanked Vice Chair Hyer and the entire Council for acknowledging Constitution Day; she advised everyone to learn more about the Constitution and provided information about upcoming training opportunities and citizenship classes. Chair White encouraged the residents of West Ogden who have spoken on their concerns about other transportation improvements in their neighborhoods to meet with Mr. Rypien to discuss the matters further.

column3: presented the Council with a petition from the Edgehill Neighborhood Coalition; she noted she represents 91 percent of t
column4: Gina Shafer presented the Council with a petition from the Edgehill Neighborhood Coalition; she noted she represents 91 percent of the households on her street who have signed the petition opposing the proposed traffic detour through their street – Edgehill Drive. She spoke of the nature of the neighborhood and the presence of young children and indicated the residents there are being asked to absorb commuter traffic that cuts between Weber State University (WSU) and the Dee Events Center that was deemed unsafe for Taylor Avenue. Taylor Avenue benefits from sidewalks, two bike lane shoulders, and multiple speed monitor signs; Edgehill has none of these protections. She expounded on the concerns of herself and other residents and stressed that public safety is not negotiable. The following individuals echoed the sentiments communicated by Ms. Shaefer and asked that the Council take action to protect their neighborhood: Janetta Kramer, William Shafer, Sean May, Brianna McMullen, Kalie Copenhaver, Chandler Copenhaver, Logan Iverson, Phil Nastoriak, Autumn Iverson, and Royce McMullin.

column3: stated he and many others were devastated by the news of the deadly shooting near the Ben Lomond campus today. He then s
column4: Heath Satow stated he and many others were devastated by the news of the deadly shooting near the Ben Lomond campus today. He then stated he is a strong supporter of local businesses, which includes the local newspaper – the Standard- Examiner. He also fully supports the Mayor’s efforts to better interface with Ogden residents, and he genuinely believes the new newsletter is a step in the right direction. However, he has been concerned about the execution; a City publication should be clearly defined as just that and calling it Ogden City News gives the impression of independent journalism where none exists. The line is blurred when the company paid to print and distribute the newsletter is the very same company the public relies on to be an independent watch dog. He stated his concerns are fundamental and lie with the erosion of the public trust in the government and in the press. There must be a clear separation between government and press and the current arrangement will cause residents to wonder if there is a financial motivation for the Standard-Examiner to keep in the City’s ‘good graces’. He then referenced Council member Myers’ comments during tonight’s work session regarding the Union Station campus project; he noted there is still a lingering lawsuit regarding the project and he advised the Council to look into that issue.

column3: stated she listened to the recent City Council candidate debates and she was pleased by the questions that were asked of
column4: Linda Sanchez stated she listened to the recent City Council candidate debates and she was pleased by the questions that were asked of the candidates. She thanked the Council for what they do and indicated they are not thanked often enough. She stated that she will miss Council member Choberka greatly; she reaches out to the Council with questions on a regular basis and Council member Choberka consistently responds to her. She also thanked Mayor Nadolski for responding to a question she asked him over the weekend. She also thanked Chair White for answering her question today as well but noted she does not always answer questions as consistently as others.

column3: stated she is very sorry to hear that a student was shot and killed near Ben Lomond High School. She then noted the Stat
column4: Theresa Bramwell stated she is very sorry to hear that a student was shot and killed near Ben Lomond High School. She then noted the State of Utah had a homelessness convention last week and she asked if any representative of Ogden City attended that event and will be making any changes in terms of how the City deals with its homeless population. She also referenced the action tonight regarding middle income housing program guidelines; she doubts that there is a single person who earns a $102,000 per year that wants to live in a rental apartment. She believes that person would rather live in a home, something they own, and she wondered if the program includes any incentive or funding for home ownership. Chair White asked Mayor Nadolski to respond to the public comments regarding the traffic detour on Edgehill Drive. Mayor Nadolski thanked the residents who spoke regarding this issue and indicated he is committed to finding solutions to ensure the safety of children in the area. He emphasized the current traffic detour is temporary in nature and the improvements being made to Taylor Avenue will potentially impact traffic flow in the area. He then stated the purpose of the City newsletter is to serve as a communication tool, not a form of independent journalism; other cities do something similar to what has been done in Ogden City and that is because they are pursuing transparency and community engagement. The newsletter is a fully staff-written document printed by the Standard-Examiner with a contract in place. He has nothing to hide and is concerned about the negative rhetoric surrounding the matter; he will ignore this rhetoric and prioritize people and progress. He then discussed recent challenges faced by the City that have highlighted the need for responsible decision making; the City is committed to responding to crises that are occurring and wishes to provide safe and supportive environments for Ogden’s residents. He noted his thoughts are with the family of the young person who was tragically killed after school and with the officers who responded to the scene. He also addressed the negative comments about the City’s response to homelessness and middle-income housing issues in the community; he expressed frustration with the lack of support from other cities in addressing homelessness in the community and hopes to see them step up in providing resources and support in the future.

column3: addressed the erosion of public trust related to the project at the corner of Quincy Avenue and 25th Street; she read an
column4: Theresa Bramwell addressed the erosion of public trust related to the project at the corner of Quincy Avenue and 25th Street; she read an advertisement for the project listed in KSL that she found on Facebook. The advertisement was very positive and communicated the apartments are only open to people who earn 60 percent or less of the area median income (AMI), which is approximately $50,600. She attended the meeting during which this project was approved, and she has also spoken with the developer, who addressed income thresholds for potential residents. She feels 60 percent AMI is too close to the very low- income apartments already located on the same block as the subject property. This is allowing and promoting too much poverty in her neighborhood, and this is very problematic. Chair White attempted to address the comments made during the public hearing; she addressed Ms. Lewis’s comments about the Wall Avenue Corridor Plan and reiterated that action on the matter was tabled, possibly for up to six months, and the Administration and Council will be examining all options available to the City. She stated the reason the City is working on the project is to increase safety for motorists and pedestrians in the area. She thanked those who made comments about recycling programs and believes the City will continue to examine the viability of those programs. She referenced Mr. Pate’s comments about the implications of the backflow prevention ordinance and noted there are programs that can help people finance any improvements needed at their property to ensure compliance with the ordinance. She thanked Mr. Satow for his comments about the massage business regulations and noted that a member of the Council did ask about the implications of the ordinance amendments for small businesses; she believes Staff will carefully evaluate those issues before the ordinance moves forward. Council member Graf stated that the cross-connection ordinance has been advertised in previous meetings, and it would have been much more helpful for him to be contacted by residents earlier than tonight so that he has more time to look into those concerns and provide appropriate representation. Vice Chair Hyer agreed and stated that all Council members are available and reachable many different ways and are willing to talk to residents about these types of issues.

column3: expressed concerns about an incident on November 12, 2025 ,when she witnessed and recorded U.S. Immigration and Custom’s
column4: Asinet Garza Caballero expressed concerns about an incident on November 12, 2025 ,when she witnessed and recorded U.S. Immigration and Custom’s Enforcement (ICE) agents detaining young adults. She stated she was later pulled over by an Ogden police officer who indicated the stop was requested by ICE agents. She requested clarification of Ogden Police Department’s (OPDs) policy regarding collaboration with ICE and interactions with citizens exercising First Amendment rights. Nick (no last name given), stated he is representing the “Ogden Strong Towns” group; he proposed implementing "leading pedestrian intervals" at intersections, which would give pedestrians a three to seven second head start before cross traffic begins. He noted this would improve safety, especially for children, elderly, and disabled pedestrians.

column3: thanked Council member Richey for running a good campaign for re-election to the City Council. He then expressed his dis
column4: Heath Satow thanked Council member Richey for running a good campaign for re-election to the City Council. He then expressed his dissatisfaction with the graphical representation of election results, arguing that the graphs made his closely contested race with Council member Richey, which only had a 148-vote gap, appear as though there was a significantly larger difference. He concluded by expressing support for the Council's decision to table the massage business regulations. He also expressed support for planning efforts and an increased focus on housing density, suggesting the need for smart, strategic developments in the City. He thanked outgoing Council member Blair and Chair White for their service to the community and indicated he hopes they will stay involved in the community. In response to the public comments, Chair White expressed gratitude to the Strong Towns Group, noting it is crucial for the City to focus on transportation improvements with new ideas; she asked the group to stay engaged. She thanked those who commented on the Council’s action regarding massage therapy ordinance amendments for their support and indicated she agrees it is important for HIPAA concerns to be thoroughly addressed. In response to Mr. Satow, she stated the City Recorder’s Office may have created the graphs, but there was no intent to slight Mr. Satow and his election returns. She then invited Mayor Nadolski to respond to the comments regarding the ICE enforcement in the community.

column3: expressed her concerns about instances where Ogden Police Department (OPD) officers were observed collaborating with ICE
column4: Kim Haslam expressed her concerns about instances where Ogden Police Department (OPD) officers were observed collaborating with ICE. She pointed out that previous assurances had been provided to the community, indicating that OPD would not participate in immigration enforcement activities. Through her observations and interactions, she questioned whether the police department's policies had changed regarding working alongside federal agents in immigration-related operations. Kim highlighted an incident where ICE and OPD were reportedly working together at a traffic stop, raising concerns about the nature of their collaboration. She sought clarification on whether Ogden Police routinely attend ICE operations or follow federal directives, which could potentially contradict the City's commitment to its residents. Her comments echoed a broader community unease regarding transparency and consistency in the City's enforcement policies.

column3: expressed her apprehension about the proposed massage therapy regulations, particularly concerning privacy and HIPAA imp
column4: Laura Lewis expressed her apprehension about the proposed massage therapy regulations, particularly concerning privacy and HIPAA implications. As a customer of a massage therapist operating within a chiropractic office, she noted that her visits are related to medical conditions and thereby should be protected under HIPAA rights. She was concerned that the requirements outlined in the ordinance could potentially violate her and others' medical privacy.

column3: addressed the council to express her concerns regarding past incidents involving the Ogden Police Department's (OPD) tre
column4: Linda Sanchez addressed the council to express her concerns regarding past incidents involving the Ogden Police Department's (OPD) treatment of citizens engaging in First Amendment recording activities. She pointed out a lack of professionalism exhibited by some officers towards individuals exercising their constitutional rights to record and show courage in doing so. Additionally, she emphasized the need for police to manage such situations with respect and without infringing upon citizens' rights. She also echoed Ms. Lewis’s comments and concerns about the City’s proposed massage therapy ordinance amendments. She concluded by expressing gratitude to the Council for their service to the community.

column3: thanked Mayor Nadolski for his community engagement and expressed concerns about the focus on housing development in the
column4: Laura Lewis thanked Mayor Nadolski for his community engagement and expressed concerns about the focus on housing development in the City. Rob Allred praised Mayor Nadolski for listening to residents’ concerns but expressed disappointment in the communication process regarding the Taylor Canyon property. He disputed the notion of "buying the property twice," explaining that it was a reallocation of resources. He also pointed out that the space had functioned as a park for over 50 years and already had infrastructure like fencing and sprinklers. Kurt Clausse suggested that the City purchase the Taylor Canyon Elementary property now and give Ogden City Schools first right of refusal for a future school, noting that Polk Elementary was overcrowded. He believed amenities, like restrooms, could be provided at the property through donations and volunteer labor. column3: commented on the difference between national politics and local politics; it is important to endeavor to strengthen loca
column4: Linda Sanchez commented on the difference between national politics and local politics; it is important to endeavor to strengthen local communities by working together as elected leaders and residents. Once open space is lost, it cannot be recovered; it is necessary to make hard decisions in order to strengthen the community. She then asked how the City will communicate with residents regarding winter parking enforcement regulations over the next several months. She also encouraged the City to provide additional information about the “My Hometown Ogden” initiative, which can help residents to comply with property maintenance regulations in order to avoid code enforcement action. She concluded that the 250th birthday of the country will be celebrated in 2026, and she asked how Ogden City will be participating in that celebration. Chair White stated that Ms. Sanchez’s question regarding winter parking enforcement will be relayed to Administration in order for them to provide a response. She asked Vice Chair Hyer to respond to Ms. Sanchez’s question about the City’s participation in the America 250 Celebration. Vice Chair Hyer stated he is a member of the Ogden-Weber America 250 Committee and efforts are underway to plan for the upcoming celebration. He highlighted some of the events planned for the coming year as part of the celebration but noted that no concrete plans have been adopted. Council member Graf added that Ogden will celebrate its 175th birthday during the upcoming year and he anticipates special events surrounding that celebration as well. Council member Richey provided brief information about the “My Hometown Ogden” program, citing online resources and information about the program.

column3: thanked the Council and noted the positive chemistry of the team that worked on the Airport policies. He specifically ac
column4: Ed McKinney thanked the Council and noted the positive chemistry of the team that worked on the Airport policies. He specifically acknowledged Chief Administrative Officer Brown for her role in keeping the process on track and mentioned that the airport's performance will be measured through various vital signs. Mayor’s Comments Mayor Nadolski thanked the outgoing Council members for their service, noting the difficulty of serving on the Council and the amount of information they must consider in their deliberations. He expressed gratitude for their open-mindedness, willingness to listen, and ability to make decisions based on data and rationale rather than politics.

column3: addressed the Council, providing a detailed account of an alleged incident of assault that occurred on December 31, 2024
column4: A. Voorhees addressed the Council, providing a detailed account of an alleged incident of assault that occurred on December 31, 2024, involving a police officer. Ms. Voorhees described being assaulted, both physically and sexually, twice by the officer, although specific names couldn't be mentioned due to pending civil and criminal cases. Ms. Voorhees highlighted the difference between a crime and a presumption, emphasizing the lack of a victim in their situation and stating that the incident began with flashing lights blinding them, implying there was no legitimate cause for police intervention. Ms. Voorhees expressed deep frustration with the complaint process, recounting how their attempts to report the incident to various authorities, including the Mayor, Lieutenant, and local police departments, were met with indifference or laughter. Ms. Voorhees stated that although she submitted a complaint verbally and in writing, it seemed to have been taken lightly by the officers involved. She relayed intentions to escalate the matter to federal authorities, asserting that they had evidence, including clothing from the incident, in federal custody. Linda Sanchez distributed materials that will aid the Mayor and Council in engaging in constitutional discussions, and she praised the Council's work session dialogue regarding communication with the public and the proposed joint resolution affirming community trust through public safety. She suggested creating a resource archive with constitutional documents to guide decision-making.
